#9023. US and China share a love of "new things and innovation" says Ma Yansong

Chinese architect Ma Yansong has completed one of the highest-profile US buildings of 2026 – the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art, in California. In this interview, he explains his architecture’s international appeal as a “bridge between imagination and reality”.

Speaking over video call on the occasion of the Lucas Museum’s opening, Ma told Dezeen that the building has acted as a stable point in a rapidly changing world, with trade wars, AI races and a US federal government that has enshrined classical architecture as a national norm.

“This project took 12 years, across two countries, and the world changed around it. The building didn’t,” he said.

The long-anticipated project, funded by Star Wars creator George Lucas, was first planned for San Francisco, then Chicago, before landing in Los Angeles.

“What made it possible is that George and I come from different roots, but both love the same kind of thing – stories that belong to ordinary people, not to high culture,” said Ma.

Ma believes this shared tendency toward exploration between himself and the American filmmaker applies more widely, and the 51-year-old architect spoke positively about the potential for architecture to illuminate the similarities between China and the United States.

“I see a lot in common between the two countries,” he said. “They both like innovation and new things, and they focus on young people, on education.”

“I think architecture is a bridge between the imagination and reality”

His own life mirrors this outlook. Attracted by innovation as a youth in Beijing, he travelled to Yale, where he graduated with a master’s degree in 2002.

At Yale, Ma became interested in Zaha Hadid’s parametric architecture and eventually worked at her firm in London.

Despite teaching and working mostly in the United States and Europe, Hadid cultivated her signature parametric style working in China’s early 2000s building boom.

The completion of the Lucas Museum represents a Chinese architect taking these principles abroad, a full-circle moment as Ma moved from the US to the UK, back to China, where he has completed dozens of projects, bringing his honed sensibility to California.

Buildings created in the parametric style, or design based on the specific geometries allowed by computer calculations, have been criticised for their lack of relation to sites, and for being self-referential.

The museum’s curved exterior is covered in thousands of white polymer panels, giving it a futuristic look.

Nevertheless, Ma pushes back on Dezeen’s description of the building as “spaceship-like”. Instead, he compares it to a cloud, as an enduring symbol for the imagination – an aspect of consciousness that the architect hopes is provoked by his buildings.

He worked with landscape studio SLA to design an expansive park to serve as an extension of the museum, and the building itself, according to him, features organic curves. He called the effect of these combined elements “surreal nature” and said he aims to bring the natural into the urban environment.

The suggestion of the surreal also points to his aim of provoking the imagination in his design – something the architect said he shares with Lucas and science fiction storytelling.

“I think architecture is a bridge between the imagination and reality,” he said, adding that he hopes the Lucas Museum functions like the narrative art that it holds.

The relationship between Ma and Lucas developed around the question of narrative art since the filmmaker first tapped the architect for the project in 2014.

Ma had actually referenced a scene from Star Wars in his bulbous 2005 museum for Ordos, though he didn’t advertise the influence in his early meetings with Lucas.

“On the personal level, me and George have very easy communication,” said Ma, who famously wanted to become a science fiction director before his career in architecture.

“[George and I] are always talking about ideas, and he’s always supportive. We were constantly discussing what is narrative art,” he continued, adding that the question has led Ma to ask a question that has helped clarify his own practice – “what is narrative architecture?”

Ma said that the project has allowed him to “kind of achieve my goal as a movie maker”.

“You create a dream,” said Ma. “That’s important.”

“It’s why I like science fiction movies – because you put your imagination on the screen, and when people watch it, they believe in something.”

For Ma, this narrative approach to architecture is about opening up to different perspectives, and like science fiction and fantasy, this bridge to the imagination requires a certain suspension of disbelief.

“I’m not interested in everyone receiving the same message,” he said. “I think good public space lets everyone reflect their own experience or knowledge or thinking and share with other people.”

“So I’ve had to find a balance between abstraction and emotion.”

At the Lucas Museum, this intersection of abstraction and emotion is most evident in the massive open-air dome, where visitors can stand on the ground and look up through the panelled apex at the sky.

The space has almost a cathedral-like quality in its grandeur, but it is without ornament and other traditional figurative elements of storytelling in architecture, such as statues or text.

“The architectural space is a trigger for different people to have their own stories. I think that’s a little different from the classic buildings.”

“When you frame it and bring the light into the space, people start to look up, and they will see this connection between individuals and the universe beyond the building, so I think that’s something narrative to me.”

“I like the future, but not the cold future”

The building was also designed to evoke well-proportioned natural elements and bring nature into the city, literally in the case of the green roofs and surrounding park.

Other projects by Ma’s studio have had similar ambitions, such as the Shenzhen Bay Culture Square and One River North in Denver.

And if his architecture is futuristic, Ma hopes that a greener version of the city is the future it evokes, he said.

“I like the future, but not the cold future,” said Ma. “It’s more important that the building is warm and welcoming.”

Ma hopes that Lucas Museum will be inspiring to people, just as his younger self was inspired by the innovative architecture coming out of Yale when he was starting.

“When people see a building that’s so idealistic, that is pushing the boundary, everyone will be encouraged,” he said.

What's your FI number? Calculate it in 60 seconds

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Your net worth is the single most important number in personal finance. Not your salary. Not your credit score. Not how much you have in checking. Your net worth — the gap between everything you own and everything you owe — tells you exactly where you stand financially and whether you are moving in the right direction.

Net Worth = Total Assets - Total Liabilities

That is it. Add up everything you own that has monetary value. Subtract everything you owe. The number that remains — positive or negative — is your net worth.

In the FI community, net worth is not just a number. It is the scoreboard. Your FI number (25 times your annual spending) is a net worth target. Every dollar you save and invest moves you closer. Every dollar of debt you pay off does the same. Tracking your net worth turns the abstract concept of "financial independence" into a concrete, measurable goal.

Let's walk through exactly how to calculate yours, what counts as an asset, what counts as a liability, and how to use this number to accelerate your path to FI.

Calculating your net worth requires two lists: everything you own (assets) and everything you owe (liabilities). The difference between these two numbers is your net worth.

An asset is anything you own that has monetary value. Be honest and conservative — list items at what they would actually sell for today, not what you paid for them or what you hope they are worth.

A note on your home: The FI community debates whether to include your primary residence in net worth calculations. The pragmatic approach is to include it but recognize it is an illiquid asset that does not generate income. For FI planning purposes, many people track two numbers: total net worth (including home equity) and investable net worth (excluding home equity). Your investable net worth is what actually funds your financial independence.

A liability is any debt or financial obligation you owe to someone else.

A surgeon earning $400,000 per year with $600,000 in student loans, a $1.2 million mortgage, and $50,000 in car loans might have a lower net worth than a teacher earning $55,000 who has been investing 30% of her salary into index funds for 15 years. Income is what flows in. Net worth is what you keep. The FI community learned this lesson early: it is not about how much you earn — it is about the gap between earning and spending, compounded over time.

Let's walk through a real example. Meet Sarah, a 32-year-old software developer earning $95,000 per year. She has been saving and investing for 5 years since paying off her credit cards.

Sarah's net worth is $140,700. If her annual spending is $45,000, her FI number is $1,125,000 (25 x $45,000). She is 12.5% of the way there. More importantly, she is tracking her number every month and watching it grow — which means she can project when she will reach FI and make strategic decisions about how to accelerate the timeline.

Her investable net worth (excluding the car, which depreciates) is $155,200 - $30,500 = $124,700 in productive financial assets. This is the number that matters most for FI planning.

A negative net worth means you owe more than you own. This is completely normal — and far more common than people realize. According to Federal Reserve data, the median net worth for Americans under 35 is $39,000, but this is skewed by homeowners. For young renters with student loans, a negative net worth in the range of -$20,000 to -$80,000 is typical.

A negative net worth does not mean you are failing. It means you are early in the journey. If you graduated with $80,000 in student loans and have $5,000 in savings, your net worth is -$75,000. But if you are earning income, paying down debt, and starting to invest, your trajectory is positive — and trajectory is what matters.

The FI community is full of people who started with six-figure negative net worths and reached financial independence in 10-15 years. The key was tracking the number, seeing the progress, and letting that momentum fuel consistent action.

Calculating your net worth once is useful. Tracking it monthly is transformational. Monthly tracking turns financial independence from an abstract goal into a visible, measurable trajectory.

The FI community's favorite: Many FI practitioners use a simple spreadsheet. Create columns for each account, update balances on the first of every month, and chart the total over time. The visual of a steadily rising line graph is one of the most powerful motivators on the FI path. Some people prefer Empower for automated tracking — it links to your accounts and updates your net worth in real time.

Your net worth will not increase in a straight line. Market drops will temporarily reduce your investment balances. Large purchases (a car, a home down payment) will create short-term dips. The number to watch is the 12-month trend. If your net worth is higher than it was a year ago, you are moving in the right direction.

Early in the journey, debt payoff drives most of the growth. A $30,000 student loan shrinking to $18,000 adds $12,000 to your net worth just as effectively as saving $12,000 in new investments. Later, compound growth takes over and your net worth starts increasing faster than your contributions — that is the magic inflection point where your money starts working harder than you do.

Complete this in one sitting — it takes about 30 minutes.

Log into every bank account, retirement account, brokerage account, and HSA. Write down the current balance. For your home, use Zillow's estimate minus 10%. For vehicles, use Kelley Blue Book private party value.

Pro tip: Do not include personal belongings like furniture, clothing, or electronics unless a single item is worth more than $1,000 at resale.

Log into every loan servicer, credit card account, and any other creditor. Write down the exact payoff balance — not the monthly payment, but the total remaining balance including any accrued interest.

Total assets minus total liabilities equals your net worth. Whether this number is positive, negative, or zero, write it down. This is your starting point.

Multiply your annual spending by 25. This is how much investable net worth you need to be financially independent using the 4% safe withdrawal rate. Divide your current investable net worth by your FI number to see your progress percentage.

Pro tip: Use your actual spending, not your income. If you earn $80,000 but spend $50,000, your FI number is $1,250,000 — not $2,000,000.

Choose a tool — Empower, a spreadsheet, or a notebook — and schedule a recurring monthly reminder to update your net worth. The first of each month works well. Track the number, chart the trend, and watch your progress compound.

The most common habit among people who have reached financial independence is consistent net worth tracking. It takes 5 minutes per month and creates a feedback loop that keeps you motivated and accountable. When you see your net worth climb from $50,000 to $100,000 to $250,000, the progress becomes its own fuel. Start tracking today — your future self will thank you.

Yes, but with context. Your home is an asset and your mortgage is a liability, so both should be included for an accurate net worth picture. However, for FI planning, track your investable net worth (excluding home equity) separately — because you cannot live off your home equity unless you sell or take a reverse mortgage. Many FI practitioners track both numbers.

Monthly is the sweet spot for most people. Weekly is too frequent and causes unnecessary anxiety about market fluctuations. Quarterly is too infrequent to maintain the motivational feedback loop. Set a recurring reminder on the first of each month, update your numbers in 5 minutes, and move on.

The median net worth by age (from Federal Reserve SCF data): under 35 is $39,000, 35-44 is $135,600, 45-54 is $247,200, 55-64 is $364,500, 65-74 is $409,900. FI community members typically far exceed these benchmarks because they prioritize saving and investing. See our average net worth by age guide for detailed breakdowns.

Yes. Your 401(k), IRA, Roth IRA, 403(b), TSP, and any other retirement accounts are assets and should be included in your net worth calculation. Some people adjust for taxes (since traditional 401(k) withdrawals are taxed as income), but for tracking purposes, including the full balance is standard practice.

A negative net worth simply means you owe more than you own — it is common for recent graduates, new homeowners, and anyone early in their career. What matters is the direction. If your net worth is -$50,000 but was -$65,000 a year ago, you are making significant progress. Focus on the trajectory, not the absolute number.

Yes, include your car at its current resale value (Kelley Blue Book private party value, not dealer retail). Cars are depreciating assets, which means their value decreases over time, but they still have monetary value and should be counted. If you have an auto loan, both the car (asset) and the loan balance (liability) should appear in your calculation.

Calculating your net worth is the first step on the path to financial independence — and it takes less than 30 minutes. Add up everything you own, subtract everything you owe, and you have the single most important number in your financial life. Whether that number is positive, negative, or zero, it is your starting point. Track it monthly, watch it grow, and use it to measure your progress toward your FI number. The formula is simple: assets minus liabilities. The habit of tracking it is what separates people who talk about financial goals from people who achieve them.

#9021. Works from US pavilion at Venice Biennale could be stuck in limbo due to fundraising shortfall

Installation view of Alma Allen’s Call Me the Breeze at the US Pavilion, Venice BIennale 2026 Photo: © Agostino Osio, Alto Piano Studio, courtesy Perrotin

With a little less than a month left of this year’s Venice Biennale, the US pavilion is in the news again—this time not for aesthetic but financial reasons. According to Zachary Small of The New York Times, the non-profit responsible for the pavilion has sounded the alarm that it needs to raise $1m or it will not be able to ship Alma Allen’s hulking sculptures back to the US.

“We are facing an urgent funding need associated with the final deinstallation and safe return of the artworks to the United States,” Jenni Parido, the director of the American Arts Conservancy (AAC), wrote in a plea to donors. She added that the organisation had only been able to raise $1.4m out of the $2.5m total needed for the pavilion.

While the State Department provided its usual $375,000 grant for the US pavilion this year, the rest was left up to Parido—a former pet-store owner with little background in art outside of a degree in graphic design—and her brand-new non-profit to raise. (Parido is a friend of the director of the State Department’s Art in Embassies programme, Erin Scavino—a former contestant on Donald Trump’s television programme The Apprentice.)

The funding shortfall comes even as this year’s US pavilion was lauded for costing much less money than usual. (The 2024 pavilion's budget was $5m, and in 2022 the pavilion cost $7m.) The AAC did most of its fundraising via private events with donors including the fashion designer Tommy Hilfiger and the art collector (and former US Navy secretary) John Phelan.

“Budgeting normally is very careful,” Katy Siegel, an art historian who co-curated the 2017 US Pavilion, told the Times. “Maybe there is no oversight now. This is crazy.” She added that finding space in Venice to store Allen’s sculptures—some of which weigh almost a ton—would be very difficult.

As for the Mexico-based Allen, he told the Times that he was unaware of the AAC’s financial woes. “I received only reimbursement for travel and my Airbnb,” he said, “which was cheap.”

#9020. Photographer Syncs Camera With Fan and Freezes the Blades

Photographer Syncs Camera With Fan and Freezes the Blades

A YouTuber’s playful photography experiment has already racked up over one million views in just a few days.

Pavel Mamontov, aka Lensevision, tried to perfectly synchronize a fan with his video camera.

The theory, known as the stroboscopic effect, holds that if a camera is recording at 30 frames per second, a fan with three blades rotating at 10 revolutions per second should appear completely stationary, as each blade occupies the position of the previous one in successive frames. The phenomenon also works with helicopters.

Mamontov drew symbols on each of the three blades of his fan, then turned it on to find the right speed when the fan appears motionless and the symbols are clearly visible.

“I’m using a potentiometer to control the speed,” Mamontov explains. “So the RPM keeps fluctuating, and I have to find just the right moment.”

Initially, he manages to freeze the blades, but not the symbols. He explains that the symbols keep changing because, between two frames of video, “the fan rotates just enough for the next blade to take the place of the previous one.” This is why the fan appears to be standing still on camera even though it is actually spinning. Since each blade carries a different symbol, however, we can see them changing from frame to frame.

Interestingly, as Mamontov alters the speed of the fan, the blades appear to start turning counterclockwise instead of clockwise. This is due to slightly faster synchronization.

“By slightly adjusting the speed, you can even make the blade appear to move back and forth,” he adds.

Mamontov doesn’t reveal which shutter speed he’s using, but the effect can be made even more convincing by using a faster shutter speed, which reduces motion blur and makes the blades and symbols appear sharper.

Eventually, Mamontov nails the shot and captures the blades and their symbols remaining in the same positions from frame to frame.

“There can be a whole lot of different speeds where the fan appears completely still,” adds Mamontov.

More of his camera experiments can be found on Instagram and YouTube.

#9019. Controlled Chaos: Getting Creative with Psychedelic Blues Films

Controlled Chaos: Getting Creative with Psychedelic Blues Films

This Film Friday brings you a whole family of fun films with Psychedelic Blues. A great tagline for these experimental films could certainly be “expect the unexpected.” It could also be, “loosen up and have some fun!”

Psychedelic Blues kind of combines both of those ideals, encouraging you to embrace chance and serendipity while also demonstrating that everything you may have once thought could go wrong with film may actually be kind of right in certain situations. So let’s get into looking at these films, shall we?

Psychedelic Blues is a line of small-batch, pre-exposed films produced by Dustin Adams. Dustin publicly launched the first Psychedelic Blues film back in 2016 after having experimented privately for several years prior. Over time, the family has grown to include variants such as Blues #2, #3, #4, #5, #6, #7, and #8. There is also a 120 version labeled as Psychedelic Blues A and even combination batches such as Blues #5/6. Each version produces a different fogging pattern or effect, so it is kind of like standing at the ice cream counter trying to figure out which flavor to indulge in.

In regard to how the films are actually produced, Dustin is understandably a bit cagey about revealing all his secrets, but generally speaking, he is working with Kodak film stock as his base emulsion (generally either Gold or Ultramax for the 35mm versions, or Gold and Portra 400 for the 120 format) and then fogging or exposing the film in a controlled environment before repackaging it and selling it on to all of us. The exact process no doubt differs from type to type, as some Blues films have simple colorful fogging at the edges while others, like Blues #4, are exposed to light reflected off of holographic paper.

Given that the look and feel of these films can vary from type to type, let’s do a quick overview of the variations and what to expect from each. Then we can discuss some overall strategies for having the most fun possible with Psychedelic Blues.

From what we can tell, this was the first Psychedelic Blues film offered on a regular basis. Its effect is the result of hand-fogging the film in a fashion that creates a red/orange bleed emanating from the top of the frame with a corresponding green bleed coming in from the bottom of the frame. The effect for each is generally limited to the top/bottom third of the frame, usually leaving the center relatively untouched, though the fogging varies from frame to frame, roll to roll, and batch to batch, and sometimes bleeds as far as the center of the image.

Blues #2 probably looks the closest to traditional film light leaking, especially that of 120 film when it is spooled loosely in-camera, such as by a Holga or Diana. In that sense, it has a weird nostalgic element to its experimental look. It is also well suited to a variety of subject matter, from landscapes to cityscapes to portraiture to weird multiple exposures.

Blues #3 takes a less structured approach compared to Blues #2. With this version, the frames are unpredictably riddled with splashes and splotches of color, varying from red to blue to purple to orange. Similar to Blues #2, the effect hangs out mostly at the edges of the frame, but unlike Blues #2, it commonly ventures into the center area with occasional splashes of color ranging across much of the frame.

The fogging has a more organic look and feel. The best results we have seen with this film are with simpler compositions with lots of shadow area where the colors of the fogging can really stand out. With more complicated scenes, the fogging can feel a bit busy.

Here is where the Psychedelic Blues line starts to get really fun. Blues #4 is pre-exposed using holographic paper and apparently has been one of the techniques Dustin Adams has been experimenting with the longest, but only made consistent enough to market after the release of Blues #2 and #3. The effect is quite varied, but could be described as splashing your film with rainbow fogging. Beyond that, the effect is very unpredictable, with colors showing up all over the place and changing placement from frame to frame.

Because of this, it is a good idea to bracket your shots with this film just to have multiple options to pick from when you develop your roll. In terms of which scenes work best, we would kind of say the same thing we did about Blues #3: simpler, cleaner scenes with strong central elements tend to do better. More negative space also gives room for the fogging effect to stand on its own without feeling too busy or cluttered.

Psychedelic Blues #5 kind of rehashes Blues #2, but with a new twist. Once again, the fogging is limited mostly to the edges of the frame, with the color bleed often blowing out the edges then fading off toward the center, leaving the middle of your image nicely framed. But what Blues #5 does differently is occasionally throwing in speckles of color, usually green, that produce a bit of a “galaxy” effect or “radioactive firefly.”

Because the fogging is relatively tight to the edges, Blues #5 does a bit better with busier scenes and is generally good for a variety of subject matter; however, the green speckling really looks its best when shot in low light, such as twilight, nighttime, or dim interiors.

Blues #6 is quite distinct from previous Psychedelic Blues films. Here, the fogging is tightly constrained to circles and windows of color moving through the middle of the frame with occasional splashes of color thrown in for good measure.

The exact placement of the patches of fogging varies from image to image. Sometimes you get a circle dead smack in the middle of the photo, and sometimes it is a half circle cropped off by the left or right edge of your frame. This is another Psychedelic Blues that benefits from bracketing for that exact reason. Do two or three takes of important compositions to give yourself a variety of fogging placements to choose from.

Just when you thought it was safe to go back into the film store, along comes Blues #7. This crazy iteration leaves squiggly waves of color running down the middle of your images. Resembling sine waves, the fogging can range from sharp peaks to gentle rolling waves, while the colors shift through the entire spectrum from red to blue. It is a film that pairs best with scenes that are either very graphic in nature or simpler with more negative space and strong central elements.

Psychedelic Blues A is the first, and thus far only, form of Psychedelic Blues in 120 format. It features a more mellow fogging heavily steeped in reds and blues that originate at the edges of the frame but fade in all the way to the middle. Here and there you get hints of pinks and greens, just for variety.

That covers the majority of the Psychedelic Blues films currently available, though it is not an exhaustive overview. There is a Blues #8 and a combination Blues #5/6 that we have not had our hands on yet. Once we have a chance to try those films, we will be sure to add them to this list.

As promised, let’s round up with some general tips and tricks. Psychedelic Blues is available in both ISO 200 and 400 speeds. The ISO 200 uses Kodak Gold 200 as the base film, while ISO 400 is Kodak Ultramax (except in 120 where it is Portra 400). Because the 35mm version uses these consumer emulsions, it is worth noting that it is naturally going to have visible grain. The fogging treatment seems to accentuate the visibility of the grain even more, giving Psychedelic Blues a definite gritty look. Psychedelic Blues A, being a medium format film and with the ISO 400 using Kodak Portra, is naturally finer grained in its appearance, but keep the graininess in mind when shooting the 35mm format. Also, the fogging of the film does affect its sensitivity somewhat. While nominally an ISO 200 or 400 stock, it responds a bit slower post-fogging. This leads Psychedelic Blues to easily underexpose. This can sometimes be a good thing as the deeper shadows can help make the colorful fogging pop more. But at the same time, it is not a bad idea to perhaps rate this film a stop slower or use it with a strong flash to help ensure good exposures with nice contrast.

As we noted in a couple of the descriptions for the individual types above, Psychedelic Blues really appreciates bracketing. We don’t mean this in the usual exposure sense, though you can do that too, but rather making multiple, redundant exposures of the same scene. Since the fogging varies from frame to frame, having multiple shots of the same composition will ultimately produce different results. In one frame, the colorful circle may be right in the middle, and in the next, there is a red window of fogging leading in from the edge. It is less film-efficient—and this is a relatively expensive film to be less efficient with—but the multitude of options on the tail end of processing will give you more opportunity to pick favorites.

We would also be remiss not to talk about scanning and printing of this film. Fogging such as this can wreak havoc with the automated calculations of film scanners. If you are scanning Psychedelic Blues at home, you will notice this right away, but you’ll also be able to apply any adjustments immediately. If you are having your film scanned at a lab, then your mileage can really vary depending on how much attention your lab is paying and how much time and effort they are willing to put into adjusting scanner corrections. This is not a knock against labs that don’t do this, mind you, but scanning this film really can be tricky. Film scanners prescan a frame of film and gauge automatic corrections based largely on what they see in the frame. If that frame has heavy red fogging bleeding across it, they often will try to compensate for it by introducing a significant cyan color cast. Many labs rely heavily on this automation to help keep labor costs and hence retail prices lower, but this will result in images with heavy off-color casts. More professional labs generally incorporate more human intervention in their scanning, like we do, where a scanning technician reviews the initial scanner settings and corrects them to produce more accurate images, or they correct post-scan to eliminate unintended color casts. The YMMV aspect of film scanning is always true, of course, but much more so with experimental films like Psychedelic Blues. Just keep that in mind.

Finally, we have to close this review on a philosophical note. The look of Psychedelic Blues is certainly not going to be for every photographer. But as a photographer, or a creative individual if you will, we think it is important to remember that adding some unpredictability and experimentation into your creative process is a very healthy thing to do. It is easy to adopt a mentality that an art like photography should only be done in certain ways, whether those are ways we have defined for ourselves through time and experience, or have been defined for us by teachers, peers, or social media. It is a good thing to make a point now and again to let go of those preconceptions and strike out into unknown territory just to see what you find. The worst thing that happens is you find nothing and you are out the cost of a roll of film. But the best thing that happens is you learn something new or create something you never thought or imagined you would. These are the moments that broaden our creative horizons. This is the path that a film like Psychedelic Blues offers up; whether we decide to go down that path to see what is around the bend is up to us.

We are going to have all the Psychedelic Blues on sale today, just in time to stock up for the Halloween weekend! Hit our online shop, or visit our store in St. Johns, Portland, Oregon to get a few rolls of this crazy film for yourself.

#9018. Cinga Samson "Ukuphuthelwa" @ White Cube Gallery, NYC

South African artist Cinga Samson’s exhibition of new paintings is titled ‘Ukuphuthelwa’, an isiXhosa word in the artist’s native language that translates as ‘unable to sleep’. Unlike the English word ‘insomnia’, the isiXhosa term carries no negative connotation and accordingly, for Samson, sleeplessness is not a condition to be cured but a state of spiritual alertness, a sensitivity that deepens in the dark. Rendered in the artist’s signature occluded palette of near-blacks, carbon and deep Prussian blues, Samson’s scenes depict men-like figures, dogs in overgrown fields and portraits of plant life native to South Africa. Encouraging slow, contemplative looking, a sense of existential gravity pervades Samson’s new series of oil paintings, attempting to depict a vast reality that is continuously in motion. As the artist has it, his quandary pertains to the existential question of how to create a ‘true and honest painting'. The exhibition will be on view through April 18, 2026.

With ‘Ukuphuthelwa’, Samson considers his role as an artist in relation to his inability to represent the whole truth of reality, and the fact that he can merely make symbols. Between the static, painted sign and the fluid experience it gestures towards, he contends that there exists a gulf that no image can close. Though the technical mastery and convincing realism of these paintings appear to invite interpretation, the artist asserts that his work confronts the very dilemma of representation: that the image can only ever be a relative symbol of what it reflects, never its equivalent. Acknowledging the open-ended nature of symbols and their subjective interpretation, Samson takes the figure of the dog as an example. The viewer may, for instance, look at Intsingiselo II (2026) and perceive the loyalty conventionally associated with dogs, while an amaXhosa understanding might highlight the dog as signifying the guiding, protective principles of ancestors. Comprising painstaking detail and deft brushwork, Samson’s paintings do not disguise the limits of representation but, rather, aspire to harness his skills towards that which exceeds the representable. Above all, the artist’s work seeks out the authority of the unnameable and the territory of the sublime, one in which the divine is not found elsewhere but present in the vernacular of all things.

Samson’s larger compositions carry a palpable sense of reverence and ceremony. In Umlindo (Watcher) (2026), figures are gathered in a forest clearing with wildflower bouquets and lengths of fabric, a scene that carries the visual grammar of ritual without specifying its addressee or terms. For Samson however, ‘the ritual itself is not the important thing – it’s an opening to what exists beyond’, and the paintings use the aesthetics of ritual to speak to a collective need for orientation, as well as the capacity of ritual to mediate an encounter with a vast unknown. That the works are titled with enigmatic words and phrases in isiXhosa, such as Imfihlo (Secret) and Intsingiselo (Meaning) (both 2026), infer the same problem the paintings contend with – the instability of interpretation as it pertains to the knowable and unknowable. Each word carries a weight in isiXhosa that its English translation approaches but can never fully reach; here, just as between the painted sign and living referent, meaning slips between the interstice of two languages.

The objects, people and settings that recur in these paintings and across Samson’s oeuvre are identifiable and quotidian, yet Samson corrals in each an unexplained mystery. In Tshee (2026), a vast field stretches out, the silhouetted trees meeting a murky sky, though the void of the night is interrupted by a moonwashed cloud, its brilliant white destabilising the eerie, cold atmosphere suffused with majesty. ‘The sky can be so friendly, but sometimes so heavy, dark, so scary. It’s the same energy, but it exists in different forms’, Samson notes, conjuring an oscillation between the approachable and the overwhelming that recalls the affective register of the sublime. Sithini ngelilitye (2026), distils the same sensation: a rocky crag emerges from arid undergrowth, its surface rendered in forensic detail against a sky of barely-there wash, charging the scene with the same quality of mute enormity.

Marshalling light ‘like a magic trick’, Samson imparts a unique kind of rhythm to his paintings – a flickering that emerges and disperses across the picture plane, granting varying degrees of visibility to the dark, nighttime scenes. Producing an unsteadiness that is at once optical and psychical, the artist leaves large sections of the painting’s under-drawing visible to lend moments of transparency to the work. In Isiganeko (2026), for example, thin layers of glaze are applied and wiped back in his typical style, a means of building colour that lends the figures a brooding chromatic density, whilst elsewhere, in the undergrowth and the bird caught mid-flight, the under-drawing is left entirely exposed. In all Samson’s figures, the pupils of the eyes are left unpainted and allow ‘light’ to further circulate, a decision that renders them porous, so they are ‘completely one with the whole painting’. Without pupils, these figures are not personified identities, but ‘human’ forms enmeshed with the painting’s landscape and atmosphere, no element ever possessing full mastery over the other. In places where the ‘trick’ of painting reveals itself, it is as if Samson’s works were stepping back from the pretence or promise of representation. What ‘Ukuphuthelwa’ reaches towards is not individual transcendence in subordination, but rather the mystery that can be unearthed in ordinary forms, whose immanent magic is available to those who are sensitive to it. This is the condition that ‘Ukuphuthelwa’ ultimately describes: not an absence or deficit, but a hypersensitivity that affords everything in existence the same potential for eliciting wonder or fear. Samson’s pupilless figures do not ‘look’ outward because the figures’ knowing comes from within the world they inhabit, a shared knowledge that exists between the bowing foliage, the vigilant dog, the bird in flight and the foreboding of the night sky enshrouding them all. In Samson’s hands, each optical device and representational motif prises apart what it cannot contain, in service of painting ‘a thing that links us to God – by God, I mean everything’.

#9017. Luminous viewpoint by Ryue Nishizawa rises within Japanese landfill site

Photography by Setouchi Art and Industry

A giant orange cone designed by Japanese architect Ryue Nishizawa acts as an observation platform at this large recycling complex on Shikoku island in Japan.

Nishizawa, co-founder of Japanese studio SANAA, positioned the cone to overlook a large landfill basin at Oono Associates, a recycling complex in the city of Toon, and open up this closed-off industrial space to the public.

Named Observatory, it was created for the inaugural edition of Setouchi Art and Industry 2026, an art and architecture festival held across industrial sites in Japan.

Specifically, it is part of the Landscapes of Waste – A landscape shaped by nature, industry, and people exhibition, curated by architect Kazuyo Sejima, who co-founded SANAA with Nishizawa in 1995.

Nishizawa positioned the cone to overlook a large landfill basin within the vast recycling complex in Toon, Ehime, revealing the closed-off industrial setting to the public.

The bright orange cone measures 33 metres in diameter and four metres in height. Its size was intended to emulate an artificial hill.

Its luminous orange finish was chosen to deliberately contrast the blue-green hues of the surrounding landfill lining and landscape beyond it.

The platform encourages visitors to observe how the landscape is shaped by nature and human activity, and experience the processes of material circulation at the recycling plant.

Alongside Nishizawa’s observation platform, the Landscapes of Waste exhibition includes bus stops by architectural studio Shingo Masuda + Katsuhisa Otsubo, as well as a bus and visitor wear by architect Suzuko Yamada.

Visitors are required to take this bus to the site and put on the clothing, as seen in the photos. The festival team said this brings “visitors themselves into the composition of the landscape”.

“Together, these interventions invite a closer encounter with the relationship between nature, industrial infrastructure and human activity,” it added.

Setouchi Art and Industry 2026 was organised by the Japan Industrial Art Foundation. Artists and architects were invited to work with industrial sites across Okayama and the Ehime prefecture on Shikoku to create a “decentralised museum” that opens these settings to the public.

Its inaugural edition runs until 31 October across seven venues, which also include a salt production site, a textile factory, a shipbuilder and a battery manufacturer.

“Developed through collaboration between artists and participating companies, the exhibitions offer access to industrial spaces usually closed to the public, revealing the technologies, materials and people behind everyday life,” said Setouchi Art and Industry.

“We hope that many people, including the younger generation, will re-examine Japan’s industries from a fresh perspective and discover the charm and potential hidden within them,” added Japan Industrial Art Foundation director Masahiro Ito.

Other recent projects by SANAA include the Taichung Green Museumbrary in Taiwan and a proposal for the National Museum of Ecuador.

Observatory: Ryue NishizawaPlaza (roundabout, forest path, elevated path, rest area) and bus stop: Shingo Masuda + Katsuhisa OtsuboBus and visitor wear: Suzuko Yamada (in collaboration with Kazuya Suzuki, Posa)Supervision: Kazuyo SejimaAdvisors: Yuko Hasegawa, Yusuke Okura, Atsuhiro MiyakeBus video cinematographer: Kenji AgataBus video music and sound engineering: Takayuki Noami (Non-REM Studio)

#9016. Art Toronto reflects Canadian art community’s focus on sustaining domestic ecosystem

Lynn Donoghue's Untitled (Watching) (1996) at Art Toronto Photo: Jenna Marie Wakani

There is something strangely comforting about this year’s edition of Art Toronto (until 1 November), Canada’s biggest art fair. In spite of the vast 20,000 sq. ft of space it inhabits at the Metro Toronto Convention Centre, there is a sense of warmth and grounding in Canadian landscapes made manifest in the installation that welcomes visitors to the art fair’s 27th iteration: Untitled (Watching) (1996) by the late Lynn Donoghue and the first of her Caribou Tarp series to be shown in public, installed here on top of a pile of dirt.

Inspired by the artist’s time in Alberta in the mid 1990s, when she encountered discarded caribou antlers scattered across the tundra, the work speaks to one of the overarching themes at the fair this year, of a return to natural roots. But this Art Toronto is also about uniting the often-scattered Canadian art landscape and, as per the title of one series of talks at the fair, “Building a Stronger Arts Ecosystem”.

These are trying times for Canadian artists and galleries, hammered by a trade war with the US and larger macro-economic forces such as inflation, war and related fuel costs. Happily, though the fair’s new director Emily Jean Alexander tells The Art Newspaper that this year’s Art Toronto is “only down in capacity by 5%”, while some other international art fairs have pared back their exhibitor numbers more drastically. She says there are far fewer US galleries this year than in past editions, while 80% of the 105 exhibitors are Canadian. A commercial gallery from New Brunswick is participating for the first time, alongside dozens from British Columbia, Québec and Ontario. There is a pervasive tariffs-be-damned, “elbows up” sense of artistic solidarity afoot and, Alexander says, a renewed commitment to creating a sustainable art market in Canada.

Rich Loen's Databells (2025) at Art Toronto, presented in partnership with Artist Project Photo: Jenna Marie Wakani

There is a nostalgic, McLuhanesque installation on the convention centre’s ground floor (presented with Art Toronto’s sister fair, Artist Project) by the Ottawa-based former software engineer Rich Loen. Titled Databells (2025), it connects a collection of bells with statistics ranging from the whimsical (the number of female orgasms per minute) to the digital (the number of TikTok videos played globally per minute) to the serious (amount of carbon dioxide removed from the earth’s atmosphere). The installation’s church and door bells chime at numerically precise intervals, creating a balm for our information-overloaded minds and sparking a meditative state akin to a Balinese temple. It is the perfect hybrid analogue-digital cleanse before the throng of Art Toronto’s main floor.

As visitors ascend into the fair, they can contemplate Kathy Slade’s monumental tapestry Sinking in the West (2023), presented by Mónica Reyes Gallery, which considers recurrence, time and landscape. Turning the corner, visitors will find the McMichael Canadian Art Collection stand; the Kleinburg, Ontario-based museum is currently closed for an expansion and renovation. At the fair it is showing off a recent acquisition, My First Medicine Teacher, a large-scale painting by the Métis artist Christi Belcourt.

A view of Art Toronto including, at centre, the McMichael Canadian Art Collection's stand with My First Medicine Teacher by Christi Belcour Photo: Jenna Marie Wakani

Nearby, the Toronto-based Nicholas Metivier Gallery has two stands: one featuring a selection of works by gallery artists, the other showcasing four decades of work by the Canadian photographer Edward Burtynsky. The solo stand includes two new photographs from the artist’s forthcoming project, Mining: For the Future. Burtynsky tells The Art Newspaper that he got his start in aerial photography in Western Australia two decades ago and he returned there last year to revisit a subject he has explored since the mid 1980s. The textural, painterly images in vibrant colours reveal both the brutality and beauty of mining materials such as lithium, copper and cobalt that are needed for components in the technologies that will enable a more sustainable future.

Another highlight of the fair, on the stand of Montreal’s Galerie Nicolas Robert, is Ascension (for Bakers) by the artist Sameer Farooq. An extension of his ongoing Flatbread Library, a long-term research project centred on the political and social significance of the tandoor, the new work connects the forms of collected bakeware with the Buddhist stupa reliquary. The appetising installation features a gathering of vessels, bread forms and tools that honour bakers as sculptors, tracing how ideas, objects and food move across cultures.

Next to it is the Vancouver-based gallery Wil Aballe, whose stand includes a work that has been attracting curatorial interest: Karin Jones’s The Bond (dress) (2023) is a mixed-media take on Queen Victoria’s wedding gown re-imagined with blonde hair extensions as a brilliant expression of the politics of adornment and beauty within contemporary material culture.

Additional eye-catching installations at the fair include Douglas Scholes’s (This is) What happens when a thing is maintained (?) (2024), a large-scale sculpture made from beeswax (presented by Galerie Robertson Arès), and the Montréal-based artist Karine Giboulo’s whimsical environment Joy is a Resistant Bacteria (The Living Room) (2026), presented by Art Mûr. Taken together, they convey a sense of the power of the organic overcoming the antiseptic aesthetics of the digital.

Douglas Scholes's (This is) What happens when a thing is maintained (?) (2024) at Art Toronto, presented by Galerie Robertson Arès Photo: Jenna Marie Wakani

The booth of Toronto’s Nia Centre for the Arts, Canada’s first professional Black arts centre, features the wonderful painting Califia by the Congolese Canadian artist Heritier Bilaka, paying homage to the warrior Queen Nzinga. (Concurrently with Art Toronto, Nia is hosting A Black Art Fair at its headquarters on Oakwood Avenue.)

The Vancouver-based gallery Ceremonial Art is showing works by five artists on its booth, including a remarkable woodblock print by the Tofino-based artist Marika Swan. Titled Embraced in Interdependence, it is both a rare example of West Coast Indigenous art in Toronto and a neat metaphor for the current socio-political climate in Canada and at the art fair.

A nearby stand is devoted to Portfolio, a nonprofit run by a collective of Vancouver artists and dedicated to helping emerging artists via scholarships funded from a percentage of their sales. Among others, the organisation is showing new paintings by Angela Grossman and new works from the Predator series by Lawrence Paul Yuxweluptun—who will open a solo exhibition at the Art Gallery of Ontario in February 2027.

A few booths away, Vancouver’s Equinox Gallery is showing early paintings by the late artist Gathie Falk, mid-century prints from the Fred Herzog archive and a work by Sonny Assu that playfully subverts the colonial landscapes of Emily Carr by overlaying them with Kwakwaka'wakw formline designs.

During the fair’s gala preview on Thursday (29 October), benefiting the McMichael Canadian Art Collection, it was revealed that the federal and provincial governments would provide C$50m ($35.7m) each in funding for the renovation of the existing building and construction of a new wing, all designed by Hariri Pontarini Architects. In a video marking the occasion, Canada’s first lady, Diana Fox Carney, proclaimed: “The world needs more Canada.” At this year’s Art Toronto, there is plenty to go around.

Canada’s largest art fair spotlights a growing market for work by Indigenous artists while challenging stereotypes and expectations

The country’s biggest art fair, with more than 100 exhibitors, is both a centre of commercial activity and a sprawling diorama of a national aesthetic

True to the fair’s mission, many exhibitors are showing works by long-overlooked practitioners of abstract art

Amid trade war between US and Canada, Toronto’s largest art fair strengthens ties with Latin America’s art scene

#9015. Canon May Raise Camera Prices Due To Increased Memory Costs

Canon May Raise Camera Prices Due To Increased Memory Costs

In August, Fujifilm mentioned the impact of rising raw materials prices in its routine financial reporting, and PetaPixel speculated that Fujifilm would be far from the only camera maker affected. It was the first domino to fall. Sure enough, Canon mentioned it during a Q&A on its FY2026 Q3 financial results, and the company will not be the only one to cite rising costs over the next few weeks.

As Digital Camera Life reports, Canon held its usual Q&A session after publishing its latest financial results. While the results themselves are fine and not especially noteworthy — overall operating profit and net income increased quite a bit year-over-year — the tangential analysis and information are very interesting and, frankly, concerning.

Someone asked Canon how the “shortages of circuit boards and electronic components” are impacting various segments, and Canon responded that Printing and Imaging are both facing “component shortages.”

These supply shortages typically raise costs, as seen across the flash memory space amid increased demand from AI data centers. Companies are bidding for a shrinking supply, driving prices up. Fujifilm alluded to this months ago, and now Canon is discussing it.

“For components that are in short supply, we are using every possible means to secure the quantities we need for next year. As a result, we expect higher procurement costs, but our policy is to offset those increases through price increases from next year onward,” Canon says.

“We have already been making pricing adjustments in response to cost increases as they occur, and we will continue to make decisions on passing on costs from a long-term perspective, while considering the potential impact on sales volumes and balancing that against profitability.”

So there are two really important things to pull out of this quote. First, Canon expects its costs to increase next year. And second, Canon’s modus operandi is to offset increased costs by passing them to the consumer, ergo, increasing product prices. It’s shrewd business, if the market will support it.

It’s not always possible to fully offset increased costs by raising prices. Sometimes markets won’t tolerate the necessary price increases, or a company may be willing to absorb some costs for its long-term prospects. For example, selling more cameras is good for Canon long-term, as it maintains more market share, sells more lenses, etc.

Canon says it will be a balancing act, but, notably, the company is coming right out and telling investors that yes, its policy is to pass increased costs to consumers. This makes perfect sense, but photographers need to hear the news and prepare accordingly.

Canon adds, in response to another question, that it doesn’t expect memory and raw material prices to decline in 2027, so this may be a long-term problem in the photography industry. Much like SSD and memory card prices have continued to increase, cameras may be the next victim.

Canon projects a significantly lower operating profit ratio in its Imaging business in Q4, which the company says is primarily due to higher memory costs and cost increases following the geopolitical strife in the Middle East. “At this point, we have not been able to fully pass these higher costs on through pricing,” Canon says. “If these higher costs persist next year, we will absorb them through price increases.”

If these higher costs persist next year, we will absorb them through price increases.

As DPReview observes, photographers have seen many price increases in recent years. Beyond higher memory card and SSD prices, even more obvious hikes have hit cameras and lenses because of President Trump’s tariff policies. These price increases may prove prescriptive, as that was effectively a company passing higher operational costs directly to their customers.

Earlier this year, Nikon discussed “higher costs” resulting from higher memory prices. Sony blamed increased memory costs for hurting its bottom line in the Imaging business. Canon may be the most open so far about how it will deal with these rising costs — passing them on to consumers — but it will very likely not be the only company to use this strategy. It’s basically the go-to strategy across the technology space.

“Photographers, many of whom were exhausted by the seemingly unending tariff-induced price increases last year, must unfortunately brace themselves for the impact of memory prices. They are coming,” PetaPixel predicted in August.

Memory is integral to digital cameras, and there’s simply no way to get around using it. Manufacturers need the memory, and it is getting pricier. More expensive cameras are, frankly, inevitable.

#9014. Sophia Huitema "Prussian Blue" @ Harper’s Apartment

Harper’s is pleased to announce Prussian Blue, New York–based artist Sophia Huitema’s first solo exhibition with the gallery. The presentation features new works by Huitema and will be on view through April 25, 2026.

Across the seven oil paintings on view, the visual and chemical properties of the pigment Prussian Blue function as a metaphorical anchor, tying together a cast of watchful female figures within Huitema’s hazy, dreamlike worlds. Working within a restrained range of blue and green tones, the paintings evoke a moody atmosphere through cool harmonies and dimly lit interiors. Prussian Blue, derived from chemical processes historically linked to cyanide while also used as an antidote to certain forms of poisoning, embodies a rare duality in which toxicity and protection converge, mirroring the emotionally guarded, ambiguous presence of Huitema’s figures.

The tension between beauty and menace permeates Huitema’s subjects. Elongated figures with exaggerated limbs and slender necks slink through each scene, often directly confronting the viewer’s gaze. Set within opulent surroundings that recall Gatsby–era decadence, Huitema’s women bear the markers of high society themselves, dressed in elegant gowns and adorned with pearl necklaces or jewel-studded headdresses. Moving through film-noir settings with poise and a quietly calculating air, these femme fatales seem either to lure their audience into a seductive ruse or to deploy their own cunning to evade danger. In Sleeper Car, for example, a woman fitted in a backless evening gown tilts her head slyly over her right shoulder in a relaxed pose while her right hand appears braced and ready to strike. As rain streaks across the coach’s windows and the narrow aisle stretches into an uncertain depth, a moment of cinematic suspense emerges, evoking the apex of a psychological thriller. In this way, Huitema constructs a world of heightened atmosphere and theatrical tension that opens onto the broader visual traditions and painterly languages informing her work.

Huitema’s paintings draw on a range of art-historical and visual references while maintaining a distinct internal coherence. The attenuated proportions and stylized poses of her figures recall traditions of early twentieth-century fashion illustration and Art Deco design, where gesture and embellishment echo the streamlined finesse of illustrators such as Erté and the theatrical poise found in interwar couture and stage design. Her compressed spaces also suggest affinities with aspects of Symbolist and Surrealist painting, in which shallow interiors and phantasmagoric backdrops function less as coherent environments than as psychological realms shaped by subconscious experience. Rather than aligning with a single historical framework, Huitema synthesizes these influences into a contemporary visual language that moves fluidly between illustration, painting, and cinematic staging. Working outside formal academic training, she has developed this vocabulary through sustained studio practice and close observation, resulting in a body of work that situates itself in dialogue with art history while remaining grounded in a self-directed approach to image making. In this context, Prussian Blue operates not only as a chromatic throughline but also as a conceptual one, binding together Huitema’s historical references and recurring motifs of protection and threat in constant tension.

#9013. Hacked Hasselblad X2D II 100C Shoots Video, Has ChatGPT, and Runs Linux

Hacked Hasselblad X2D II 100C Shoots Video, Has ChatGPT, and Runs Linux

A few weeks ago, PetaPixel posted a Snap about someone who got Doom running on a Hasselblad X2D II 100C. At the time, creator Radium Wang said they were working on more open-source projects for the X2D II 100C. Well, that’s certainly proved true.

As Mirrorless Rumors writes, people have used Radium Wang’s Github work to do all sorts of interesting things with Hasselblad’s newest medium format mirrorless camera, including getting it to record video.

Video recording on the Hasselblad X2D II — a demo by 奶酪 on Xiaohongshu by r/hasselblad

A Chinese creator, 奶酪, has built experimental firmware for the X2D II 100C that adds video recording, something that the X2D II 100C cannot do out of the box and Hasselblad has signaled no intention of adding.

While that is probably the most interesting thing people have done so far to the X2D II 100C using custom firmware, Radium Wang has also gotten Apple CarPlay running on the camera for whatever insane reason and installed ChatGPT to it. Reddit user u/Unable_Ad_1804 even loaded up a Linux kernel on the camera.

Got XFCE running on my Hasselblad X2D II! by r/hasselblad

There are many other possibilities, too, including a wide range of practical applications that actually benefit photographers. Radium Wang has created a bunch of repositories on Github related to individual camera features and functions, like LiDAR, autofocus, IBIS, AF-C, and more. It is certainly possible for someone to enhance aspects of the camera or create custom software for niche photographic applications.

A natural comparison is Magic Lantern for Canon cameras. People have achieved some pretty incredible things through open-source firmware updates before, including adding new video features, improving performance, and unlocking impressive time-lapse capabilities. Magic Lantern even enabled HDR video recording on select Canon cameras long before Canon itself ever added it to its cameras.

If it is not already obvious, anyone who hacks their camera must do so with an understanding of the potential risks. There may also be legal implications to tinkering with any source-level camera code. PetaPixel is sharing this information because it is interesting, not as any endorsement of the behavior described herein. Loading open-source software onto a camera can cause issues, violate terms of service, and potentially cause headaches when trying to get a warranty honored if something goes wrong and the camera bricks.

#9012. Sam Taylor-Johnson’s ‘Crying Men’ Photo Series Featured in Major Solo Exhibition

Sam Taylor-Johnson’s ‘Crying Men’ Photo Series Featured in Major Solo Exhibition

An exhibition presents the career-defining work of internationally celebrated British photographer Sam Taylor-Johnson, including a selection of works from her iconic Crying Men series.

Taylor-Johnson’s solo exhibition She Was I is on view at Jackson Fine Art in Atlanta through January 23, 2027. The exhibition coincides with the publication of the photographer’s new monograph Sam Taylor-Johnson: The Self and the Portrait, published by Rizzoli.

The exhibition explores Taylor-Johnson’s long-standing interest in identity and the self through photography and film. It centers on her self-portraits, beginning with early black-and-white photographs she took in London in the 1990s while she was a student.

More than a decade later, Taylor-Johnson returned to self-portraiture with images of herself suspended in her London studio, appearing weightless and seemingly held aloft by balloons. In Wired, photographed in Joshua Tree, California, in 2020, she makes the fragile support mechanisms holding her body above the ground an integral part of the composition.

The exhibition will also present Self Portrait in Dark Water, a more recent series in which Taylor-Johnson uses water to suspend her body in unusual positions. The series will be shown to U.S. audiences for the first time.

A selection of works from Taylor-Johnson’s Crying Men series will also be on view. Created between 2002 and 2004, the series features leading male actors whom the artist invited to sit before her camera in moments of private reflection. The portraits capture the subjects crying, exposing a more vulnerable side of their public personas.

Taylor-Johnson photographed more than two dozen subjects for the series, including actors Daniel Craig, Laurence Fishburne, and Philip Seymour Hoffman. The images document the men in unguarded moments of emotion.

Alongside these portraits, the exhibition includes photographs of Taylor-Johnson’s family and friends in private, familiar settings. These works have a semi-autobiographical quality, offering another perspective on the relationships between identity, personal experience, and portraiture.

Together, the works in She Was I examine Taylor-Johnson’s career-long interest in the self and the ways in which the complexities of individual identity can be both revealed and concealed.

Sam Taylor-Johnson’s solo exhibition She Was I is on view at Jackson Fine Art in Atlanta through January 23, 2027.

#9011. There’s a New M-Mount Pancake Lens in Town

There’s a New M-Mount Pancake Lens in Town

DJ-Optical, which sells its lenses on eBay, has a new ultra-slim manual-focus pancake lens that looks quite stylish.

Shown off earlier this year at the 2026 China P&E Imaging Show, per Leica Rumors, the new DJ-Optical Ultra Slim 35mm f/3.5 Pancake Lens is a manual focus prime for Leica M mount. It is just 15 millimeters (0.59 inches) long, not counting the mount itself.

Online retailer Shotenkobo describes it as a “body-cap-style lens.” PetaPixel has reported on other similar lenses over the years, including most recently the TTArtisan AF 24mm f/3.8 Mini for full-frame E-mount cameras. The idea is that instead of protecting the image sensor with a standard body cap, users can attach a pancake lens that protects the camera, adds little weight, and can also be used to take photos.

In this case, a 35mm f/3.5 lens suits a wide range of photographic applications. It can be used for street photography, travel, and portraiture, to name a few. While it isn’t super-fast, it’s fast enough for many casual scenarios. It also doesn’t add much weight to a kit, since the lens is just 140 grams (4.9 ounces).

As Digital Camera Watch adds, DJ-Optical has about 30 years of optical experience. The company’s most recent lens is the NyctaLux 50mm f/1 for M Mount. It’s also on eBay and costs about $700.

The manual focus lens has eight elements arranged across five groups. That’s quite a bit of glass for such a thin lens. It includes one ED element and a trio of high-refractive index elements. The aperture ranges from f/3.5 to f/16, with eight aperture blades. Although it is rangefinder-coupled and focuses down to 0.7 meters, it can focus as close as 0.5 meters in live view. It can also be easily adapted to non-M cameras, though any adapter adds a bit of length to the pancake lens.

“Combining classic metal craftsmanship, multi-coated optics, and rangefinder-coupled manual focusing, it is an ideal everyday companion for street photography, travel, and casual shooting,” Shotenkobo says.

It’s not super cheap, priced at about $520, but it’s not an especially high price for an all-metal Leica M-mount design. The lens is available to purchase now.

#9010. A Van Gogh hidden away for over 50 years and a vibrant Cezanne harlequin: our pick of the November auctions

Vincent van Gogh painted Châtaigniers en fleurs (blossoming chestnut trees) during the final weeks of his life, having just moved to the French village of Auvers-sur-Oise after spending the previous year in a psychiatric asylum in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence. Initially he took to painting with a renewed optimism at his surroundings and work. The painting at hand depicts flowering chestnut trees blooming into a blue sky, with women passing through with parasols and Japanese-inspired dress. Châtaigniers en fleurs is expected to fetch in the region of $180m, Sotheby’s says. The artist’s current record at auction is $117.2m, set by Christie’s New York in November 2022 during the Paul Allen sale with Verger avec cyprès (orchard with cypresses, 1888). Châtaigniers en fleurs has not been seen in public since entering the Argentinian Blaquier-Arrieta collection in 1975.

Arlequin is a rare appearance on the market of one of Paul Cezanne’s paintings from his harlequin series, modelled on his son, Paul, and inspired by Mardi Gras parades from the artist’s childhood in Aix-en-Provence, France. It is one of only four such examples, according to Sotheby’s. When the painting was unveiled at Sotheby’s in London, it was the first time it had been seen in public since 1975, when it was acquired by the sugar magnates Carlos Pedro Blaquier and Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier. Before it entered their collection in Argentina, it belonged to legendary dealers like Ambroise Vollard, Paul Durand-Ruel and Paul Rosenberg. It also hung for two decades at Merton Hall in Cambridge, the then-family home of the British branch of the Rothschild family. Another version of the painting is part of the collection of the National Gallery of Art in Washington, DC. If it exceeds its estimate, Arlequin could set an artist record at auction. The most valuable Cezanne to sell at auction was a view of his beloved Sainte-Victoire mountain, for $137.79m, at Christie’s New York in 2022 during the sale of Paul Allen’s collection.

Man Ray’s Le Baiser (the kiss) comes from the collection of Roger Therond, the journalist and longtime editor of Paris Match, whose holdings included photographs by some of the leading artists of inter-war Paris. Therond was particularly drawn to Man Ray, whom he nicknamed “the Frenzied One”. In Le Baiser, two figures are captured in ambiguous poses, leaving the relationship between the two sitters deliberately unclear. According to Christie’s, Therond encouraged his children to look at the photograph from a distance and imagine different possibilities and circumstances for the subjects. The sitter on the left side is the American photographer Lee Miller, who began her career as a fashion model and later worked as a correspondent for Vogue during the Second World War. Miller was one of the first journalists to arrive at the Dachau concentration camp after its liberation in 1945, and recorded some of the most haunting photographic evidence of the Holocaust. She famously posed for a photo while bathing in Adolf Hitler’s personal bathtub at his Munich apartment.

“Blossoming Chestnut Trees”, which has been hidden away for over 60 years, is being sold by Sotheby's for the Blaquier-Arrieta family of Argentina

#9008. Two Telescopes Team Up To Photograph a Spooky Space Cat

Two Telescopes Team Up To Photograph a Spooky Space Cat

What better way to celebrate Halloween than with a ghostly cat comprised of a nebula? NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope and the Hubble Space Telescope joined forces to capture the Cat’s Head Nebula.

“Like a spectral form rising out of a cold mist, NASA’s Hubble and James Webb Space Telescopes have captured a hauntingly dynamic star-forming scene,” NASA writes.

The Cat’s Head Nebula is located 7,500 light-years from Earth in the Carina Nebula, a popular target for Webb and other space telescopes. The Cat’s Head Nebula, unsurprisingly, got its name because it resembles a cat. Specifically, it looks like a cat sitting with its back to the viewer, with its head turned to the right, glowing eye and all.

As NASA says, the Cat’s Head Nebula will eventually disperse, with its growing stars changing the region’s complexion. In the meantime, it is fertile ground for studying star formation.

The cat’s head shape specifically was likely formed by the intense ultraviolet radiation and winds emitted by massive stars in the Carina Nebula.

“As this stellar feedback erodes the surrounding gas and dust, denser material within the feline-shaped pillar resists erosion, at least for now,” NASA explains.

The James Webb Space Telescope and Hubble have different strengths. In this case, Hubble’s visible-light view of the Cat’s Head Nebula shows the opaque cosmic dust that forms the cat’s body.

Meanwhile, Webb’s exceptional ability to peer through interstellar dust in mid-infrared and near-infrared wavelengths lets it see beyond the dust. For my money, the spookiest rendition of all comes from Webb’s Mid-InfraRed Instrument (MIRI).

Image creditsNASA, ESA, CSA, STScI; Image Processing: Joseph DePasquale (STScI)

The cost of a will varies dramatically based on how you create it and how complex your estate is. Here is a comprehensive comparison of every method, from free options to premium attorney packages.

Several factors push will costs toward the higher end of each range:

The will vs trust decision is primarily a financial calculation: does the upfront cost of a trust save more than it costs by avoiding probate?

When you die with only a will (no trust), your estate must go through probate — a court-supervised process where a judge validates your will, your executor inventories assets, debts are paid, and remaining assets are distributed. Probate costs include:

Probate also takes 6-18 months on average and is a public proceeding — anyone can look up your will, your assets, and who inherited what.

A revocable living trust costs $1,500-$5,000 upfront but avoids probate entirely. The math is straightforward:

For most FI-focused households who are building wealth toward financial independence, the trust pays for itself many times over. If your net worth exceeds $100,000-$200,000 and you own real estate, a trust is almost certainly the better financial decision.

Even with a trust, you still need a pour-over will — a short document that catches any assets not transferred into the trust during your lifetime and directs them into the trust at death. You also still need a healthcare directive and durable power of attorney. Most estate plan packages include all four documents together.

The sticker price of a will is only part of the total cost of estate planning. Several hidden costs catch people off guard:

The FI-optimized approach to estate planning minimizes cost without sacrificing protection:

Start with an online will now. A $159 Trust & Will plan gives you a will, healthcare directive, and power of attorney today. Do not let perfect be the enemy of done — having a basic will is infinitely better than having no will while you save up for an attorney.

Upgrade to a trust when your net worth exceeds $200,000. At this point, the probate avoidance savings justify the $1,500-$3,500 cost of adding a trust.

Shop attorney fees aggressively. Estate planning is a competitive market. Get quotes from at least three attorneys. Many offer flat-fee packages, and prices can vary by 50-100% for the same work in the same city. Ask specifically whether the quote includes trust funding assistance and deed transfers.

Use online services for updates. Rather than paying an attorney $200-$500 for a codicil, many online platforms let you update your will for free or for a small annual subscription ($19-$39/year). Trust & Will, for example, includes one year of free updates.

Bundle documents. An estate plan package (will + trust + POA + healthcare directive) typically costs 20-40% less than purchasing each document separately. If you are going to see an attorney, get everything done in one engagement.

Here is the counterintuitive truth: the most expensive estate plan is the one you never create. Dying without a will (intestate) triggers state default rules that may not match your wishes, longer and more expensive probate proceedings, and potential family conflict. For parents of minor children, it means a judge — not you — decides who raises your kids. The $0-$259 cost of an online will is trivially small compared to these consequences.

Yes. FreeWill (freewill.com) offers a free basic will funded by nonprofit partners. Some states also accept handwritten (holographic) wills that cost nothing. Military personnel can get free wills through the JAG office on any military installation. Many bar associations and legal aid societies offer free will clinics several times per year. While these free options work for simple estates, you may want to pay $99-$259 for a more comprehensive online service that includes healthcare directives and power of attorney.

Attorneys charge $300-$750 for a simple will and $750-$1,500 for a complex will with special provisions. A complete estate plan package (will, trust, power of attorney, healthcare directive) runs $1,500-$5,000. Fees vary significantly by location — attorneys in major metros charge 2-3 times more than attorneys in smaller cities for the same work. Always ask for a flat fee rather than hourly billing for estate planning.

For straightforward estates, yes. Major online will makers like Trust & Will, Nolo WillMaker, and LegalZoom produce documents that are legally valid in all 50 states and cover the same core elements an attorney would include. The difference is that an attorney can provide customized advice, handle complex situations, and anticipate issues specific to your state law. If your estate is simple, an online will is functionally equivalent. If your situation has any complexity, the attorney consultation is worth the additional cost.

Online services typically include free updates for one year and then charge $19-$39 per year for ongoing access. An attorney charges $100-$500 for a codicil (formal amendment) or $300-$1,000 to draft a new will. For minor changes, a codicil is sufficient. For major changes (new spouse, additional children, significant asset changes), creating an entirely new will is cleaner and reduces the risk of conflicting instructions.

The most expensive part of estate planning is NOT the documents — it is probate. Probate costs 3-7% of your estate value ($15,000-$72,000 on a $500,000-$1,000,000 estate) and takes 6-18 months. By comparison, even the most expensive estate plan package ($5,000-$10,000) is a fraction of what your family would spend navigating probate without a trust. The second most expensive mistake is outdated beneficiary designations on retirement accounts, which can send six or seven figures to the wrong person with no legal recourse.

The cost of a will ranges from $0 to $10,000+ depending on your method and complexity, but the most expensive option is always having no will at all. For most FI-focused households, start with an online will for $0-$259 to get basic protection in place immediately. As your net worth grows beyond $200,000, invest $1,500-$5,000 in a comprehensive estate plan with a revocable living trust — the probate savings alone deliver a 300-1,000% return. Update your beneficiary designations today (free), review your plan every 3-5 years, and remember: the goal of estate planning is not to create perfect documents. It is to protect the people you love from financial chaos during the worst moment of their lives.
