#9006. Molly Bounds "The Light That Loses, The Night That Wins" @ Mrs Gallery, Maspeth, NY

Mrs. is pleased to present The Light That Loses, The Night That Wins, Molly Bounds’ New York debut solo exhibition, on view at the gallery’s 6040 56th Drive location. This exhibition marks the Los Angeles-based artist’s second presentation with the gallery following The Armory Show in September 2025. The show will be on view through May 2, 2026.

Opening on the vernal equinox, a rare moment when the hours of daylight and night are equal, Molly Bounds offers light as the protagonist in her new series of paintings. It is versatile and ever-changing; it both conceals and reveals, and reminds us of the unrelenting forward movement of time. Depicting her subjects both in contemplation and in the midst of candid movement, Bounds continues her investigation into liminal moments where stillness and urgency shape the mood. Much like the transition from winter to spring, these figures appear on the threshold of a transformative shift.

There are also moments of escapism. In both It Sings in Me and Among of Green, Again a figure moves freely amongst rolling green hills, illuminated under the sun. The landscape appears bucolic and perhaps overly so - is this real or imagined? For Bounds this is less important; the ability to build optimism and a belief in renewal and rebirth is paramount. Contrasting with the scenes of pensive interiority, these landscapes communicate urgency, celebration, possibility, and fantasy. After the darkness of winter, spring wins.

#9005. Page\Park uses local stone and timber for school wellbeing hub in Edinburgh

Photography by David Barbour

Scottish architecture studio Page\Park has completed The Allardice Centre, a health and wellbeing hub for Fettes College in Edinburgh, which is topped with a lantern-like roof.

Named after the independent day and boarding school’s alumnus David Allardice, the 469-square-metre centre brings together medical and pastoral care services in a fully accessible building nestled into a wooded plot.

According to Page\Park, the centre’s design was informed by the late Allardice’s interest in Eastern philosophy, in particular the elemental philosophy of Wuxing, which led to a palette of timber, stone and metal.

The building’s structure is made from Scots-grown timber, while Darney stone quarried nearby forms the external load-bearing cladding, which is contrasted by a bronze roof.

“Allardice spent much of his working life in East Asia, and was drawn to ancient Chinese philosophy and the five essential elements, fire, water, wood, metal and earth,” the studio told Dezeen.

“This narrative directly influenced the design, materiality and construction approach, which can be seen through the strata-like stone cladding, burnt bronze metal roof, and connection to the outside,” it added.

The Allardice Centre is organised across a single storey, with an open wellbeing hub at its centre, wrapped by a series of individual treatment and counselling rooms overlooking the surrounding woodland.

Illuminating the central hub is a mono-pitched, lantern-like roof. This creates a ring of clerestory windows, framed by the exposed glued-laminated timber (glulam) structure designed in collaboration with Scottish engineering firm Will Rudd.

“Fitting the full brief for both medical and pastoral functions into this constrained site, while avoiding level changes to maximise accessibility, forced the plan to be quite deep,” explained the studio.

“Bringing natural light into this deep plan therefore became a challenge. To resolve this, the glulam structure extends and branches out at high level to reveal a triple-glazed clerestory lantern formed of timber curtain walling,” it added.

Inside The Allardice Centre, white walls allow the timber structure to come to the fore. In the treatment rooms, leaf-print and green fabrics create a visual connection to the surrounding site, which was developed by landscape architects Harrison Stevens.

“We were interested in the didactic implications of exposing the glulam timber frame, offering an insight into how the building was crafted, celebrating its sustainability principles and the elemental philosophy underpinning the design,” said the studio.

“The Darney stone chosen for the project was quarried only 75 kilometres away, and had fantastic mineral veins through it which paired neatly with the varying course sizes, leaning into the earth element theme, and giving a sense of permanence,” it added.

Other projects in Edinburgh recently featured on Dezeen include the extension of a Georgian townhouse by Pend, which complemented the existing stone structure with skinny red brickwork.

Elsewhere, Page\Park recently completed a teaching building for the University of Stirling, which was shortlisted for the 2025 RIAS Andrew Doolan Best Building in Scotland Award.

Photography by David Barbour

#9004. Viltrox 35mm f/1.4 Pro Review: A Beautiful Behemoth

Viltrox 35mm f/1.4 Pro Review: A Beautiful Behemoth

Viltrox has made huge waves in the world of optics, with many saying that it is the Sigma of China. Of course, this is a huge compliment given that Sigma is now famous for making affordable optics that easily compete with OEM lenses. I’ve reviewed many Viltrox lenses now, and I always enjoy the process. They are solid lenses, with ambitious optical goals, and they usually meet these lofty expectations.

The Viltrox 35mm f/1.4 is sharp and exceptionally well-designed for shallow depth of field performance. The only real price you have to pay is in its bulk.

I’m a particular fan of the Pro series of Viltrox lenses because it delivers fast optics with excellent correction for a good price. In fact, the 85mm f/1.4 Pro is easily one of my favorite portrait lenses, but can the new $829 35mm f/1.4 Pro have this same impact on me? When I use 35mm lenses, I want them to have faster apertures so that I can get some separation from my subjects. I went into this review hoping that this latest offering from Viltrox could keep the ball rolling.

Viltrox takes a very clean and practical approach to the Pro lens design. Nothing flashy, but everything is built reliably and with ease of use in mind. The 35mm Pro definitely keeps the trend alive with a rugged chassis and professional weather-sealing. However, it also keeps the larger size and bulk of the Pro lenses as well. This is a big chunk of glass weighing in at 26.8 ounces (760 grams), as tested on the Sony E-mount. You can also get this lens for the Nikon Z mount, which turns out to be quite important to the success of this lens. More on this shortly. The filter thread is 77mm, which is not unusual, but there is no denying that the 35mm Pro feels a little larger than it needs to be. At least this size comes with fantastic physical controls.

The manual focus ring is tuned beautifully, with just enough resistance to make focusing accurate. There is a customizable button and controls for switching between autofocus and manual focus. You also get a really nice aperture ring with third-stop increments and a noticeable point of resistance before it clicks into auto aperture control mode. You can also set the aperture ring for smooth operation with the flick of a switch.

Everything on this lens feels solid, works smoothly, and is quick and easy to adjust. The autofocusing experience is also quick and easy, thanks to a powerful voice-coil motor to drive the heavy glass elements. There is a supplied hood that bayonets onto the front of the lens and a USB-C connector built into the lens mount for lens updates.

I distinctly remember shooting the test charts for this lens, evaluating them, and immediately texting the team a simple “wow”. I expect Viltrox lenses to be sharp, as I do with any modern lens, frankly, but I didn’t expect the consistency I was finding. The center of the image is full of usable detail at f/1.4, with only a slight improvement noticeable as you stop down. However, the corners are equally impressive, with good clarity right to the edge at f/1.4 and very little vignetting. Stopping the lens down will tighten things up and cover even the extremes of the corners, but this lens is made to shoot at f/1.4 and still deliver impressive sharpness anywhere on the image.

Flare resistance is good thanks to the Viltrox lens coatings, with some very minor green ghosting wide-open. Stopping the lens down will create a more sizable field of green across the frame, but it is manageable nonetheless. Contrast is also well maintained, and due to a grey and cloudy day, we torture-tested the lens coatings with a strong COB light up close. It still did pretty well.

Bokeh matters on a lens with such a wide aperture, and the Viltrox 35mm lens handles it well. I like the cat’s eye effect at f/1.4, but the lens does exhibit a bit of a strong halo around the highlights. You will also see some very minor onion rings, and the specular highlights have a polygonal look when stopped down. The bokeh looks fine, and you can absolutely get shallow depth of field at will, but the backgrounds can have a touch of distracting harshness.

Where this lens will show some weakness is in the LoCA department. Longitudinal chromatic aberrations are difficult to get rid of in the editing process, and the color fringing can be very distracting when shooting at wider apertures. The Viltrox isn’t out of control, but it does exhibit a noticeable green/magenta split, and this will show up in some of your pictures.

Okay, so earlier I stated that the mount is really going to determine how popular this lens will be. The Viltrox is delivering excellent image quality with just a few compromises, and I’d happily use it for even demanding professional photography. However, if you get this lens in Sony E-mount, there is lots of strong competition. The Sony G-Master 35mm f/1.4 is better, but it’s also wildly expensive. The Sigma 35mm f/1.4 Art is not that far off, though, and it is a near-perfect lens. You will still save a bit of money going to the Viltrox, but it might not be enough to justify the loss of image quality in comparison.

At $829 the Viltrox is a good bargain, and Nikon Z-mount users don’t have as many options. There is an affordable Nikkor 35mm f/1.4 lens, but it is specifically targeted at a lower price range and doesn’t quite have the same sophistication as the Viltrox.

I’d definitely recommend it on the Nikon mount, where Sigma is not currently supported. Regardless, the Viltrox has some really strong points and is a good value in the fast optics arena. I’m happy to say that the Viltrox Pro series continues to impress as it expands the options available, but make sure you are okay with the weight and size.

In E-mount, the Sigma is a better lens if you don't mind spending a little more money. It's probably worth it, especially when considering that the Sigma is much smaller and lighter too. In Nikon Z-mount, the Viltrox makes more sense and outperforms the Nikkor Z 35mm f/1.4 at a fairly similar price.

Yes. No matter how you look at it, the Viltrox 35mm f/1.4 Pro delivers professional results at a great price. Just be ready for its hefty proportions.

#9003. Fifth generation Indian weaver launches luxury cashmere brand

Kadri’s ‘Triangle Twill’ two-tone, hand-painted scarves are 100% cashmere and retail for $400 each. Designs for the brand’s inaugural range were created in a studio in Paris Mickaël Llorca

Art of Luxury magazine, published twice per year by The Art Newspaper, explores how grande marque fashion, jewellery, travel and lifestyle interact with artists, the art market and the museums and heritage sector.

Mujtaba Kadri’s family has produced cashmere for five generations and his atelier in Srinagar, the largest city in Kashmir, is just 50m away from where his great-grandfather had his own. “I’ve been involved since I was a child,” Kadri says. His spinners and weavers are still based exclusively in Srinagar, mostly women working from home. Hand spinning creates a slightly uneven texture in the fibre, which leaves tiny air pockets once it is woven. It is this that makes the fabric both very light and incredibly warm.

Kadri studied at university in Mumbai but returned immediately to his home city, albeit with a more international outlook. “Our cashmere is the finest quality, which means its micron count is always below 14.5,” Kadri says. “I knew it had potential in foreign markets.” He went on to work with Carolina Herrera, Oscar de la Renta and Marni, making custom-ordered textiles. Later, he met Mary-Kate and Ashley Olsen, and collaborated closely with their label, The Row, when they launched their home line.

He is now launching the Kadri brand, using his own name, in outlets including London’s Dover Street Market. On sale will be scarves, blankets and other home and fashion accessories. “I’ve wanted to do this for a long time,” he says. Designs are developed in a small Paris studio where the creative team includes colour specialist Maeva Elfassi. “Colour can be the element that cashmere brands get wrong,” Kadri says.

Hand-woven cashmere is expensive due to the rare raw materials, from a special breed of goats in the Jankan region, and its time-consuming production. A shawl, which sells for $1,000, will go through 12 processes, undertaken by a number of artisans, and takes 40 days to make. “It really is slow fashion,” Kadri says. But more importantly, for him, it is a way to sustain a community where weaving has always been a way of life.

#9002. Images by Nadar and Man Ray Feature in Auction Celebrating 200 Years of Photography

Images by Nadar and Man Ray Feature in Auction Celebrating 200 Years of Photography

A major collection of groundbreaking 19th- and 20th-century French photography, featuring works by Henri Cartier-Bresson, Nadar, and Man Ray, will be offered.

France is celebrating 200 years of photography, marking the pioneering work of French inventor Nicéphore Niépce, who captured View from the Window at Le Gras which is widely considered the oldest known photograph made with a camera in 1826–1827.

To celebrate France’s bicentennial of photography, Christie’s will present more than 350 photographs in the Roger Therond Collection: A French Passion. The works will be offered across three sales in Paris, France, on November 13 and 14, and online from November 6 to 17 to coincide with Paris Photo, the world’s largest international art fair dedicated to photography.

Roger Therond, a journalist who served as editor of Paris Match for half a century, spent decades building a collection that brings together major works from the history of French photography. While his work at the magazine focused on current events, collecting offered him a different perspective on the photographic medium, which he valued for its ability to reveal hidden worlds.

Therond’s collection includes works by some of the leading figures in 19th-century photography in France, including Auguste Belloc, Gustave Le Gray, Édouard Baldus, and Nadar. Therond also built an extensive collection of 20th-century photography, acquiring works by artists who helped shape the medium’s history. These included images by Man Ray (who became a French naturalized citizen), Dora Maar, Brassaï, Henri Cartier-Bresson, Helmut Newton, and Guy Bourdin — several of whom were friends of the Therond.

One work that held particular significance for Therond was Man Ray’s Le Baiser (The Kiss), estimated at $280,000–$392,000 (€250,000–350,000). Man Ray’s photograph depicts two sitters, including photographer Lee Miller on the left, but leaves their identities and relationship open to interpretation. Therond encouraged his children to look at the photograph more than once, considering the different possibilities it might suggest.

“A man and a woman? Two women? Two men wearing make-up? Let us not try to know,” Therond would say, according to a news release by Christie’s. “Instead, let us half-close our eyes and allow into our field of vision the black-clad Gypsy woman who emerges, beyond the photographer’s intention, a dancing silhouette whose skirt billows like a corolla. And where are we? In another world, the world of the strange, the world of the unknown.”

More information about Christie’s auction of the Roger Therond Collection: A French Passion can be found here.

#9001. Nat Meade's "Franklin" @ HESSE FLATOW, NYC

HESSE FLATOW is pleased to announce the opening of Franklin, an exhibition of paintings and works on paper by Nat Meade, marking his third solo presentation with the gallery. The show is on view through April 18, 2026.

The emotional arc of life’s struggles and triumphs take shape within Meade’s figurative works, reflecting the artist’s everyday experiences as he navigates being a father, son, partner, and academic. Far from portraits of actual individuals, his protagonists mirror timeless archetypes. At times, we encounter a lone traveler searching for existential validation; at other times, we see through intergenerational dynamics. This allegorical distance via painting provides a realm for Meade to explore personal challenges through absurd, somber, and humorous tropes, while also furnishing a space rife with human nature that bears unequivocal resonance.

Meade’s reflections on his relationship with his father after his recent passing, and subsequent reevaluations of his own role as a parent percolate throughout the works in the exhibition. Vulnerability, pain, and mortality are themes Meade does not shy away from, yet the introduction of younger males in this body of work casts a sense of hope, acceptance, reconciliation, and renewal.

Faced with a pair of dangling legs from a cloud in Poise, we question whether a figure is ascending or descending from the heavens, a suggestion perhaps on the interchangeability of birth and death, be it physical or spiritual. Ghostly specters hover over certain individuals – a metaphor for inherited trauma and release. In the same way that a soul peels away from an expiring body in classic cartoons, we observe a spirit looking back on itself with what might be  happiness or regret. The exhibition’s title Franklin is a subtle nod to the 1974 horror film Texas Chainsaw Massacre, known for its portrayal of a deranged patriarchal family. Meade embraces this inner turmoil of contending with one’s violent and antagonistic impulses as his characters are visibly sublimated or put in their place. A vulture picking away at a corpse recalls the eternal punishment of Prometheus by Zeus, while a bearded figure on his hands and knees echoes William Blake’s portrayal of Nebuchadnezzar, condemned for his lust for power.

In contrast to the adults, Meade’s younger figures appear more harmonious. A young boy charts his own path as he steers a boat with a radiant torch, unclouded by societal and familial pressures. A sense of childlike wonder and adventure beholds an adolescent ankle-deep in a secluded cove, reaching in to touch the sea floor brilliantly covered in starfish, anemones, and mussels. In a related work, we observe two pairs of legs belonging to father and son in the same shallow pool, one tenderly guiding the other. Having in the past shown his figures wrestling with or victims of forces of nature, physically being overtaken by turbulent wind and crashing waves, Meade’s focus on calmer seas signals a turning point. He recognizes the need to acknowledge one’s rocky histories in order to heal and release future generations from similar burdens. Despite what may seem like an insurmountable heaviness, he reminds us of the stubborn resilience of human nature, making progress attainable.

#9000. Why the Habitat Matters as Much as the Animal in Wildlife Photography

Why the Habitat Matters as Much as the Animal in Wildlife Photography

Wildlife rarely exists in isolation, yet it’s easy to overlook the environment when you’re trying to capture a compelling portrait. Learn how environmental wildlife portraits use habitat, composition, and animal behavior to tell a bigger story without losing focus on the subject.

Wildlife photography often emphasizes getting close enough to capture fine detail, from the texture of a bear’s fur to the expression in a bird’s eye. But some of the most compelling wildlife images leave more room around the subject, showing an animal within the environment it inhabits. A wider composition can reveal how an animal interacts with its surroundings, communicate scale, or capture the conditions that shape its daily life.

Creating an effective environmental wildlife portrait requires more than pulling back or switching to a wider lens. The habitat should support the photograph without overwhelming the animal, and every element in the frame should help tell the story. From researching an animal’s behavior to using foreground elements and negative space, balancing the subject with its surroundings can add another dimension to wildlife photography.

I also incorporate environmental wildlife portraits into my portfolio to add variety beyond traditional, tightly framed animal portraits. Showing wildlife in its natural habitat provides context, shows these animals were photographed in the wild rather than in captivity, and offers a more complete picture of the experience behind the image. I also share behind-the-scenes clips from my time in the field, giving viewers another look at the real environments, conditions, and moments that went into capturing the photograph, particularly as AI-generated imagery and accusations become increasingly common.

Traditional wildlife portraits often emphasize the animal itself, using a long focal length and shallow depth of field to isolate the subject from its surroundings. Environmental wildlife portraits take a different approach, giving the habitat an active role in the composition. Rather than blurring the background, the photographer uses it to establish a sense of place and provide context for the animal.

The difference is not necessarily how much of the frame the animal occupies. A relatively tight composition can still communicate a strong connection to the habitat, while a wide photograph can feel disconnected if the surroundings contribute little to the story. What matters is the relationship between the subject and everything around it.

A bear moving through the tundra, a fox standing among tall grasses, or a shorebird feeding along a tidal flat can all make compelling environmental portraits. Each setting tells the viewer something about where the animal lives and how it interacts with that environment. The landscape becomes part of the subject rather than simply a backdrop.

This approach also creates opportunities to communicate scale, atmosphere, and behavior. An animal photographed against a vast mountain range might appear small in the frame, yet its placement within the landscape can make the image more powerful than a close-up. The surrounding environment helps viewers better understand the world the animal inhabits.

Creating a compelling environmental wildlife portrait starts before you raise the camera to your eye. Learning about the animal, its behavior, and its habitat can help you recognize which elements belong in the frame and which distract from the story. A landscape might look visually appealing, but understanding what makes it important to the animal gives you a more meaningful reason to include it in your composition.

Research can help you anticipate the moments and environmental details worth photographing. Understanding seasonal migration, feeding habits, nesting behavior, or preferred habitat can reveal opportunities you might otherwise miss. An elk photographed among autumn grasses tells one story, while an elk standing in a snow-covered landscape during the rut communicates something different. The setting is not merely a backdrop. It provides context that helps viewers understand what the animal is doing and how it lives.

This knowledge also helps you decide what to leave out. A photograph of a bird in its nesting habitat might benefit from including the surrounding vegetation and nesting materials, while distant human structures or unrelated objects could weaken the intended story. In other situations, evidence of human activity may be essential, especially when documenting habitat loss, conservation challenges, or the relationship between wildlife and developing landscapes. The key question isn’t whether an element is attractive, but whether it supports what the photograph is trying to communicate.

Observation in the field is just as important as research beforehand. Watch how the animal moves through its surroundings, where it pauses, what it interacts with, and how the light changes across the habitat. These observations can help you anticipate where to position yourself and when to make a photograph. They can also reveal details easy to overlook when you focus only on the animal, from tracks in fresh snow to feeding signs in the vegetation.

Ultimately, an environmental wildlife portrait works best when the photographer understands the relationship between the subject and its surroundings. Research helps you recognize the story, while careful observation and composition determine how much of that story makes it into the frame. The goal is to include enough information for the viewer to understand the animal’s world without overwhelming the image with unnecessary detail.

One of the first decisions when creating an environmental wildlife portrait is determining how much space to give the surroundings. There is no universal focal length or framing rule for this type of photograph. Instead, the composition should reflect what you want the viewer to notice about the animal and its environment.

A moderately wide composition can show the animal interacting with nearby vegetation, rocks, water, or other habitat features while keeping it prominent in the frame. A much wider view can establish the scale of a landscape, show the animal moving through a larger territory, or emphasize the isolation of a subject within an expansive setting.

I also use environmental portraits to show a sense of scale, highlight natural camouflage, and capture how an animal appears within its habitat. Seeing a wildlife subject in context can reveal just how well it blends into its surroundings, how small it is against an expansive landscape, or how its colors and patterns work with the environment. These details can be difficult to convey in a tight portrait, but they help tell a more complete story of the animal in the wild. So thinking of the end goal helps me decide how much habitat to include.

Consider what would be lost if you cropped the photograph more tightly. If removing the surrounding landscape eliminates important information about the animal’s behavior, habitat, or scale, those environmental elements are doing useful work. If a tighter crop tells essentially the same story, you may not need the extra space.

Distance also influences the relationship between the subject and its surroundings. Moving farther away can include more of the habitat, but it may also change the animal’s apparent size and introduce additional distractions. Changing focal lengths from the same position produces a different framing effect than physically changing your position, so consider both options when working out a composition.

Remember that an environmental portrait doesn’t have to be a landscape photograph with a tiny animal in the distance. The animal can remain a substantial part of the frame while still allowing enough room for the habitat to provide context. The goal is to find a balance that serves the story rather than following a fixed formula.

A wider composition introduces more opportunities to work with layers. Foreground vegetation, a middle-ground subject, and distant mountains can add depth and guide the viewer through the scene. These layers can also establish the animal’s position within its habitat, making the image feel more immersive than a straightforward portrait.

Foreground elements can be particularly useful when photographing wildlife in forests, wetlands, and grasslands. Blades of grass, leaves, or branches can frame an animal and provide a sense of being present in its environment. However, they need to be used carefully. Vegetation that obscures the animal’s face or creates confusing shapes around its body can weaken the composition.

Pay attention to how foreground and background elements overlap with the subject. A tree trunk emerging from an animal’s head or a bright branch crossing its body can be distracting, even if the surrounding habitat is otherwise attractive. A small shift in your position may separate those elements and produce a cleaner composition.

Negative space can be equally important. Open water, snow, fog, or an uncluttered stretch of sky can give an animal room within the frame and establish a particular mood. A bird flying across a broad expanse of sky, for example, may communicate movement and freedom, while a solitary mammal surrounded by snow can emphasize the harshness or quiet of its environment.

The amount of negative space should reflect the subject’s position and behavior. Leaving room in front of an animal that is walking or looking in a particular direction can create a natural sense of movement. Placing it near the edge of the frame may instead communicate tension, isolation, or an intentional sense of imbalance. Neither approach is automatically better, but the placement should feel deliberate.

Even when the habitat is an important part of the photograph, the animal should remain the clear visual anchor. Without a strong focal point, a wider composition can become a collection of environmental details rather than a cohesive wildlife image.

One way to establish visual hierarchy is through contrast. An animal’s color, shape, or texture may stand out naturally against its surroundings. For example, a dark mammal against pale snow can remain easy to recognize even when it occupies only a small portion of the frame. In other situations, the subject may blend into the habitat, requiring more careful positioning to create separation.

Light can also help direct attention. An animal illuminated by a break in the clouds may stand out against a darker background, while a rim of light along its fur or feathers can distinguish its outline from the surrounding vegetation. These opportunities often require patience, as the photographer waits for the light and the animal’s position to align.

Body language and behavior also contribute to visual emphasis. A bird turning its head, a fox looking toward something outside the frame, or a bear pausing mid-stride can give the viewer a clear point of interest. When the animal is small within a landscape, recognizable posture or movement can be especially important.

Focus remains critical. Environmental portraits sometimes benefit from enough depth of field to preserve the habitat’s detail, but the animal’s eye should generally remain sharp when it is visible, and the composition calls attention to its face. If the subject is too small for facial detail to be meaningful, a distinct silhouette or recognizable body position can still give the photograph a clear focal point.

One of the biggest challenges of environmental wildlife photography is that a wider frame includes more opportunities for visual clutter. Branches, grasses, bright patches of sky, rocks, and distant objects can all compete with the animal. The challenge is not to eliminate every detail, but to recognize which ones strengthen the photograph and which ones pull attention away from its central idea.

Start by scanning the edges of the frame before taking the photograph. Bright objects near the corners, partially visible branches, or high-contrast patches can draw attention even when they have little relevance to the subject. Looking beyond the animal to the entire composition helps identify these distractions before they become difficult to correct.

Changing your shooting angle is often more effective than changing camera settings. Moving a few feet to the left or right may place the animal against a darker background, separate its outline from a tree, or remove an unrelated object from the frame. Lowering the camera can also change the relationship between the animal and the background, while a higher viewpoint may reveal patterns in the terrain or water.

Depth of field offers another way to manage competing elements. A wider aperture can soften a busy background while retaining enough environmental detail to establish the setting. However, excessive background blur can undermine the purpose of an environmental portrait. If the habitat is essential to the story, use a smaller aperture or adjust your distance to preserve more detail.

Sometimes, the best solution is simply to wait. Wildlife moves through its surroundings, and a small change in position can reveal a clearer view of the animal. A few seconds of patience may allow a bird to move beyond a distracting branch or a mammal to step into a patch of cleaner light.

There will also be situations where distractions are unavoidable. Dense vegetation and complex habitats are part of wildlife photography, and not every scene needs to be simplified into a perfectly clean composition. The key is to distinguish between details that create a sense of place and those that obscure the subject without adding useful context.

Light and weather can change how the habitat contributes to an environmental portrait. Clear conditions may reveal texture in the landscape, while fog, rain, snow, or mist can simplify the scene and create a stronger sense of atmosphere. Instead of treating these conditions as obstacles, consider how they shape the story.

Fog can reduce background detail, making it easier to isolate an animal while retaining the surrounding landscape’s presence. Snow can simplify a composition through broad areas of similar tone, allowing the subject’s shape and color to stand out. Rain can add texture and reflect light from the environment, while overcast skies often produce softer illumination that helps preserve detail across the animal and its surroundings.

The direction and quality of light matter, too. Side lighting can emphasize the texture of a rocky hillside, the structure of a forest, or the contours of an animal’s body. Backlighting can create a striking silhouette or highlight fine details in fur and feathers, though it can make exposure more challenging.

Pay attention to how light falls across the entire scene, not just on the animal. A brightly lit background may compete with a shadowed subject, while a patch of sunlight on the ground can become a distracting highlight. Waiting for the light to change or repositioning yourself may produce a more balanced image.

Weather can also add important behavioral and ecological context. An animal moving through fresh snow, feeding during a rainstorm, or navigating a misty shoreline can appear more connected to its environment than it would under neutral conditions. These details work best when they contribute to the story rather than simply making the photograph look dramatic.

Environmental wildlife portraits don’t require a specific lens. Wide-angle lenses can exaggerate the relationship between a nearby subject and its surroundings, but they generally require photographers to work closer to the animal to maintain its prominence. That isn’t always possible or appropriate, so a wider focal length should never come at the expense of the animal’s welfare.

Telephoto lenses can be equally effective. They let photographers maintain a respectful distance while still including distant landscape features in the composition. Longer focal lengths can also compress layers of habitat, making mountains, trees, or other background elements appear closer to the subject. This can create a different visual relationship than a wide-angle view, even when the same elements are present.

A post shared by Kate / Torva Terra (@torvaterra)

For environmental wildlife portraits, my lens of choice is a superzoom telephoto. The flexibility to quickly widen the frame to include more habitat, then zoom back in when the moment calls for a tighter composition, makes it easier to adapt without swapping lenses. This is especially useful with unpredictable wildlife, where even a small change in the animal’s position can affect the composition.

Another option is to use two camera bodies, one fitted with a 500mm or 600mm telephoto and the other with something like a 70-200mm lens. This setup lets you capture tighter portraits with one camera and wider environmental compositions with the other, so you can switch perspectives quickly without missing a moment.

Aperture should be chosen according to the amount of environmental detail you want to preserve. A wide aperture can help separate an animal from a busy background, while a smaller aperture can keep more of the habitat in focus. Be mindful of shutter speed when stopping down, especially in low light, and increase ISO when needed to keep a shutter speed appropriate for the animal’s movement.

Autofocus settings also deserve attention. Continuous autofocus and animal eye detection can help maintain focus as wildlife moves, but tracking systems may struggle when the subject is small in the frame or surrounded by complex vegetation. Check that the camera is focusing on the animal rather than a foreground branch, and be prepared to adjust your focus area when needed.

Ultimately, equipment should support the composition rather than dictate it. The right focal length, aperture, and autofocus settings are the ones that allow you to preserve the relationship between the animal and its habitat while capturing the moment effectively.

A post shared by Kate / Torva Terra (@torvaterra)

Environmental portraits are a valuable addition to a wildlife photographer’s portfolio, but they do not replace close-up images. Both approaches serve different purposes, and the strongest coverage of an animal or location may include a variety of compositions.

A close-up can reveal details of the animal’s expression, plumage, fur, or behavior that would be lost in a wider frame. An environmental portrait can provide the context those details lack, showing where the animal lives, how it moves through the landscape, or what conditions it faces. Together, the images can communicate a more complete story.

When framing a scene, consider what the photograph needs to convey. If the animal’s expression or a subtle behavior is the defining moment, a tighter composition may be the best choice. If the relationship between the animal and its surroundings matters more, giving the habitat room in the frame may create a stronger image.

Whenever possible, make deliberate variations in your composition without disturbing the animal. Photograph the scene wider, then consider whether a tighter frame offers a different perspective. You may discover that an environmental portrait captures the atmosphere of a moment, while a closer image reveals a detail that would otherwise go unnoticed.

The important thing is to avoid treating proximity as the ultimate measure of a successful wildlife photograph. A small animal in a carefully composed landscape can be as compelling as a tightly framed portrait, as long as the environment adds meaning and the subject remains visually important.

Environmental wildlife photography ultimately asks the photographer to look beyond the animal and consider the larger story unfolding around it. Research helps identify the details that matter, observation reveals how the animal interacts with its surroundings, and thoughtful composition determines what the viewer sees. When those elements work together, the habitat becomes more than a background. It becomes an essential part of the photograph.

#8999. Chris “Daze” Ellis "Orchid Rain on the Underground" @ PPOW Gallery, NYC

PPOW are pleased to present Orchid Rain on the Underground, Chris “Daze” Ellis’s third solo exhibition with the gallery. The show is on view through April 25, 2026. Featuring a new series of paintings, multimedia installation, and a site-specific mural, the exhibition harnesses the passion and spontaneity of the graffiti movement of the 1970s and 80s while demonstrating a thoughtful and meticulous practice honed over the past five decades. While the version of New York City that fostered Daze’s beginnings as a fine artist may feel like a bygone era, the works in this exhibition are evidence of its enduring legacy. By revitalizing that foundational energy for the present moment, Daze affirms the continued relevance of those figures and places, and their profound influence on the creative spirit that persists throughout the city today.

Born in Brooklyn in 1962, Daze became inspired by early graffiti writers like Blade, Lee Quiñones, and PHASE 2 while attending High School of Art and Design in the mid 1970s. As he began to establish his own name as an artist, he was also a frequent visitor to what would become historic landmarks of the city’s nightlife, including the Lit Lounge in the East Village, Danceteria on West 21st Street, and the Mudd Club in Tribeca. These nightclubs, which often doubled as art galleries and performance venues, functioned as generative sites of social and artistic experimentation and part of the driving force behind Daze’s early works. By the early 1980s, he had begun transitioning from tagging subway cars to developing a studio practice that encapsulates the ethos of the city.

Inspired by early 20th-century urban realist artists, including John Sloan of the Ashcan School and Reginald Marsh of the WPA era, Daze’s works honor New York City’s streets and subways as important sites of his creative evolution. Simultaneously influenced by the lyrical abstraction of works by Joan Mitchell and Willem De Kooning, Daze combines gestural swaths of acrylic and spray paint with detailed renderings of train car interiors, tunnels, and stations. In Gem Spa In the 80s, 2025, Daze depicts the now iconic newspaper stand and candy store that once operated on the corner of St. Mark’s Place and Second Avenue. Gem Spa was a central destination and meeting place for members of the city’s subcultures and is referenced by literary figures like Jack Kerouac and Allen Ginsberg (who called it a “nerve center” of the city). Important people from Daze’s life can be found throughout the composition, among them critic and curator Carlo McCormick as well as artist Martin Wong, who both emerge amongst the crowd in the painting’s foreground. In other works, technicolor throngs of flowers ascend from heaps of urban rubble, representing optimism amidst inequality and the beauty that can arise out of destruction. Throughout the exhibition, these varied combinations of tropical flora and local flowers from the artist’s home in upstate New York function as poignant memorials to what has been lost and hopeful testaments to the beauty and creativity that can still be found around every corner.

The exhibition will also include a site-specific mural, bringing an aspect of Daze’s practice often relegated to the outdoors into the interior setting of the gallery. Covering the walls of a hallway, the mural gives way to the final room of the gallery, featuring a multimedia installation that transports viewers into a composite scene from the artist’s youth. Combining a light-up dance floor and disco ball, actual subway car seats, and a curated track fusing house, disco, hip-hop, and club music, the installation emphasizes the freedom and creative inspiration that arose from these settings, and their importance to Daze’s personal and artistic development. Combining elements from throughout his career, Orchid Rain on the Underground showcases Daze’s never-ending exploration of daily life in New York City while paying homage to the people and places that comprise its vibrant cultural heartbeat.

#8998. Flokk's design-forward seating features on Dezeen Showroom

From distinctive task chairs to sprawling modular systems, the following seating has been released this year by Scandinavian furniture manufacturer Flokk‘s sub-brands.

The HÅG X Recouture Capisco task chair features the original HÅG Capisco task chair’s distinctive cruciform backrest, developed by designer Peter Opsvik and originally released by Flokk-owned ergonomic chair brand HÅG in 1984.

In the this version, created in collaboration with textiles brand Recouture, the rear side of the backrest is upholstered in traditional Norwegian vintage åkle textile, characterised by bright colours and scintillating patterns.

Users can select from various base colour and finish options, while the åkle material itself is vintage, meaning that each is one of a kind and is matched with a complementary block-coloured wool upholstery covering the seat.

Design studio Webb has created an flexible, snaking sofa system for Flokk-owned, UK-based furniture brand Connection.

Terrain modular seating comes in various colourways and module options, which can be reconfigured to facilitate relaxation and informal meetings in across lobbies, workplaces and education interiors.

#8997. Photographer Captures International Space Station and Jupiter in the Same Frame

Photographer Captures International Space Station and Jupiter in the Same Frame

A photographer captured a rare shot of the International Space Station (ISS) as it whizzed past Jupiter.

“This photograph had been on my radar for nearly two years, and this past Sunday, I finally brought it to life after driving over an hour north of Seattle to Burlington, Washington, just before sunrise,” AJ Smadi tells PetaPixel.

Remarkably, the ISS and Jupiter appear nearly identical in angular size, a coincidence caused by the fact that Jupiter was approximately 1.3 million times wider than the ISS, yet also 1.3 million times farther away at the moment of capture.

“Every month or so for the past couple years, I would check the ISS’s path across the sky and see if it would be close enough to any planets that I could align them from within Washington State,” Smadi says.

“At precisely 6:03 AM PDT, the International Space Station zipped directly past the gas giant Jupiter. After I carefully calculated the exact location from which to observe the transit, I managed to capture both objects in a single frame.”

“Within this photograph are seven human beings aboard the ISS (Jessica Watkins, Luke Delaney, Joshua Kutryk, Sergey Teteryatnikov, Pyotr Dubrov, Anil Menon, and Anna Kikina),” Smadi adds.

“Far beyond them lies a detailed view of Jupiter with its storms and belts, accompanied by all four Galilean moons: Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto.”

The photos of the ISS and Jupiter are part of an ongoing series Smadi calls “ISS Meets.” The astrophotographer has previously captured Venus and the orbital lab, as well as Saturn and Mars.

“As far as I’m aware, I have the only known ISS-Venus transits ever recorded, and have also captured it alongside Saturn and Mars,” Smadi says. “This week, I finally got the opportunity to photograph it with Jupiter.”

Aside from the distant planets of Uranus and Neptune, Mercury is the only planet left in the Solar System that Smadi hasn’t captured.

Smadi used a 9.25-inch Celestron Schmidt-Cassegrain Telescope that has a focal length of 2,350mm. The camera was a ZWO ASI662MC that uses Sony’s IMX662 sensor. He also used a UV/IR filter to block out ultraviolet and infrared light.

More of Smadi’s work can be found on his Instagram and Reddit.

#8994. Bart Simpson Could Have Been the Best Photographer of His Generation

Bart Simpson Could Have Been the Best Photographer of His Generation

Diane Arbus. Helmut Newton. Bruce Gilden. If the world was just, Bart Simpson would have been counted among them, all legendary photographic talents of the 20th century.

Sadly, unlike Arbus and Newton, Bart Simpson’s photographic career ended nearly as soon as it started, lasting but a single day.

As Dr. Eldon Tyrell from Bladerunner put it, yet another totally real person worthy of legitimate critical analysis: “The light that burns twice as bright burns half as long.” Truer words have rarely been spoken of one Bartholomew Jo-Jo “Bart” Simpson.

Armed with a dream, $1.99 in coins, and a mail-in flier for a “genuine spy camera,” Bart Simpson’s photographic career got off to an auspicious start. The brilliant artistic mind quickly unwrapped his tiny camera, which clearly takes sub-35mm format film, fired off a test shot, and got to work.

Many photographers require significant training and extensive practice to truly bring their vision to life. Not Bart Simpson. Within minutes, he had fired off two exquisite frames, capturing his subjects at their most vulnerable in stark black and white.

Simpson’s work is like a cross between Sally Mann, whose seminal 1992 series Immediate Family actually arrived after Simpson’s career ended (coincidence?), and Bruce Gilden.

Like many photographers before him, Simpson even turned his camera on himself. Self-portraiture is such a powerful way to flex creative muscles and truly explore oneself.

Although Simpson undoubtedly made his most influential photos pointing his camera toward his family, he, like many before him, dabbled in wildlife photography. Powerful. Poignant. The squirrel is like the artist himself, living under the thumb — or tire — of an unseen force, perhaps society itself. A remarkably mature voice from such a young photographer, and on his very first day with a camera, no less.

But that night, during a family dinner at The Rusty Barnacle, Bart Simpson truly made his mark on the art world.

After ducking away from his plate of squid tentacles, Simpson heard a ruckus in a private event area. True artists like him never shy away from danger, and Simpson cracked the door open, revealing a scene of debauchery, drama, and intrigue. Bart Simpson’s father, Homer, was dancing atop a table with a burlesque dancer, Princess Kashmir, dollar bills in hand.

Never one to leave home without a camera, long before the days of cell phones, Simpson whipped out his spy camera and fired off the single frame that would make him famous. Or infamous, depending on who you ask.

The following day, inside Springfield Elementary’s darkroom — yeah, schools used to have those — Simpson developed and printed his film. His peers in the Future Photographers of America club instantly recognized greatness.

“My goodness, quite exciting,” Martin Prince exclaimed.

“Extremely sensual,” another budding photographer added.

“The subtle gray tones recall the work of Helmut Newton,” said another.

“He brings to mind the later work of Diane Arbus,” a shrewd student remarked.

The club instantly wanted a print of his work, but Simpson, knowing his value, declined. At least for about 30 seconds, after which he made a single print for his best friend, Milhouse Van Houten.

Then, long before the concept of internet virality, Bart Simpson, a 10-year-old master photographer, went truly viral in Springfield.

One print quickly became a dozen, then hundreds. Bart Simpson not only lost his ability to monetize his masterpiece, but he quickly got his prized subject, his father, Homer Simpson, into very hot water at home.

Bart’s mother, Marge, saw the photo of her sleazy husband at her jazzercise class and promptly kicked him out of the household.

Presumably scarred by the experience and the immense power he had behind the lens, Bart Simpson hung up his camera for good. The world truly lost something that day.

It is impossible to know what type of photographic career Bart Simpson could have had. He was en route to live among the all-time greats. But alas, instead, for just one brief moment, Bart Simpson was the best photographer in Springfield. He used his camera to reveal the seedy underbelly of his family, and for that, he paid a steep price, capped his lens, and pivoted to skateboarding, baseball, and general tomfoolery.

#8993. F1 Photographer Has $30K Worth of Camera Gear Stolen at Mexico Grand Prix

F1 Photographer Has $30K Worth of Camera Gear Stolen at Mexico Grand Prix

A Formula 1 photographer covering the Mexico Grand Prix had “tens of thousands” of dollars worth of equipment stolen from him this weekend.

The Australian photographer, identified as Ryan, reportedly went to the media center on Wednesday before it was fully operational and, along with several other photographers, dropped his camera bag there before stepping out.

Fellow photographer and social media star Kym Illman says that when Ryan returned to the media center just five minutes later, he grabbed his bag and noticed it felt very light.

“Well indeed it was light because there was hardly any camera gear left in there,” Illman explains. “Initially, he thought his mates were playing a joke, but it turns out he was robbed of two cameras and a range of lenses worth tens of thousands of dollars.”

Security cameras at the media center captured two men who appeared to be installing wiring under the desks, but were actually rummaging through Ryan’s camera bag and stealing expensive cameras and lenses. Exterior cameras caught them sprinting away from the media center.

Ryan had two Canon R1s taken off him along with a range of lenses including a 100-300mm, 85mm, and a 14-35mm. Illman notes that the total loss was roughly $30,000.

A post shared by Kym Illman F1 (@kymillman)

The F1 Media Center is made available to accredited press at every circuit. Each event has a unique setup; photographers often get their own area that’s separate from written and visual media.

Illman notes that on Wednesday, tradespeople were still setting up the media center, and flooding had affected the press conference room, meaning there was plenty of work still going on.

All this activity gave the thieves the cover they needed to not arouse suspicion. Illman notes that it is a “painful reminder about equipment security” and says it’s not the first time thefts have happened at F1 races.

“At Le Castellet [Paul Ricard Circuit in France], two lockers were completely emptied on one occasion,” Illman writes on his blog. “A long lens was taken from the Hungaroring media center, and photographers have also had camera straps cut to steal their cameras.”

Illman adds that it is devastating for a photographer to discover that the gear they rely upon for their work has been stolen.

“After the theft [in Mexico], people were taking greater care to lock away laptops before leaving the room,” Illman says.

“The immediate change in Mexico was noticeable. Laptops were being put into lockers when their owners went out, and everyone was a little more alert. The practical lesson was not to assume that a familiar working environment made unattended equipment safe.”

#8992. The iPhone Camera Makes Fall Colors Look Better When There’s a Hand in the Frame

The iPhone Camera Makes Fall Colors Look Better When There’s a Hand in the Frame

Autumn is here, meaning the leaves are turning golden and falling to the ground. Many people can’t help but whip out their smartphones and take a photo.

However, the resulting image can sometimes be disappointing and one X user went viral this weekend after she pointed out that the “iPhone can’t handle anything colorful unless there’s a hand in the frame.”

Cherry (@mclIark) shared side-by-side photos of a wooded area covered in leaves. The before picture shows the green, brown, and yellow colors looking flat and washed out. But the second photo of the same scene, with Cherry’s outstretched hand, shows much warmer, inviting colors that are associated with fall.

iphone can’t handle anything colorful unless there’s a hand in the frame https://t.co/C8FVp17gko

PetaPixel attempted to recreate Cherry’s results. Finding some colorful foliage that was succumbing to the onset of winter, I held out my hand and watched the colors of the trees in the background become deeper and more saturated.

Beneath Cherry’s post, many people complained that the iPhone camera simply can’t recreate the colors of fall that they are seeing with their own eyes. So why is that?

It’s not clear which iPhone model Cherry is using, but I used the iPhone 16 base model, which doesn’t allow the user to pick the white balance, and herein lies the problem.

Most iPhone cameras rely on auto white balance (the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are the exception). White balance is a camera setting that adjusts the colors in a photograph to compensate for the color temperature of the light illuminating a scene.

The color temperature of light is measured in Kelvin (K). Virtually all modern cameras allow photographers to manually set the K value by selecting a specific temperature. Cameras also have the option of selecting preset white balance options; “Daylight,” for example, is roughly 5,500 K.

But since this is not possible on most iPhones, apart from the new 18, smartphone photographers are left at the mercy of Apple’s computational photography system, which many argue is focused on getting humans looking right, and less so landscapes.

It’s possible that the iPhone incorrectly interprets warm autumn light as an unwanted color cast and compensates by cooling the image. When a hand is introduced into the frame, it likely influences the camera’s color calculations, changing the white balance and making the foliage appear warmer.

Apple has previously discussed the issue of how ambient lighting can significantly alter the colors in photographs. While it’s great that it has introduced white balance controls to the iPhone 18, serious photographers know that setting the white balance correctly before shooting pictures leads to better results, and this can generally only be done with a real camera.

#8991. All-New Free Affinity App Brings Photo Editing, Sketching, and Vectors to iPad

All-New Free Affinity App Brings Photo Editing, Sketching, and Vectors to iPad

Canva has announced that popular and free photo editing, illustration, and vector app Affinity is coming to the iPad.

When Affinity was owned and operated solely by Serif, back before Canva bought Affinity in March 2024, Serif released multiple iPad apps. Affinity Designer, Affinity Photo, and Affinity Publisher all had separate, distinct iPad apps. However, while these older apps are compatible with the new Affinity app released last year, the old iPad apps have been languishing. They languish no longer.

The new Affinity app for iPad brings all the latest and greatest features from Affinity on desktop to Apple’s popular tablet, adding new tablet-friendly features that take full advantage of the Apple Pencil.

“Creative work doesn’t stay in one discipline, so your tools shouldn’t either,” says Duncan Clark, CEO of Pro Design at Canva. “Since we brought Affinity together on desktop, our biggest user request has been the desire to bring it to iPad. Today we’re delivering it: a fully-fledged, professional app built for touch.”

A key highlight is the brand-new Sketch Studio. This supports freehand drawing and promises to utilize artificial intelligence (AI) to simplify the sketch-to-vector workflow. It has new iPad-first features like a full-featured Mask Tool and Sketch to Shapes.

Affinity for iPad also includes robust photo editing features borrowed from the desktop, including RAW processing and editing, powerful selection tools, retouching, compositing, and more.

“Users can even sketch over a photo first to plan where a subject or prop should sit. The Mask Tool finds the boundary as the Apple Pencil pixel precision runs along a challenging edge, so hair, fur and foliage take a stroke rather than an afternoon,” Canva says. “Every mask, grade and retouch stays live and undoable, even thousands of layers deep.”

Photographers can use things like motion blur and noise reduction in real time directly on their photos and build complex, layered edits directly on their iPad.

Affinity for iPad offers powerful vector editing tools, a full layer-based workflow, layout tools, text editing, and more. It is a full-blown creative suite in a single iPad app.

A key part of bringing any app to iPad is ensuring its user interface and layout remain powerful without compromising the touch-first iPadOS interface. Not everything that works well on a Mac translates well to iPadOS. Canva describes the new Affinity for iPad as “built for touch, not shrunk to fit.” This means that the new interface is designed from the ground up for iPad but carefully arranged to be familiar to longtime Affinity users. The app also supports all major file types, per Canva.

The Apple Pencil Pro is a powerful companion, too. Affinity for iPad supports the Pencil Pro’s pressure, tilt, barrel roll, squeeze, and hover functionality.

“Affinity has built groundbreaking tools for iPad for almost a decade, and our community has shaped every step,” adds Clark. “This is the result of everything we’ve heard and learned, worked over until every gesture and panel felt right under the hand.”

“Affinity for iPad delivers the full power of Affinity, together with the versatility and portability of iPad,” says Affinity Head of Product Design, Neil Ladkin. “Every development decision was made by people who create on iPad themselves, from how the Apple Pencil responds to where the tools sit. If you’re the sort of person who rotates the canvas 40 times to get one line right, Affinity for iPad was made by people who’ve done exactly that.”

All of Affinity for iPad’s core functionality, including photo editing, sketching, vector, and layout tools, is free for individuals. Canva’s AI features, which are implemented in various ways across Affinity, require a Canva premium subscription.

The all-new Affinity for iPad is available now.

#8989. Norman Foster creates first-ever watch in collaboration with Lebond

British architect Norman Foster has unveiled his first watch, designed with watch brand Lebond in a process he said was “very similar to architecture.”

The mechanical watch has a sleek silhouette with an integrated strap. According to Foster, the design process began with a reevaluation of what we assume a watch should look like.

“We wanted to look again at something very familiar and reconsider it as a complete object, with the case, the strap, the dial and the movement all part of a system,” Foster told Dezeen.

“Normally, you have a watch case and then you attach a strap to it. We started to question the obvious. Why should they feel like two separate objects? Once we began thinking of the strap as a continuation of the case, the whole watch started to come together.”

As a result, the Lebond Norman Foster has a 38.5-millimetre-wide Grade 5 titanium case that widens to 40 millimetres where it connects to the integrated strap, creating a streamlined design.

The architect also got rid of the traditional watch lugs, wrapping the strap around the timepiece’s titanium case instead.

“Removing the conventional lugs gave us the continuous profile, but it also made the watch more comfortable and more integrated,” Foster explained.

The Lebond Norman Foster, with its distinctive rotor, also evokes aviation design – a reference to Foster’s interest in flying, as well as to his history of international travel.

This comes across in a very practical way, with the watch’s bidirectional rotating 12-hour bezel allowing the wearer to read a second time zone using the main hour hand.

Its dial is protected by a domed sapphire crystal with anti-reflective coating, and the watch is water-resistant to 50 metres.

It is currently available in two versions: the Natural Titanium Edition, which has a micro-sandblasted titanium case, a brushed-metal dial and a grey rubber strap, and the Black Edition, which features a matte black DLC-coated titanium case matched with a black lacquered dial and hands and a black rubber strap.

Foster designed the watch to allow people to customise it, swapping cases and straps at will, and more versions will be released over time.

“A watch is intensely personal. You wear it, you travel with it and it becomes part of your everyday life,” Foster said. “This led to the potential for a wide range of colour combinations and the ability to customise the watch”

“By designing an easy attachment mechanism, the user is able to interchange elements and create personal versions,” he continued.

“I proposed a watch that could move naturally between very different situations, working in the studio, being on a building site, travelling or going somewhere formal. It should not feel precious or limited to one particular setting.”

This marks the first time that Foster, who is known as the most successful architect in history, has designed a watch, but he didn’t find the process daunting.

“I have never really thought that scale changes the nature of design,” Foster said. “Whether it is a city, a building, a chair or a watch, you are still asking the same questions: how does it work, how is it made, and how do all the parts come together?”

“The process is also very similar to architecture,” he continued.

“It becomes one of refinement, sketches, prototypes, adjustments and then more adjustments. You explore options to finally arrive at the essential idea and then you keep refining it until everything seems inevitable.”

Last year, in celebration of Foster’s 90th birthday, we looked at twelve defining projects from his long career. Next month, the architect will give the keynote speech at the Dezeen Awards party.

#8988. Fujifilm Spending Over $63 Million to Quintuple Magnetic Tape Production

Fujifilm Spending Over $63 Million to Quintuple Magnetic Tape Production

Magnetic storage tape may seem like old hat in the age of massive, ultra-fast flash storage. However, magnetic storage tape is still a big deal in the archival data space, and archival data demands have only increased in recent years. What’s old is new again.

Photographers may know Fujifilm best for its popular digital cameras, Instax cameras, and photo film, but the company is also the world’s largest producer of magnetic storage tape, and it wants to grow even bigger.

As NewsShooter reports, Fujifilm has announced it intends to increase its production capacity for magnetic data storage tape by a whopping five times. To increase its already high market share, Fujifilm says it is spending about 10 billion yen ($63.367 million at current exchange rates) at its Kanagawa Factory in Odawara.

“The investment will strengthen Fujifilm’s stable supply system for magnetic tape in response to growing data archiving demand accompanying the spread of generative AI,” Fujifilm says. “This investment, to be made from fiscal 2026 through fiscal 2028, will be used to expand manufacturing facilities and increase personnel to strengthen the production structure.”

As Fujifilm explains, the “rapid spread of generative AI and cloud services” has significantly increased the amount of data. Companies have more data than ever, and they need to store it somehow.

Magnetic tape, although it may seem archaic, remains an exceptionally cost-effective and reliable way to store huge amounts of data for a very long time. Typical modern digital media is great and useful, but it inevitably fails, and often after not that many years. Data stored on magnetic tape, in contrast, lasts decades. It can also be isolated from networks, which is very important from a security standpoint, as Fujifilm says.

“In recent years, the use of magnetic tape has been expanding, particularly among major cloud service providers and data center operators,” Fujifilm notes. “Furthermore, given the sophistication of cyberattacks, magnetic tape is attracting increasing attention as a means of protecting data from threats such as ransomware.”

Fujifilm says it began researching magnetic tape in the 1950s, long before anything resembling modern computer infrastructure was a glimmer in anyone’s eye.

In 2000, Fujifilm launched LTO Ultrium1 data storage magnetic tape. Since then, the company has continued to invest significant resources into magnetic tape development and production.

In 2011, Fujifilm became the first company to commercialize Barrium Ferrite (BaFe) magnetic particles for use in magnetic tape.

Back in December 2020, Fujifilm introduced new magnetic storage tape that can store a whopping 580 terabytes of data, which is an absurd amount of data in a relatively small physical space.

Last year, the company introduced its latest-generation LTO Ultrium10 magnetic storage tape, which uses proprietary “fine hybrid magnetic particles” that combine BaFe and Strontium Ferrite (SrFe) magnetic particles.

“Through such technological innovation, Fujifilm has led advances in magnetic tape capacity and currently holds the top global share of the magnetic tape market,” Fujifilm says.

#8987. William N. Copley "X-Rated (1972–1974)" @ Galerie Max Hetzler, Berlin

Galerie Max Hetzler, Berlin, is pleased to announce X-Rated (1972–1974), a solo exhibition of paintings and works on paper by William N. Copley. This is the fourth presentation of the artist’s work at the gallery, and the show will be on view through April 22, 2026.

Copley came to painting from an unusual position. He had ambitions to become a writer before becoming a painter, and, for a brief period in the late 1940s, he co-founded and operated a gallery in Beverly Hills that focused on the Surrealists. The Copley Galleries – which he ran with his brother-in-law, the artist John Ployardt – brought him into close contact with exiled Surrealists such as Man Ray, Max Ernst and Marcel Duchamp, as well as the dealer Alexander Iolas, who encouraged him to pursue his nascent art practice. Adopting the signature CPLY around the time the gallery closed, he debuted his first exhibition at a bookstore in Los Angeles in 1951, shortly before he moved to France.Even though he was a generation younger than the Surrealists, Copley’s work is deeply informed by the movement on a conceptual and personal level. While his bold black outlines and self-taught figurative style recall comics and Pop art, Copley approached painting with a literary sensibility, using narrative strategies that both embodied Surrealist principles and drove the structural evolution of his compositions. Like many Surrealists, Copley embraced humour, psychology and eroticism as fundamental to his creative process, yet his engagement with overtly sexual subjects went far beyond the playful eroticism of his peers.On view in the exhibition are works from Copley’s prolific ‘X-Rated’ series, created between 1972 and 1975, and first exhibited in 1974 in an eponymous show at the New York Cultural Center. This body of work draws on erotic imagery and ritualised motifs from adult magazines, seeking, in the artist’s own words, to ‘break through the barrier of pornography into the area of joy.’ 1In a decade when the sale of hardcore pornography was still illegal in the United States, Copley would buy ‘adult magazines’ under the counter, using them as a source for inventive figurative and narrative paintings that explored eroticism, sexual politics and the pursuit of pleasure. The artist was able to convey a wide range of tone in the ‘X-Rated’ paintings: some, such as The Seven Year Itch, 1973, are tender; others, including  Viridiana, 1973, are exuberant; and almost all of them are openly humorous. Underscoring the open-endedness of sexual expression, Copley stated: ‘That’s what makes sex so much fun: since nobody really understands it, the possibilities for originality are endless.’ 2Copley typically produced two stages of preparatory drawings before starting a painting: an initial, small-scale study, followed by a larger version in which he refined the composition, introduced changes, and heightened the work’s pictorial dynamism. The resulting paintings maintain a deliberately slapdash style, with figures treated loosely rather than meticulously rendered. The exhibition makes this developmental process visible through multiple pairings of preparatory drawings and completed paintings, including Calcutta, 1973, and its counterpart Untitled, 1973.Scenes of copulations and orgies are set against vivid, brightly coloured backgrounds animated by bold, geometric patterns, making them almost ‘too artful to be libidinous, let alone lascivious’, as critic James R. Mellow has remarked. 3 It is both this treatment of the backgrounds and the contorted, entwined bodies with their attenuated limbs and schematic outlines that has prompted critics to draw a link between Copley and Henri Matisse more than once. Yet, while depictions of the nude and sexual imagery throughout art history have traditionally relied on suggestion and idealisation, Copley presents the sexual act directly, leaving nothing to the imagination.With titles borrowed from Hollywood movies such as Les Quatre Cent Coups, The Exorcist or Tobacco Road, Copley tempered the shock of the pornographic image through comic playfulness and pop cultural sensibility. Manifesting a Surrealist disjunction, the movies rarely align explicitly with the images’ content, but the titles nevertheless set in motion a cascade of associations for the viewer. The title of the series, likewise, draws on terminology from the film industry: until the 1990s, the film-classification term ‘X-rated’ was used in the US for films only suitable for adults. Despite the cautionary notices that some visitors might find the subject matter offensive, the 1974 exhibition at the Cultural Center – curated by the newly appointed and strikingly progressive director Mario Amaya – received a notably positive critical response. Art in America writer Peter Schjeldahl hailed the presentation as a ‘uniformly gorgeous exhibition,’ noting that it marked ‘a highly satisfying development in Copley’s work’. 4The ‘X-Rated’ series represents a singular chapter in Copley’s oeuvre, deliberately set apart from the prevailing currents of the early-1970s art scene. Even in today’s uncensored and image-saturated world, Copley’s suggestive canvases retain a subversive charge. By merging art and eroticism, Copley challenged conservative norms and rejected the notion of artistic neutrality, clearing away moralistic constraints in favour of directness and humour.

The $30,000 average wedding figure you see everywhere is misleading. That number is skewed upward by luxury weddings in expensive metros like New York, San Francisco, and Los Angeles. The national median — the number where half of weddings cost more and half cost less — sits closer to $10,000 to $15,000. That distinction matters because it means a beautiful, memorable wedding is absolutely possible without spending five figures you do not have.

The FI perspective adds another layer: every dollar spent on a wedding is a dollar that cannot compound for decades. A $30,000 wedding invested for 30 years at a 7% average annual return grows to roughly $228,000. That does not mean you should elope in a courthouse (unless you want to), but it does mean you should spend intentionally on the categories that matter most to you and cut ruthlessly everywhere else.

Here is where the typical wedding dollar goes:

The biggest takeaway from this table: venue and catering are 60-70% of the total. If you can reduce those two categories, you change the entire math.

Not all wedding spending creates equal memories. Research consistently shows that couples remember three things most vividly years later: the ceremony itself, the food and drinks, and the photographs. Almost nobody remembers the chair covers, the napkin folds, or the custom monogram on the cocktail napkins.

That insight creates a clear FI-aligned strategy: splurge on what creates lasting memories (photographer, food, music) and minimize everything else.

The golden rule of wedding budgeting: if you cannot remember whether a detail was present at the last three weddings you attended, your guests will not notice either. Cut it without guilt.

The biggest financial mistake couples make is not setting a firm budget before visiting any vendors. Venues and vendors are skilled at upselling, and without a hard number in mind, costs spiral quickly. Start with a number you can pay in cash — wedding debt is one of the worst ways to begin a marriage and a direct threat to your FI timeline.

Follow this payment timeline to manage cash flow without credit card debt:

A practical savings strategy: divide your total budget by the number of months until the wedding and automate that transfer to a dedicated savings account. If your budget is $15,000 and your wedding is 15 months away, that is $1,000 per month. Treat it like any other savings goal on your FI path — automate, do not touch, and watch it grow.

For couples on the FI path, consider this reframe: every dollar you shave from the wedding budget is a dollar that starts compounding immediately. Cutting $5,000 from a $20,000 wedding and investing that savings at 7% for 25 years creates roughly $27,000 in future wealth. You can have a wonderful wedding and build wealth simultaneously — but only if you plan intentionally from the start.
