Before finalizing your wedding budget, run the compound interest math on any amount you are considering spending. A $30,000 wedding invested at 7% for 30 years becomes roughly $228,000. A $15,000 wedding invested at 7% for 30 years becomes roughly $114,000. This is not an argument against celebrating — it is an argument for spending intentionally on what matters to you and cutting everything else. The couple who spends $15,000 on a joyful celebration and invests the other $15,000 gets both the wedding and a significant head start on financial independence.

There is no single right number, but the median US wedding cost of $10,000 to $15,000 is achievable for most couples without going into debt. Focus on what matters most to you and cut everything else. A $10,000 wedding with great food, a good photographer, and people you love is better than a $30,000 wedding that starts your marriage with financial stress.

No. Wedding debt is one of the worst forms of consumer debt because it funds a single day with no residual asset value. The average couple who finances their wedding on credit cards at 22% interest turns a $20,000 wedding into a $28,000 expense over 4 years of payments. Set a cash budget and stick to it.

Any contribution from parents is a gift, not an obligation. If parents offer to contribute, have an honest conversation about the total amount and whether it comes with expectations about the guest list or style. Budget based on what you can afford independently, then treat any parental contribution as a bonus.

Yes. Friday and Sunday weddings typically cost 20-30% less than Saturday weddings for the same venue and vendors. Some venues offer discounts of 40% or more for weekday weddings (Monday through Thursday). Off-season months like January, February, March, and November also offer significant savings.

Tips for vendors (plan 15-20% for catering staff, bartenders, and drivers), alterations for wedding attire ($200-$500), marriage license fees ($30-$100), and overtime charges if the reception runs past the contracted time. Build a 10% contingency buffer into your total budget for these surprises.

Set your budget privately as a couple before discussing with family. Present it as a decision, not a discussion. If family members want upgrades, they are welcome to fund those specific additions. Protect your financial foundation — the marriage matters more than the wedding, and starting debt-free sets up your partnership for success.

A meaningful wedding does not require $30,000 or any specific dollar amount. Set a cash budget based on what you can afford without debt, allocate spending toward what creates lasting memories (food, photography, people), and cut everything else. Every dollar you save on the wedding is a dollar that starts compounding toward your financial independence. The couples with the strongest financial futures are the ones who celebrate joyfully within their means and invest the difference.

#8985. KPF completes Texas's tallest skyscraper in Austin

Photography by Jason O'Rear (unless otherwise stated)

New York architecture studio KPF has completed Waterline in Austin, Texas, a supertall skyscraper with a mixed-use programme that slopes away from Lady Bird Lake as it rises. It has a form that resembles a “cowboy boot”, according to its designers.

KPF, which is known for its skyscrapers around the world, was not originally meant to design the 1,025-foot-tall (312-metre-tall) structure.

The building’s original developer was the coworking real estate company WeWork, which selected a design by its collaborator, architecture studio BIG, through a competition.

However, after WeWork’s failed IPO in 2019 and governance scandals, KPF was brought back in to take up the mantle on the project, which had already begun its early construction.

KPF president James von Klemperer told Dezeen that the concept of a “we-building” or a mixed-use building with overlapping functions remained part of the DNA of the building as the project was awarded to KPF by its new development team.

“Space isn’t as proprietary,” said von Klemperer of the project and concept. “No, it weaves together with other things, and with the spaces that are shared at the rooftop of the base of the building.”

The structure features hotel and office programmes at the bottom, with luxury residences at the top. Double-height exterior floorplates supported by massive columns mark changes in the programme from the exterior, and the whole building slopes up and away from Lady Bird Lake, a wide section of the Colorado River that flows through Austin.

Deference to the waterway was one of the main goals of the project, as were nods to the regional heritage, and a desire not to “strangle” the low-lying historic Rainey District to the southeast of the site.

It was originally supposed to be multiple towers, but the studio decided that shoring its density into a single tower allowed for these goals to be achieved.

“The project grew into the design, if you will, the way it inclines down like a cowboy boot at the base,” said von Klemperer

“It inflects towards Lady Bird Lake, and I think that was a powerful profile in everybody’s estimation, because it says something about a vertical structure becoming a piece of landscape or geology.”

Von Klemperer also contrasted the skyscraper, with its wide-grid facade and columns, with black-glass skyscrapers with wide bodies that block urban view corridors, referencing recent skyscraper construction in New York.

It’s not often or always that a tall building is also seen as a kind of supple building that is good for the community.

“It’s not often or always that a tall building is also seen as a kind of supple building that is good for the community,” he said, adding that Waterline’s facade, which features rust-coloured details to reference Texas geology, is “lacy” and full of moments “where your eye can see through or see some depth or see pattern”.

“We hoped to make a beautiful little piece of waterway facade.”

Working closely with landscape architecture studio TBG Partners, the structure steps up from the creek, with massive columns meeting the ground plane.

These columns form what von Klemperer compared to an amphitheatre of sorts, adding “urban drama”.

“Cities should have places that support urban drama, and I think already this has shown it really works,” he said.

At the centre of the structure’s stepped podium is a paseo from the city to the water that is lined with stone and makes the lower part of the structure, mostly retail and parking, more porous.

On top of the podium, amenity spaces serve the 1 Hotel, which is taking over the middle part of the programme.

The columns at the base and at the breaks were designed with oak trees in mind.

The studio included some V-shaped columns to add to this character, but also to structurally aid the building as the floorplates changed to accommodate the programme shifts.

“From an office grid to the residential grid, those misalignments along the perimeter were actually beneficial for getting a better column placement in the residential above,” said KPF design director Andrew Klare.

At the top of the building is a sky lounge, and the bulkhead has a slight angle that echoes the slope of the skyscraper.

Von Klemperer said both the shifts in the facade and the tilted top of the skyscraper were subtle nods to the city’s slogan – Keep Austin Weird.

“It’s not an exceedingly weird gesture that interrupts the skyline, but it’s a bit of whimsy, which is in character with the rest of the skyscraper’s geometries,” he said. “It destabilises the conventional grid of the world.”

The mixed-use programme also came to pass during the Covid-19 pandemic, which was a period of doubt in the feasibility of downtown cores.

This didn’t stop the project, but intensified the studio’s desire to create an open building with multiple uses and to “multiply” the uses of the podium.

“It restores your faith in the urban agenda of development – to make such a mixed-use project with levels of shared use throughout,” said von Klemperer.

Other recent skyscrapers by KPF include a “beaux-arts” supertall in New York that is nearing completion and a pair of skyscrapers in Istanbul.

#8984. Experimenting with Infrared Photography

Some of you who saw my star timelapse video might’ve clocked me using a GFX 100 II IR, specifically modified to pick up infrared light frequencies, and since I had it for a few more days, I decided to take it on the road. I happened to be passing through Denver, so I drove over to Golden Gate Park to capture some beautiful fall colors on the aspens, plus a neighborhood photo walk in my hometown of Portland.

Heads up: I know practically zero about infrared photography, so this project is the first installment of many into the world of infrared photography.

On top of photographing the scenery with the bare IR sensor (which picks up a full visible spectrum plus adds IR into the mix), I wanted to put a range of filters in front of it to see how they’d react. Maybe they’d make a difference, maybe not, but I brought a pile to find out.

We started with a K&F Concept Circular Polarizer, then a K&F Concept UV MRC for a bit of UV blocking to see if it shifted the colors. Then some more interesting ones: an ICE IR/UV cut, which should be intriguing because cutting IR might turn this into a regular spectrum camera, a K&F Concept Light Pollution Reduction filter, a Hoya StarScape, and finally a batch of fun color filters just to see how they’d look: orange, green, blue, red, purple, and yellow.

I should add that, as soon as I got home, I did more research and realized I’d probably missed a key component: a true IR pass filter. So I went to Pro Photo Supply in Portland and picked up one from URTH. I did some additional photography downtown in the Pearl District and around my neighborhood, capturing shots with the filter on and off to see whether it really made a difference.

As usual, let’s lock down as many variables as possible so we can judge color and exposure accurately. The plan was to fix the white balance at one point, and keep it on aperture-priority to respond to the environment while holding EV0 throughout, and keep a low ISO when possible. Most of these comparisons I captured on a tripod, but a lot of the later ones without all the different filters were handheld and on-the-fly.

The tricky part with this camera is that when you first turn it on, everything has a wild red tint. The best practice I heard is to point it at foliage, ideally bright green, and balance to that. Balancing to the green makes the image read less red and more neutral or monochrome, and that’s when colors start to pop out instead of everything drowning in red. It also helps the yellow leaves stand out more.

Back at the computer, I lined up all the Colorado frames side-by-side, to see the difference between them. The bare IR sensor images look quite interesting right off the bat. The green needles in the back read gray because we balanced to the green, and you get this cool pop off the yellow. The UV cut and light pollution filters looked fairly similar to each other, and the circular polarizer didn’t seem like it affected the colors or tone, as expected. The most interesting of the initial bunch was the ICE UV/IR cut filter. It gives the colors more pop and, by reducing the infrared, starts turning the needles and foliage green again, pulling away from our balance and looking more like a normal photo.

Then I rebalanced everything. Luckily with Capture One, it can drop manual color temperature all the way to 800K, which is around what others recommend for WB. Adobe only goes down to 2000K manual adjustment, so it would require extra profiles to drop below that extra CT floor. With some clouds around but a white aspen in frame, I used that tree as the focal point and eyedropped a white balance off it for every image. Rebalanced, some of the color filters showed a stark difference. The bare sensor became the baseline: yellow still popping, back branches muted, aspen white. The UV cut versions stayed close to that with only slight shifts in the greens, while the IR cut filter kept the greenery visible and let the yellow pop more, much like a regular photo.

During my IR research, I kept seeing links to photographer Rob Shea, whose tutorials are excellent. The basic concept, as I understand it: balance your white to actual white in frame, or to the foliage, go into levels adjustment and trim each channel so there’s no dead space on the input, then control the output channel by channel. After that, you invert the blues and reds. Capture One can’t do that swap, so the files go into Photoshop, where you pull the red out and add blue to the red channel, then flip the blue to carry only red and zero blue. The idea is that the sky reads as a normal blue while the foliage pops out red and warm.

Since the Colorado shots weren’t captured with the IR pass filter, I wasn’t sure what I’d get. Flipping the channels gave a genuinely wild result. On the IR cut image, which already looked close to a normal photo, the flip turned it stark and intense; the closer a shot was to the visible spectrum, the wackier it looked inverted. The warm filter shots, the reds and oranges, came out closer to what I’d imagine infrared looking like, with the trees in the back really popping once I dialed up the contrast.

The IR pass shots were the fascinating ones – I captured each photo with and without the filter. I had balanced the WB with the filter on by pointing at a green bush to make it read neutral, though it still came out quite warm. In one example, a car turns a completely different color while the grass around it pops. In another, trees with a mix of yellow, green, red, and orange leaves become more uniform under the filter but pop harder against the surroundings, especially the sky.

Running those through the channel flip was where it clicked. I love how certain colors change dramatically under the process while others stay put. Balanced to the greenery and changing leaves, those areas hold their tone while everything around them shifts. Pushed to black and white, I think this is where infrared really shows its strength, because the eye gravitates straight to the bright leaves.

I grabbed one quick shot off a bridge while driving (don’t do that at home, but it looked too good to pass up), balanced to the white of the bridge, and the flip gave a subtle two-tone look with the trees and windows popping gently. A lot of these images settle into that halftone, two-tone feel.

I kept learning as I edited this, and I definitely should have had the IR pass filter the whole time in Colorado, but you live and you learn. The results were not at all what I expected, which is exactly what makes it interesting to see how differently a camera can perceive the world than our own eyes do. To sum up the look: the infrared sensor alone gets you cool, unique images. The full spectrum with IR added gets you something stranger still. But if you want the starkest, strongest look, put an IR pass filter on a camera like this and it gets genuinely wild. If I hang onto this camera a little longer, I’ve got more experiments planned. Stay tuned.

#8983. An Interview with Surreal Salon 18 Winner, River Reishi

We are so excited to share our interview with Surreal Salon 18 winner, River Reishi, selected by guest juror, Swoon. On the occasion of the win, we spoke with Reishi about the work in the show, the history of Surreal Salon, and her upcoming travels.

Juxtapoz: Congrats on the big win! Talk about the winning work, what the story behind it is, the process, and even the process of submitting it to the Surreal Salon?River Reishi: The piece is called Surface Tension. It shows a figure emerging from dark water, her hands reaching forward as if she is about to break through the surface and step into our world. She is half submerged, suspended in that strange moment between two realms. Around her is an ephemeral field of black sand and amber.

From land, the surface of water looks smooth and transparent, almost empty. But of course it hides an entire world that is not ours. I have always been fascinated by that threshold. The installation tries to hold that exact moment where the two worlds meet.

The sculpture also glows faintly from within, which was a little hard to see in the bright gallery lighting but becomes visible as you approach. I like that quiet surprise. The piece looks still at first, but there is a sense that something is about to happen. Water is often a symbol of life, but it also carries danger and power. Louisiana and the Gulf region know that reality very well. I think some of that tension found its way into the work.

The black sand surrounding the sculpture is loose and hand-drawn into patterns, so the installation only exists in that form for a short time. Even small vibrations change it. I am interested in that fragility, in works that cannot quite stay fixed.

It was already an honor to be included in a show curated by Caledonia Curry (Swoon). When I arrived to install the piece and saw the other works for the first time, I remember thinking how haunting and memorable every single one was. So hearing the piece announced as Best in Show later that night felt surreal in the truest sense.

Had you followed the Surreal Salon in past years? What did you know about it? I had heard about the Surreal Salon through the pop surrealist art community for years, but this was the first time I lived close enough to attend in person. I kept hearing that it felt a little like an unofficial kickoff to Mardi Gras season, that people came in elaborate costumes and that the whole evening had this celebratory, slightly otherworldly atmosphere.

What I did not realize until participating this year was that some people actually design their costumes based on the artwork in the exhibition. That was amazing to see. At one point someone came up to me wearing a costume inspired by my piece, and getting to watch him model it and explain how the sculpture influenced the design completely made my night. It felt like the work had briefly stepped out of the gallery and into the room!

Also, it was a wonderful addition to have SWOON be the juror for this year's contest. I have done it in the past, and it was hard, fulfilling work. What did you know of SWOON's work and did that inform your submission at all? I have admired Swoon’s work for a long time, especially her installations and the way she moves between sculpture, architecture, and public intervention. I first heard about her in 2009 when she brought the Swimming Cities of Serenissima project to the Venice Biennale. A fleet of sculptural rafts floating into one of the most formalized spaces in the art world was such an unforgettable gesture.

The act of arriving that way, without waiting for institutional permission, became part of the artwork itself. That kind of boldness has always stayed with me. It is difficult to break into the art world, especially in spaces where voice is carefully selected and curated. Seeing an artist carve out space for herself so creatively was incredibly inspiring.

I also love the direction her work has been taking recently with the Sibylant Sisters project. My own work is deeply inspired by myth and storytelling, so it has been fascinating to watch her develop that world, creating her own oracle cards and building a living mythology around the work. There is something powerful about artists inventing symbolic languages that people can enter into. So having the chance to meet her and have her encounter one of my installations was a very meaningful moment for me.

You work in a few different mediums, and sculpture and installation seem to be your focus. Talk a little bit about your process and where you feel most comfortable as a maker? I am not sure I feel comfortable in any single medium, and I think that is probably a good thing. I tend to move toward whatever material feels necessary for the idea at hand. In many ways my practice grew out of practical constraints. For a long time I did not have a large studio, so I had to find ways of making work that could expand into a space temporarily and then disappear again. Sand, modular sculptural elements, and ephemeral materials all emerged from that reality.

Over time those limitations became part of the language of the work itself. I am drawn to materials that hold a sense of fragility and transformation. Installation allows me to build an environment around the sculpture where those ideas can unfold more fully, where the viewer is not just looking at an object but stepping into a moment or a story.

What sort of artists influenced you as you began to find your own voice? And, sort of as a nice anecdote, what is the last work that made you stop in your tracks and get back into the studio and create?

Voice is an interesting concept to me as a woman, because women often face particular obstacles when it comes to the emergence of voice. It takes a certain measure of audacity to say something and commit it to art. In a way you are asking the world to listen. Because of that, I am especially inspired by women who make art without asking permission.

I mentioned earlier how powerful it was for me to learn about Swoon bringing her Swimming Cities project to the Venice Biennale. That gesture has always stayed with me, not only because of the work itself but because of the confidence behind it. The willingness to claim space in a world that does not always easily offer it. Moments like that remind me that voice is not only about what you say as an artist, but about allowing yourself to say it at all. That idea continues to shape the way I approach my own work.

As for the last artwork that made me stop in my tracks, I recently visited the Museo Nacional de Antropología in Mexico City. Walking through the galleries of figurative ceramics from different regions of Mexico was completely mesmerizing. The Mayan ceramics in particular took my breath away. There is so much spirit in them, such a sense of presence. I encountered one ceramic face that affected me deeply. I have gone back to see it several times now, and each time I leave feeling more inspired to return to sculpture.

What else do you have lined up this year? Are you someone who likes to work in a gallery situation, or do you prefer alternative means to show your work? This summer I will be working with Raf Gallery in Reykjavik, Iceland during the month of August. A total solar eclipse will pass directly over Reykjavik on August 12, and later that month the city celebrates Menningarnótt, a large citywide festival of arts and culture.

Raf Gallery works with both artwork and Baltic amber jewelry, and I have always been drawn to amber as both a material and a mythological object. For the exhibition I will be installing sculpture and a sand installation that tells the myth of the birth of Baltic amber while also reflecting on eclipse mythology and the relationship between darkness and light.

The sand will come from the local shoreline, and at the end of the exhibition I invite the community to dismantle the installation with me. We carry the sand back to the ocean and return it with a wish, prayer, or intention.

I love Iceland deeply. The black sand I often use in my installations was inspired by the volcanic beach at Reynisfjara, so being able to create work there during such a rare celestial moment feels very meaningful.

As for where I like to show my work, I enjoy many different contexts. My installations have appeared in galleries, museums, empty storefronts, and even city halls. But my favorite place for ephemeral work is the beach.

When I lived near the sea in Washington State, friends and I would sometimes build temporary altars from flowers, driftwood, shells, and plants as offerings to the water. The tide would slowly carry everything away. There is something very special about building something together that only exists for that one night.

What did you like about the whole Surreal Salon experience? What were some of the highlights?The whole evening had an incredible energy. The costumes alone were extraordinary, and everywhere you looked there was another small moment of creativity unfolding. Music, conversation, artists reconnecting, people discovering work for the first time. It felt celebratory in the best way.

There was also an unexpected moment early in the night. Someone accidentally backed into the platform holding my installation, and when the platform shifted the sand vibrated and many of the detailed designs disappeared. Thankfully the person who tripped was completely fine, which was the most important thing. But in a strange way the moment also revealed something essential about the work. Some people had assumed the sand had been glued down or painted in place. When it shifted, it suddenly became clear that the entire surface was loose and hand-drawn. I sat beside the piece and carefully repaired it, re-drawing the patterns into the sand and amber while people watched.

For me that moment captured the spirit of the work. The installation only existed in that exact form on that particular night. It could be recreated, but it would never be exactly the same again. Everyone there was witnessing something temporary, something that belonged only to that moment in time. And in a way that felt very fitting for the Surreal Salon itself.River Reishi is a multidisciplinary artist whose sculptures and ephemeral sand installations explore myth, grief, and the mysterious threshold between worlds. Drawing on feminine water deities and ancient storytelling traditions, she works with materials such as sand, amber, and light to create environments that exist only briefly in time.See more at riverreishi.com and on Instagram @riverreishi.

#8981. Hybrid events help turn up Art Week Tokyo’s buzz

Works on show will include Chen Wei’s Trouble City #250504 (2025) Courtesy of Chen Wei and Blindspot Gallery; © Chen Wei; Photo: South Ho Siu Nam

A sure sign of an event’s arrival in the international art calendar is the number of collateral programmes it attracts. This year is a watershed for Art Week Tokyo in that regard, with multiple partners set to amplify the city’s November buzz.

Leading the way is a new project by the founders of the alternative art fair Basel Social Club. Tokyo Jazz Club, which takes place from 1 to 8 November in a former capsule hotel in the Jimbocho neighbourhood, will combine contemporary art, performance, music and food to create a hybrid space between an immersive exhibition, a social environment and a reimagined marketplace. According to co-founders Robbie Fitzpatrick and Yael Salomonowitz, the event is inspired by the history of jazz culture in Japan. “Jazz offers us a mode of thinking—a language of improvisation, listening and collective presence,” says Salomonowitz.

Tokyo Jazz Club will take place in a former capsule hotel in the Jimbocho neighbourhood of Tokyo Courtesy Tokyo Jazz Club

Also exploring notions of hybrid space is Project O+O: Gabriel Orozco at Higashi-Yama Tokyo. Orozco is collaborating with designer Shinichiro Ogata to turn a restaurant into an extension of his home from 6 to 29 November. Billed as a “living exhibition where artworks, specially designed objects and culinary experiences converge”, the project is co-presented by Mexico City’s Kurimanzutto and Tokyo-based producer Jam Acuzar.

Meanwhile, Serakai Studio, backer of the new Hong Kong cultural space Gold, is hosting a durational performance and installation by Taiwanese artist Liang-Jung Chen (4-5 November) as part of Certainly Tokyo, its pop-up exhibition at Path Omotesando.

These events reflect the global scope of Tokyo’s creative scene. Not to be outdone, homegrown media art and VJ duo MES is curating a lineup of DJs and performers for AWT x Shibuya Parco Art Night on 4 November.

#8980. Tiny Leica Half-Frame Camera Among Rare Items Up for Auction

Tiny Leica Half-Frame Camera Among Rare Items Up for Auction

Sebastião Salgado’s Leica R6 camera is among some of the rare cameras that are for sale in the 49th edition of the Leitz Photographica Auction.

Also on offer is an exceptionally rare Leica Box camera from the 1950s and a re-edition of the Elcan 66mm f/2 lens.

More than 400 lots will be offered at Leitz Photographica Auction 49. While Leica cameras, lenses and equipment make up the majority of the lots, numerous items from other renowned manufacturers will be offered as well. Estimates range from the three-figure to the six-figure euro range.

A rare half-frame Leica Box prototype dating back to the mid-1950s is expected to be one of the auction’s biggest attractions. Designed to shoot 18 × 24mm images, the remarkably compact camera measures just 100 × 64 × 48 millimeters, making it one of the smallest Leicas ever produced.

Only two examples were made. One is on display at the Leica Museum in Wetzlar as a non-functioning design study, while the other, bearing serial number 000.01, is fully operational and now heading to auction. The rare camera is estimated to fetch between €400,000 and €500,000 ($450,000 to $560,000).

One of the standout lots is a Leica R6 once owned by renowned Magnum photographer Sebastião Salgado (1944–2025).

Salgado used the camera to document the burning oil fields of Kuwait during the Gulf War, a series of images that helped establish his international reputation. The lot also includes two photographs from the series and a signed copy of his limited-edition photobook Workers.

The camera and accompanying items are estimated to sell for between €28,000 and €32,000 ($31,000 to $36,000).

The auction will also feature a rare Leica lens with an unusual military history. The Elcan 66mm f/2 was developed by Dr. Walter Mandler at Ernst Leitz Canada on commission for the US Navy. According to Mandler, the Navy’s intelligence service wanted a lens that “looked like any other but delivered an unparalleled level of resolution.”

Just 200 examples of the Elcan 66 were produced in the late 1960s, making it one of the rarest lenses ever made for the Leica M system. Earlier this year, Leica released a limited-edition reissue, the Summicron-M 66 f/2, with production capped at 660 units. The example heading to auction bears the particularly collectible serial number 001 and carries an estimate of €16,000 to €20,000 ($18,000 to $22,000).

Bidding is open now and will close on November 29. Information on the lots and details of the bidding process are available at www.leitz-auction.com.

#8978. Kohei Yamada: MY SCREEN TESTS @ Gr Gallery, New York (UPDATED with Installation Imagery)

GR gallery is pleased to present My Screen Tests, the first New York City solo exhibition by Kohei Yamada. The exhibition examines the enduring value of the authentic relationship between artist and artwork, engaging in themes of irony, introspection, and visual metaphor, which draw inspiration from contemporary practice and Yamada’s nuanced admiration for American Pop art.

Presenting a new suite of paintings on canvas -each paired with its esquisse on paper- In My Screen Tests, Yamada searches within New York City’s identity as the art capital of the world in order to infuse his work with a distinct vitality, revealing his admiration for Andy Warhol through motifs referencing the Silver Factory era and its entourage, and evoking tension between a sense of historical prestige and vibrant pop expressions. This interplay initiates a critical conversation between perceptions of art and is worthwhile in examining the creative directions of today’s world.

My Screen Tests is defined by motivations that comment on the ambiguous nature of art’s true value beyond its creator, while also alluding to Yamada’s need to remain bound to art for the rest of his life. The work also critiques the world’s normalization of deceit and capitalistic greed, alongside a persistent

longing for freedom that remains just out of reach. New York City lies at the core of Yamada’s practice, serving as both subject and catalyst for exploring the interplay between personal perception and nostalgia. It also functions as a cultural bridge between American and Japanese influences, tracing the artist’s journey from childhood through his engagement with the legacy of Andy Warhol, as well as other Japanese and American artists. Through a combination of brushwork, abstraction, and figuration, Yamada weaves a narrative rich in contemporary art history, while also confronting the true value of an artist’s existence.

Over half of the works exclusively made for My Screen Tests are imbued with references inspired by Warhol’s practice and artistic values, cast against New York City as a hub for experimentation where art meets and even challenges commerce. Repetition and humor are also at the core of the artist’s creative process, adding a wittiness and discipline to his work, while also connecting it on a deeper level to the Pop tradition. Yamada draws upon the city as both muse and stage, invoking a range of artistic influences as main characters, while ultimately revealing each to be a projection of his own identity.

The opening reception will take place on Friday, May 15 from 6:00 pm to 8:00 pm. The artist will participate in the opening reception.

#8977. C Next Designers EMEA brings together over 250 professionals for design conference in Almería

For the ninth edition of the C Next Designers design conference, Spanish brand Cosentino brought together designers from Europe, Africa and the Middle East for three days of talks focused on “design as a driver of change”.

The event was held from 13 to 16 October in venues across Almería, Spain and included talks by designers such as Ron Arad, Karim Rashid and design studio Studiopepe.

It is the fourth iteration of the event held in Spain and the ninth worldwide.

This year’s conference focused on the theme Design to Transform, which champions “design as a force capable of reshaping society and adding value to it”, according to the team.

The first day opened with a welcome at the Cabo Gata Beach Hotel.

On Wednesday, the event moved to Cosentino’s industrial park in Cantoria, where Cosentino CEO Pilar Cosentino gave opening remarks.

Architect and designer Ron Arad then spoke with Cosentino commercial director for Europe, Jorge Lope about his career and collaborations with the brand, before the day ended with a guided tour of Cosentino’s facilities, including a local natural stone warehouse.

The day also featured the presentation of the latest product innovations by Valentín Tijeras, global vice president of product.

The second day took place at the Almería Science and Technology Park (PITA) and included presentations by brands Novara, Jung, Speho, TECE and Gaggenau.

Karim Rashid and Studiopepe then gave keynote speeches, which were a highlight of the day.

Dezeen editorial director (special projects) Max Fraser also moderated two panels as part of the event.

The first, held with Dornbracht, focused on hyper-personalisation as a creative tool and featured C’est Ici Design founder Monica Arango, founder of Black Architecture Danko Lekic and head of global channel management at Dornbracht Sascha Bialoian.

The second panel examined how design is changing our everyday habits, and featured Fran Silvestre Arquitectos founder Fran Silvestre, ZHA associate director Bidisha Sinha and founder of AS Architect Ayşin Sevgi Karakurt Macit.

Studio Haus closed the panels, and the event concluded with a gala dinner in the Cloister of Almería Cathedral, which was informed by the Dekton Artik Nodes collection, a new Cosentino material.

Cosentino previously launched Nara, a beige-toned porcelain surface designed to celebrate natural stone and Éclos, which was designed to be free of crystalline silica.

Last year’s C Next Designers conference featured talks by Sabine Marcelis and Peter Ippolito or Nini Andrade Silva.

To learn more about C Next Designers, visit the conference’s website.

Succeeding a New Meta classic, Dunu’s latest begs the question: is less sub-bass ever a good idea?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Earphone manufacturer Dunu has just released the DaVinci Vitruvian, a follow-up to one of the most talked-about in-ear monitors (IEMs) of recent years. For the same price as the original ($299.99), it promises a cleaner, more balanced take on the DaVinci sound, and I for one am excited to hear it.

The DaVinci was one of the early high-profile IEMs associated with the JM-1 target and the “New Meta” tuning trend. In terms a normal human can understand, that means a broadly balanced sound, with a generous dollop of extra bass and a relatively relaxed treble. In practice, many people loved its warm, full-bodied sound, but others found the bass overdone and the treble a little too subdued. Still, some of the best representatives of this sound are featured on my list of the best IEMs under $500 for a reason. You'll also find them on my list of the best budget IEMs too.

On paper, the Vitruvian looks like Dunu’s answer to those critics, and suggests the brand is moving in the same direction as much of the industry: towards a more natural, neutral sound. Let's dig into what we can expect...

Interestingly, Vitruvian started life as the DaVinci 2, and the first prototype essentially turned everything up: the same big bass, extra treble drivers and even a bone-conduction driver.

But then, in response to feedback at the Shenzhen International Audio Show, the brand changed tack. Consequently, it reduced the bass, boosted vocal clarity and dropped the bone-conduction driver.

The new name – inspired by Leonardo da Vinci's Vitruvian Man; a naked male figure in two overlapping poses – reflects that shift towards balance. The design pairs two dynamic drivers, one for deep sub-bass and one for bass, with five balanced armatures handling mids and treble.

That’s one more than the DaVinci, and Dunu says the extra treble driver brings smooth, open highs with more air and no harshness. It also promises the bass hits harder and faster than before, even though there’s less of it.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

In the box, you get a modular cable with swappable 3.5mm and 4.4mm plugs and 13 pairs of ear tips. The earpieces themselves sport vintage-inspired faceplates with precision gear details.

For years, the Harman target, with its boosted bass and bright upper mids, has shaped how most headphones and IEMs sound. Lately, though, brands seem to be going for something more natural.

Sennheiser’s HD 480 Pro is a great example. In our review, we called them the best closed-back headphones we’ve heard due to their neutral, balanced sound, with just a touch of bass warmth. As for IEMs, the CrinEar Reference tops our guide to the best IEMs under $500 thanks to its balanced tuning.

The Vitruvian probably won't go that far: Dunu talks up its “enveloping warmth” and “deep bass presence”, making it sound more like a nudge towards neutral than a leap. That said, for anyone who found the DaVinci’s low end overwhelming, that nudge could make all the difference.

To no one's surprise, Samsung is throwing shade at Apple again in a new Instagram post, this time targeting the iPhone Duo. Showcasing the slick build and, ahem, notably crack-free durability of its Z Fold models, the subtly shady ad playfully roasts the competition.

Apple and Samsung have been at war for what seems like an eternity, resulting in some of the best adverts of all time. While brand beef can, at times, be a little overplayed, Samsung's latest ad demonstrates how it can be used to create a welcome bit of buzz for both brands.

#8974. Five exhibitions to see during Art Week Tokyo

Utanhole’s Plug in Baby (2025). Her paintings and drawings often use soft, pastel colours to depict scenes of violence and chaos © 2026 Utanhole, courtesy the artist and Kaikai Kiki Gallery

Rising Japanese artist Utanhole creates dreamlike, pastel-hued paintings that blend cinematic suspense with manga-style precision. Born in 2001, she graduated from the Tokyo University of the Arts in 2025. She characterises her signature style as “soft violence”, a thematic concept defined by intense emotional and visual contrasts. Utanhole’s paintings depict calm young figures with soft colours, delicate forms and innocent faces set against chaotic scenes of collapsing cities, weapon-laden spaces and deadly explosions, highlighting the stark contrast between innocence and chaos. Her work draws on chūnibyō, a Japanese term for intense, dark adolescent fantasies. Rather than shocking, the Tokyo-based artist’s solo gallery debut features new large-scale paintings and a selection of drawings that explore the inner coping strategies and desires characteristic of contemporary youth culture.

A performance of Akane Saijo’s Double Touch (2025), which will be shown at the Tokyo Opera City Art Gallery Photo: Takeru Koroda

Exploring how city residents can re-engage with nature in an increasingly artificial environment, this group exhibition uses art to investigate the new ecosystems thriving in the literal cracks of asphalt, including non-native species, self-sustaining plants and organisms that coexist with concrete and plastic. Core themes include reshaping urban nature, revitalising bodily sensations and integrating cross-disciplinary views. As human activities disrupt ecosystems, the boundary between natural and artificial blurs. The exhibition promotes coexistence with these changes rather than resisting or reverting to the past. Artworks are metaphorical seeds inspiring visitors to imagine roots reconnecting with the earth and senses. The show includes artists such as Tomoko Azumi, Yasutake Iwana, Akari Kaneko, Akiko Ikegami, Yoko Daihara, Yoji Ohno and Akane Saijo, who use everyday activities—living, wearing, eating and excreting—to reimagine our environment.

Miho Dohi makes assemblages from everyday items with industrial parts,such asbuttai 113 (2025). This is her fourth solo show at Hagiwara Projects Courtesy the artist

A celebrated Japanese artist, Miho Dohi is internationally known for her small, intricately layered, tactile abstract sculptures, which she calls buttai, a Japanese term combining the characters for thing and body. She produces enigmatic assemblages that creatively combine common natural materials with industrial parts, relying on intuition, experimentation and physical activity rather than pre-planning fixed forms. During creation, she repeatedly flips her pieces to break away from a single viewpoint. The process is complete when an original, unexpected structure naturally emerges from the chaos. Returning to the gallery for her fourth solo show, the Kanagawa-based sculptor presents new works in materials that seem heavy yet hang lightly on walls or from the ceiling, as if floating in space.

Alicja Kwade’s Tunnel-Tell (Ceci Sera Persicum) (2026) is made from granite, stainless steel, bronze and concrete Photo: Roman Marz; courtesy the artist and Pace Gallery

Alicja Kwade is a conceptual artist acclaimed for her interdisciplinary work across various media, all aimed at questioning human perception. The Polish-born, Berlin-based artist is recognised for her methodical, almost scientific approach to abstract existential questions. She uses natural materials and everyday objects to explore deep philosophical and scientific ideas, including space, time, gravity and social constructs. Kwade’s first solo show at Pace Tokyo explores empty space—the space within and between objects—and the unseen, unexperienced, unknowable in-between. Through sculptures and works on paper featuring peaches, clocks, tunnels, stones and clock hands, the exhibition addresses what constitutes the world, the transitional space between objects, and the viewer’s reflections on existence.

Nam June Paik’s New Candle (1993) is part of an exhibition marking 20 years since his death Courtesy Watari-um

Known as the “father of video art”, Nam June Paik trained as a classical pianist and musicologist before turning to visual art. A key figure in the 1960s Fluxus avant-garde movement, the late South Korean artist reshaped Modern art by using television sets, broadcasting networks and video recording devices as materials for sculpture, performance and installation. Drawing on the museum’s extensive collection, the retrospective examines how his innovative ideas—combining technology, Eastern philosophy and nature—remain relevant in today’s world of smartphones and AI. Rather than viewing him solely as a tech-focused artist, the show highlights Paik as both a performer and a deep thinker. The exhibition’s Japanese title Jugemu comes from a traditional rakugo story about endless life, symbolising the idea that Paik’s art and impact will endure forever.

#8973. Simone is a Copenhagen bookstore that doubles as a gallery, event space or listening room

Photography by Armin Tehran and Hampus Berndtson

Custom-designed furniture by Derya Arpac, Lærke Ryom, Kasper Kyster and Daniel Schofield sets the scene for this unconventional bookstore in the Danish capital.

Simone Book Services is a Copenhagen shop specialising in rare and independent books and magazines, but it can also be an exhibition gallery, a listening space, or a venue for book launches and other informal gatherings.

Turkish-born architect Arpac oversaw the intentionally “un-Scandinavian” interior, which includes modular shelves made from aluminium and cherry wood, mobile book trolleys and a counter dressed in leather.

The concept for the store was born out of conversations between Arpac, who works for furniture brand &Tradition, and founders Tugce Kayar Subay and Ibo Subay, a married couple with backgrounds in fashion media and marketing.

The Subays had amassed such an impressive collection of art, design and fashion literature that they launched a “literary branding” business in February 2026, curating libraries for exhibitions, offices and brand spaces.

Simone gives the couple a physical platform for this business and allows it to evolve further. It showcases their curation of books and magazines, but also furniture and objects related to reading culture.

“Tugce is the book nerd, and I’m the design nerd; we came up with this idea of combining our passions,” Arpac told Dezeen.

“We wanted to create a space where people would come and be inspired.”

Arpac’s own contribution to the space is a system of wall-mounted shelves crafted from cherry, a red-hued hardwood that offers a different aesthetic to traditional Scandinavian timbers like oak, ash or pine.

“The shelving appears to extend and climb through the space, almost like scaffolding or the structural skeleton of a building,” she said.

The leather-wrapped counter was designed by Ryom, who specialises in alternative methods of upholstery. Similar to the Garments chairs she developed for The Mindcraft Project, the bar’s edges feature zippers that open up to reveal storage areas.

Kyster developed a shelving system made from folded sheets of unpolished aluminium, intended for displaying magazines. The system is modular, so more panels could be added in future.

For seating, Schofield crafted a bench out of sheets of black-pigmented MDF that slots neatly into the store’s corner. It’s joined by mobile book trolleys made from the same material, encouraging visitors to move books around the space.

In addition to the four designers, artist Staffan Sundström was invited to create paintings for the bookstore. He contributed three pieces for the store opening, although the display will change as works are sold.

The store also includes an area dubbed “the red room”, a David Lynch-inspired space featuring red walls and matching floor-to-ceiling curtains. This 20-square-metre space offers scope for small-scale events and exhibitions.

Since opening, Simone has hosted various events, including a book launch for photographer Lasse Dearman, a curated library for sports brand ASICS and a pop-up for fashion label Bonnetje Recut.

Future ambitions include the launch of “reading objects”, including everything from bookmarks and paperweights to lighting and shelving.

What's your FI number? Calculate it in 60 seconds

What Americans actually have saved — the gap between average and median tells the real story.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Before comparing your balance to anyone else's, you need to know what the benchmarks actually include. Most retirement savings data from Vanguard, Fidelity, and the Federal Reserve covers:

What these numbers typically exclude: taxable brokerage accounts, real estate equity, HSA balances invested for retirement, pension values, and Social Security. For FI-minded savers, this distinction matters enormously — your total investable net worth is almost certainly larger than your "retirement savings" as defined by these surveys.

The gap between average and median retirement savings is one of the most important distinctions in personal finance. The average gets pulled upward by high-balance accounts — a single person with $5 million in their 401(k) dramatically inflates the average for their age group. The median (the middle number when all balances are ranked) gives you a far more honest picture of what a typical American actually has saved.

Notice how the gap widens with age. By 65+, the average is 3.3 times the median — meaning a small number of disciplined savers (or high earners) are pulling the average far above what most people actually have. The median tells you what a typical person in each age group actually holds. If you are above the median, you are doing better than half of Americans your age. But "better than average" and "on track for a secure retirement" are very different standards.

Vanguard's annual "How America Saves" report and Fidelity's quarterly retirement analysis provide the most comprehensive snapshots of what Americans hold in their workplace retirement accounts. These numbers reflect defined-contribution plan balances only — primarily 401(k) and 403(b) accounts.

Average balance: $13,265. Median balance: $5,400. Most savers in this bracket have been contributing for fewer than five years. The biggest advantage this group has is time — a 25-year-old contributing $6,000 per year with a 7% average return will accumulate over $1.2 million by age 65 without ever increasing their contribution. The FI community emphasizes that getting started early matters far more than starting with large contributions.

Average balance: $53,300. Median balance: $21,000. This is where employer matches start compounding meaningfully. Fidelity data shows that employees who have been contributing consistently since their 20s have balances 2.5 to 3 times higher than those who started in their 30s. The typical employer match adds 3-6% of salary — effectively free money that many employees still leave on the table. According to Vanguard, roughly 25% of eligible employees do not contribute enough to capture their full employer match.

Average balance: $142,069. Median balance: $60,763. Earnings typically peak in this decade, making it the critical window for aggressive savings. FIRE-path savers in this age bracket commonly have $500,000 to $1 million or more saved by maximizing their 401(k) ($24,500 in 2026), HSA ($4,400 individual / $8,750 family), and Roth IRA ($7,000) — then directing additional savings into taxable brokerage accounts.

Fidelity's guideline of 1x salary by 30 and 10x salary by 67 is a reasonable starting point for traditional retirement planning. But for FI seekers, these benchmarks are the floor, not the ceiling. The ChooseFI community consistently demonstrates that saving 40-60% of income — rather than the national average of 4.6% — compresses the timeline from 40 working years down to 10-17.

If your balance is below the median for your age group, you are not alone — and you are not stuck. The math of compound growth means that aggressive action in your 40s and 50s can still produce a secure retirement or even an early one.

The IRS provides additional contribution room for savers age 50 and older. In 2026, the 401(k) catch-up contribution is $7,500 on top of the standard $24,500 limit, for a total of $31,000. IRA catch-up contributions add $1,000 to the standard $7,000 limit. HSA catch-up for those 55+ adds another $1,000. Combined with employer matching, a 50-year-old couple can potentially shelter $80,000 or more per year in tax-advantaged accounts.

Most financial advice focuses on investment returns, but the variable you control most directly is your savings rate. Moving from a 10% savings rate to a 30% savings rate has a dramatically larger impact on your retirement timeline than chasing an extra 2% of investment return. A household earning $120,000 that increases from 10% to 30% savings — a shift of $24,000 per year — adds roughly $600,000 to their retirement balance over 15 years (assuming 7% average returns).

The FI community's core insight is that savings rate is the primary driver of financial independence. At a 50% savings rate, you can reach FI in roughly 17 years regardless of income level. At 60%, it compresses to about 12 years. At 70%, you are looking at under 10 years. These numbers are independent of salary — they depend only on the ratio of savings to spending.

The average American contributes 4.6% of salary to their 401(k), receives a 3-4% employer match, and saves little outside of that. FIRE-path savers typically max every available tax-advantaged account, maintain savings rates of 40-60%, invest in low-cost index funds, and direct overflow savings into taxable brokerage accounts. The result: FIRE savers in their 40s commonly have $500,000 to $1.5 million in total investable assets — 5 to 10 times the national median for their age group. The difference is not income; many FIRE success stories come from median-income households that simply saved aggressively and avoided lifestyle inflation.

If you are 40 with $50,000 saved and feeling behind, shifting from a 10% savings rate to a 40% savings rate on a $100,000 income adds $30,000 per year to your investment accounts. At 7% average returns, that alone grows to over $950,000 in 15 years — before counting the $50,000 you already have. Starting late is not ideal, but a high savings rate compresses the timeline dramatically.

Add up every 401(k), IRA, Roth IRA, HSA, and other retirement account balance. Include employer-sponsored plans from previous jobs — many people have orphaned 401(k) accounts they have forgotten about. Exclude your home equity and Social Security for now.

Use the age-bracket tables above to see where you stand. If you are above the median, you are ahead of most Americans your age. If you are below, calculate exactly how far behind and what it would take to catch up.

Most employers allow you to change your 401(k) contribution rate at any time. Increasing by 2% of salary is small enough that you will barely notice the paycheck reduction, but it compounds dramatically over time. Repeat this increase every six months until you are maxing out your 401(k).

Roughly one in four employees leaves free employer match money on the table. If your employer matches 50% of contributions up to 6% of salary, you need to contribute at least 6% to capture the full match. This is an instant 50% return on your money — no investment can beat it.

A Roth IRA provides tax-free growth and tax-free withdrawals in retirement, with no required minimum distributions. The 2026 limit is $7,000 ($8,000 if 50+). If your income exceeds the Roth limits, use the backdoor Roth conversion strategy to contribute indirectly.

Fidelity recommends having 1x your annual salary saved by age 30. For someone earning $55,000, that means $55,000 in retirement accounts. The FI community targets higher — $50,000 to $100,000 by 30 is common among aggressive savers. The national median for under-35 is only $13,000, so if you have more than that, you are already ahead of most peers.

The average is pulled upward by a small percentage of very high-balance accounts. If nine people have $10,000 saved and one person has $1,000,000, the average is $109,000 but the median is $10,000. The median gives a far more accurate picture of what a typical American has saved. Always compare yourself to the median, not the average.

Yes — employer matching contributions are part of your retirement savings balance. In a typical arrangement, an employer matches 50% of your contributions up to 6% of salary. On a $75,000 salary, that adds $2,250 per year in free money. Over a 30-year career at 7% returns, that match alone grows to roughly $213,000.

Generally no. While your home is part of your net worth, it is not liquid retirement savings you can draw from to cover living expenses. You would need to sell or reverse-mortgage your home to access that equity. Retirement planning should focus on investable assets — accounts you can convert to income without selling your primary residence.

A common guideline is 10-12x your pre-retirement income. For a household earning $100,000, that means $1,000,000 to $1,200,000 in retirement savings. The 4% rule suggests you can withdraw 4% of your portfolio annually with a high probability of not running out over 30 years — so $1 million supports roughly $40,000 per year in withdrawals.

It is never too late, but the urgency increases with age. A 40-year-old saving $20,000 per year at 7% returns will accumulate roughly $1 million by age 65. A 50-year-old has access to catch-up contributions ($7,500 extra in a 401(k)) and can still build $400,000 to $600,000 in 15 years with aggressive saving. The key is maximizing savings rate immediately rather than trying to make up ground through risky investments.

The average retirement savings benchmarks are useful directional guides, but they should not define your target. Most Americans are dramatically undersaved — the median 401(k) balance at retirement age is under $72,000, which supports only about $2,860 per year in withdrawals using the 4% rule. That is not a retirement plan; it is a supplement to Social Security at best. The FI community takes a fundamentally different approach: define your actual annual spending, multiply by 25, and work backward to a savings rate that gets you there. Whether your number is $750,000 or $3 million, the path is the same — maximize tax-advantaged accounts, invest in low-cost index funds, maintain a high savings rate, and let compound growth do the heavy lifting. If you are behind the benchmarks, the single most impactful action is increasing your savings rate, not chasing higher returns.

The need to take creative risks – make it so.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Playing it safe doesn’t get you far, and Patrick Stewart learned that the hard way. As we mourn his passing, it's worth reflecting on an actor who embraced challenges, took risks in his work, and gave us iconic film and theatre performances, from Marvel movies to Star Trek and Shakespeare. It's a devotion to the arts and trying new ideas that we can all be inspired by.

You will never achieve success by insuring against failure

One moment early in his career led to one of Patrick Stewart's most inspirational quotes. Near the end of his time at Bristol Old Vic Theatre School, his director Duncan Ross hauled him in for a dressing-down: Stewart was holding back, and it showed on stage. Ross’s advice stuck with him for years, when he was told: "You will never achieve success by insuring against failure".

As reported by Broadway World, Patrick Stewart repeated that advice over the years, and it’s easy to see yourself in it. We all have a go-to subject, a favourite brush, a style we know will land. And when a sketch starts heading somewhere odd, it’s tempting to bin it and start again. Play it safe long enough, though, and you end up making the same piece on repeat.

So next time you’re facing a blank canvas, try the thing you’re not sure about. It might flop. It might also give you something you’d never have found by sticking to what works.

Why Club Nothing (R) is more than empty philanthropy.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Tech brand Nothing has a rare upper hand that few of its rivals can claim – it is, I dare say, pretty cool. Already, the words 'brand' and 'cool' together irk me a bit; it feels antithetical to say a company trying to sell you things could ever truly be 'cool', but somehow Nothing has carved an identity that feels real, and I've been sucked right in.

From its trend-defying product design to its slick campaigns, Nothing oozes style in an effortless way that many brands will spend an eternity trying to capture. Sometimes it's not about competing for the best adverts or the swankiest product launches, but building something authentic.

Nothing has been on my radar for a while, particularly after it employed 365 party girl Charli XCX to promote its Headphone model. Nothing came out swinging, announcing Charli as its first Global Brand Ambassador, marking a distinct finger on the pulse of pop culture. With a Midas touch for all things cool, getting the BRAT composer to be the face of its brand was an instant boost in social clout.

But Nothing doesn't just embrace this party lifestyle as a fleeting trend. The return of its Club Nothing (R) initiative sees the brand support grassroots music scenes, underground parties, and alternative sound experiences with a $40,000 grant. This year's winners, Black Bass Collective, Oroko Radio, Whorechata and Signal, represent a diverse array of independent music culture, providing a much-needed boost for the struggling and uncertain status of the live music scene.

In short, Nothing's 'cool' image isn't just performative; it's productive. Often, brand philanthropy can come across as virtue signalling, but Nothing knows its place in culture and is actively helping to improve the industry that supports it. Being cool is much more than getting the latest trending celeb to rep your tech – it's about living and breathing community.

From the Kelly Clarkson's mechanical bird fiasco to Carrie Bradshaw's Dior newsprint dress, Gay Halloween speaks to the staying power of women's iconic media moments.

With everything that's happened in the 1,000+ lifetimes jammed into 2026, I think we've all been waiting for Gay Halloween to rehash the year in popular culture. #8968. How Édouard Manet's Black Cat Became a Symbol of Modernity

Long associated with witchcraft and bad luck, the black feline became an emblem of artistic rebellion and urban life in 19th-century Paris.

Every Halloween, black cats return as emblems of witchcraft, bad luck, and the supernatural. Their sinister reputations stretch back centuries: starting in the Middle Ages, people associated cats with heresy and sexual transgression, and their perceived affinity with witches intensified during the trials of Elizabeth Francis and Agnes Waterhouse and their cat Sathan between 1565-1579.

But after the Enlightenment, 19th-century French artists and writers began to reclaim the mysterious and devilish qualities foisted onto felines as desirable. Alongside a new bourgeois pet-keeping culture, where caring for animals became associated with progress and enlightenment, bohemian artists and intellectuals began incorporating black cats into their work. The black cat became a symbol of independence and nonconformity, reflecting changing attitudes toward individualism and self-expression amid industrialization and urbanization. French writer and diplomat François-René de Chateaubriand described the cat’s modern independence favorably, stating, “What I like about the cat is his character, independent and almost heartlessness […] The cat lives alone, he has no need of society.” These inherited qualities of eroticism and defiance also became synonymous with the emerging language of modern art.

No painting or artist makes this transformation more apparent than Édouard Manet’s “Olympia” (1863). Historians like T.J. Clark have long hailed it as a “founding monument of modern art,” updating Titian’s “Venus of Urbino” (1534) with a stark depiction of a contemporary prostitute, her Black maid, and a black cat. The work provoked outrage at the Paris Salon in 1865: its subject matter, combined with flattened forms, bold color contrasts, and use of black, clearly rejected academic conventions. Critics latched onto the wiry black cat, whose arched back and luminous eyes seemed to embody the painting’s perceived vulgarity by showing what Olympia’s hand covered.

Christopher Glass discusses working on Boots Riley’s absurdist crime comedy.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Boots Riley's absurdist crime comedy I Love Boosters is far from conventional. From its stunning movie posters to its action-packed trailer, it's not a movie that comes quietly. Following a group of shoplifters as they face off against fashion mogul Christie Smith, the film soon spirals into a surreal science fiction body horror with some slicing social commentary for good measure.

But such an eccentric story needs immersive production design to match – that's where Christopher Glass comes in. To understand the meticulous practical effects process behind I Love Boosters and more, I sat down with Christopher to uncover the intricate artistry of production design and the evolution of the industry.

Christopher Glass is an Art Director Guild (ADG) Award-winning and Gold Cannes Lion-winning Production Designer whose work spans feature films, television, and commercials. Known for creating visually ambitious, emotionally resonant worlds - he has collaborated with some of the most influential directors working in film and advertising today.

I think beyond the obvious technological changes that have happened in the last 25 years (iPhones, iPads, Motion Capture/LED Volumes, real-time rendering and now AI) the largest conditions that have changed in the industry are economic.

The decentralization of film work from a Los Angeles hub to being scattered all over the world, chasing the latest tax rebate; the creation of IP-obsessed streaming platforms with tech companies swallowing traditional studios via ever larger mergers and acquisitions have created an environment where there is less work in general.

When there is work, it tends to be less creative and completely risk-averse. There is a focus on collecting libraries of “content” versus actually having an interest in making great films, TV shows or commercials. That’s why movies like “I Love Boosters” and what NEON and A24 are doing is much needed today.

In an ideal world, film companies would break away from these monstrous corporations and return to smaller autonomous studios, run by people who truly care about telling unique and compelling stories.

I think miniatures and forced perspective are my favorite practical effects, overlooked not only by audiences but also by filmmakers themselves. Filmmakers sometimes don’t know or realize these are great options for getting tangible effects in camera.

People tend to think miniatures have to be small buildings and cars. I have used 70% scale miniature “backings” to eliminate the need for LED walls or traditional translight backings. You get parallax when you move the camera. You can dress or light up windows how you want and change everything in modular ways. You can design sets with forced perspective to make things look further away or more expansive. These are techniques that have been around for over 100 years.

We used miniatures on “I Love Boosters” in a different way. Almost the entire third act is a combination of full-scale and 1/6th and 1/12th scale miniatures. We have stop-motion characters running across moving vehicles, down streets and alleys. It was an intentional choice for the handmade look.

In fact, when we were shooting, our Director Boots Riley thought some of the miniature shots started looking too real and told the folks at Blind Beagle FX (the miniature company run by Christopher Warren) to make them look more “miniature.”

I have a few favorite projects for varying reasons. “I Love Boosters” stands out for sure. Its sheer madness and creativity are unparalleled for me. I also really loved doing the battlefield war sets for “12 Strong” – which was a completely different experience – and “The Jungle Book” will always be a special film for me. I learned a hell of a lot from that and really loved the people I worked with.

Hands down, the Apple short film directed by Spike Jonze starring FKA Twigs called “Welcome Home.” Every detail, from the lighting, camera, props, actor choreography, music cues, and artwork, was subject to complicated practical effects and moving set pieces.

As an example, we built the apartment twice. One was “normal” and unmoving. The other one was the magic trick set where everything moved and stretched. Each moving piece affected the next, like a domino effect.

One time Spike asked me to move the coffee table about 4 inches in one direction. I had to explain to him that the metal table, with a spring-loaded stretching magazine was attached to the stretching rug, and both were bolted into moving tracks underneath the floor connected to levers hidden just out of view of the perpendicularly moving walls at the end of the room… So it wouldn’t be easy.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Everything in that set depended on precise placement, choreography and movement. Every pattern and texture of fabric had to be precisely made and printed to achieve the “pixel” stretching effect throughout. The umbrella on a stand, a bike and a lamp had to be meticulously sculpted to be extruded by movement.

The large moving wall actually hovered on air bearings and was timed to the music. The hallway was made of ribbons stretched with so much tension, it bent the original steel frame and had to be rebuilt before shooting. The list goes on and on. Nothing was easy about that project. I thought it was the end of my career, and it was all going to go down in flames. But to my pleasant surprise, we won a Gold Cannes Lion for Film Craft.

Coming in close second for most difficult was “I Love Boosters!”

#8966. ‘Travel guides are far from neutral forms’: Art Week Tokyo video programme goes off the map

A still from Kandis Williams’s A Travel Guide: Black Gothic in South Korean Horror (2025) © Kandis Williams, courtesy the artist and Heidi

Generations of tourists have criss-crossed the world clutching dog-eared guide books. With lists of must-see landmarks, advice on local customs and listings of places to eat, drink and sleep, guide books promise to contain all that you could ever need to know about foreign places.

This year’s Art Week Tokyo (AWT) Video programme challenges that assumption, with a selection of single-channel moving image works that ask what is mapped, and what is left out of view.

“My interest in travel guides is less in them as a genre or style of literature,” says sector curator X Zhu-Nowell, “and more as a form that choreographs bodies within inhabited spaces, idealised landscapes, and any other kind of locale that has been deemed necessary to map out.” The showcase considers geography as shaped by migration, memory, labour and ideas.

Of the ten artists showcased in Your Travel Guide To…, five are from Japan and one is from the Japanese diaspora. Zhu-Nowell, who is the executive director and chief curator of Shanghai’s Rockbund Art Museum, has worked with four of the artists previously, including Berlin-based Kandis Williams, who has never shown in Japan before. “It’s important and meaningful to bring their work in this context alongside new companions,” Zhu-Nowell says.

Williams’s video A Travel Guide: Black Gothic in South Korean Horror (2025) draws upon Victor Hugo Green’s famous The Green Book guide for Black Americans during the Jim Crow era. “It identified restaurants, hotels, gas stations, soda shops and other businesses where Black travellers could expect to be served and were at less risk of harassment or price gouging,” says Zhu-Nowell. Williams reflects upon this history and frames the work around “the political reality that mobility equals power”. Showing the Black American artist moving through Korea connects the two countries’ shared “musical aesthetics, histories of suppressed mourning, and experiences of militarisation and state violence.”

Zhu-Nowell also highlights New York-based artist Ken Okiishi’s “addictive” video Brian at Home (2020-25), which consists of Zoom calls with the artist’s personal trainer, who lives in a “smart-home hellscape” in New York City called “Denizen” with “a seemingly endless array of app-based appliances and perks”. Okiishi walks the viewer through this “highly designed public/private space [to] watch its promise of frictionless inclusivity start to come apart”.

A still from Hiroyuki Oki’s Buddy Matsumae’s Picture Diary (1988) © Hiroyuki Oki, courtesy Anomaly, Image Forum and Okiiki

The exhibition also includes the Berlin- and Beijing-based He Xiangyu, while Linda Iha, Fuyuhiko Takata and Atsushi Yamamoto are based in Japan, as were the late Keiichi Tanaami (1936-2024) and Hiroyuki Oki (1964-2025), both masters of handcrafted moving images. This range of perspectives combines for a nuanced exploration of how “travel guides are far from neutral forms, and often do a poor job of concealing that lack of neutrality”, Zhu-Nowell says. “Each form they take reflects the long and complex history these objects have as difference-mediating technologies and storytelling devices.”

The curator cites as an example the “the infamous 18th-century ars apodemica guides that instructed wealthy European young men on a ‘world tour’ how to observe, behave, and even listen to ‘others’ in foreign cultures”, an entitled inverse of The Green Book. “Those pocket travel guides that proliferated at the end of the 20th century are also fairly famous,” Zhu-Nowell says. “Today, new forms, digitised and even more pocketable, have emerged from a self-described ‘nomadic’ class of travel-influencer globalists. But in every case, the framing power of travel guides underlines [philosopher] Katherine McKittrick’s point about how geography is never a neutral space.”

#8965. Büro Ole Scheeren designs winding concrete gallery in South Korea "without traditional thresholds"

Architecture studio Büro Ole Scheeren has revealed designs for the Suseong Continuum, a snaking, concrete art gallery in Daegu, South Korea.

Set to be built within the city’s Yeonhwaji park, the 364-square-metre gallery was designed specifically for showcasing digital art.

Berlin-based Büro Ole Scheeren designed the gallery as a continuous space, without any enclosed rooms and or doorways, in a bid to reflect the “flows” of digital art.

“We wanted to build a gallery without traditional thresholds: a gradient of realities that morph into one another as you gradually move through the space,” studio founder Ole Scheeren said.

“The substance of digital art is not rooted in the physical domain of distinct objects and isolated experiences… it exists in a world of overlaps and connections, where one condition potentially flows into the next.”

“Landscape, circulation and exhibition become a continuous experience,” the studio added.

The Suseong Continuum gallery was unveiled as part of this year’s Suseong International Biennale, which invites architects to realise permanent public works across Daegu.

Commissioned by the Suseong District Government, the design by Büro Ole Scheeren is expected to open for the biennale’s 2028 edition.

Once complete, visitors will access the space via a winding path, from which the gallery was designed to emerge as an extrusion.

Conceived as a “continuation of the landscape”, the gallery’s twisting volume will be partially embedded into the park’s topography and oriented toward a nearby lotus pond.

Its structure will be built using board-marked concrete to create a rough exterior texture. Inside, this textured surface will transition to smooth concrete walls for projecting media onto.

According to Büro Ole Scheeren, the gallery’s layout and materiality were designed to reflect the transition from the park’s natural landscape to the digital interiors.

“Technology is often seen as an opposite to nature,” Scheeren said. “With Suseong Continuum we wanted to explore how we can create a way of extending the way we perceive the relationship between both domains – a journey that starts in the park and that seamlessly carries you into the digital realm.”

“There is no single moment where one world ends and the other begins, it is a continuous transformation.”

“What begins as natural landscape gradually transforms into digital media,” the studio added.

Renders of the gallery’s stripped-back interior reveal its immersive exhibition spaces framed by curving walls.

A layered ceiling will run the building’s full length to conceal all lighting and technical infrastructure, which was developed by the studio in collaboration with the Center for Art and Media Karlsruhe.

“The interior unfolds as a spatial gradient in which light, sound, enclosure and immersion shift gradually along the visitor’s route,” the studio said.

“Curving walls widen into open spaces and tighten into passages; atmospheres transform rather than switch,” it added.

The design will remain on show at the Suseong International Biennale until 22 November.

In Shenzhen, China, the studio has revealed plans for skyscrapers with “waterfall” facades and its design for the Róng Museum of Arts is currently under construction.
