#8964. Documenta 16 Names Four New Curatorial Team Members

The embattled German exhibition's latest appointments, artist Catherine Opie wins a Yale University award, and Dallas Art Fair partners with … a university?

Art Movements, published every Thursday afternoon, is a roundup of must-know news, appointments, awards, and other happenings in today’s chaotic art world.

Less than eight months away from the 16th edition of Documenta, the German contemporary arts festival has appointed four new curatorial team members: artist and musician Raven Chacon will serve as curator-at-Large, and Osei Bonsu, Timea Junghaus, and Noam Segal will be curatorial advisors.

The upcoming iteration, opening on June 12 in Kassel, promises to offer a space for “study, experimentation, and awakening, where artists hold right to expression alongside their artistic creation.” But artists and free speech advocates have argued that this stated mission jars with Documenta’s adoption of a controversial definition of antisemitism that includes criticism of Israel, raising serious questions about creative freedom. In a recent interview with the German newspaper Die Zeit, Artistic Director Naomi Beckwith revealed that some artists have already declined to participate in Documenta 16 over Germany's support of Israel's genocide in Gaza.

Chacon, Bonsu, Junghaus, and Segal will join Beckwith and the core curatorial team for the 16th edition — Carla Acevedo-Yates, Romi Crawford, Mayra A. Rodríguez Castro, and Xiaoyu Weng — to help shape the program's artistic vision.

The most entertaining bit of game marketing I've seen in a long time.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Rockstar has found a brilliantly left-field way to show off Grand Theft Auto VI: by smuggling new footage into South Park. It’s one of the smartest bits of brand placement I’ve seen in a long time but its also just the right kind of unexpected disruption I'd expect from Rockstar.

Game marketing usually runs on slick trailers and carefully managed hype. A dog poo weapon demo inside a crudely animated cartoon is the opposite of that, but it works. The latest episode of South Park (or is it South America now?), ‘Guinea Pig on a Stick’, aired on 28 October and included around 20 seconds of previously unseen gameplay from the forthcoming open-world game, GTA 6.

The clip follows protagonists Jason and Lucia along a busy Vice City beach before switching to Jason, who spots a dog doing its business on the sand. The owner dutifully bags the mess, but Jason has other ideas. He throws something at the hapless dog walker, grabs the bag of poo and smacks the NPC round the face with it. Charming.

New gameplay from GTA 6 was shown in the latest ‘SOUTH PARK’ episode. https://t.co/gL2kRKUv2IOctober 29, 2026

The visual clash is half the fun. South Park’s flat, cut-out look has barely changed in decades, and dropping a few seconds of Rockstar’s richly detailed, near-photoreal world into it makes the game’s fidelity stand out more than another polished trailer would. The footage is the real thing, too, with Rockstar Games credited in the closing credits.

From a branding point of view, it’s a refreshing move. GTA 6 is the biggest entertainment release of the year, if not the decade, and Rockstar could simply keep releasing bigger trailers and let the internet amplify them (having begun with an equally unique Netflix reveal). Instead, it’s placing the game inside a piece of pop culture that already has an audience, and a voice, of its own.

It’s in keeping with a campaign that has been playful from the start, from a neon logo that reads as a love letter to Vice City and box art that leans hard into PS2-era nostalgia to cheeky parody ads that blur reality and fiction on the streets of Miami.

It also doesn’t feel like an ad. South Park has been referencing GTA 6 all season, so the appearance lands as a punchline rather than a paid slot. Both brands trade on irreverence and a willingness to go further than their rivals, so the tone matches. Nothing feels forced. That’s more than can be said for the brands trying to borrow the Vice City look, from Burger King to Shrek. Rockstar keeps official tie-ups tightly controlled, and the Miami Heat’s Vice City merchandise is a rare example.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

There’s a nice bit of brand history here, too. The narrator of the gameplay footage is voiced by Tish Hicks, who also provided the voiceover for GTA 5’s official gameplay video back in 2013. It’s a small touch, but it’s the kind of consistency that makes a brand feel coherent over time, and longtime fans will spot it.

What I like most is that Rockstar is letting a comedy show poke fun at one of its biggest selling points: the extraordinary detail of its worlds. That apparently includes weaponising dog mess.

With GTA 6 due on 19 November, there’s still time for more surprises. If this is the template, I’d take it over another dozen predictable cinematic trailers.

#8962. Montana acquires sustainable furniture maker Takt

Montana has announced its buyout of fellow Danish design brand Takt, known for its solid wood furniture and pioneering approach to sustainable design.

Founded in 2019 by trained physicist and former Lego and Bang & Olufsen executive Henrik Taudorf Lorensen, Takt makes modern Scandinavian furniture from FSC-certified wood that is low-carbon, flat-pack and designed for disassembly.

Its future launches and existing catalogue, including products such as the Cross chair by British design duo Pearson Lloyd and Anderssen & Voll’s Spoke sofa, will now be sold under the collection name Takt by Montana.

Montana CEO Joakim Lassen said he hopes they will act as an understated counterpart to Montana’s existing selection of colourful modular furniture – including the Montana System storage – and bring valuable learnings about sustainability to the table.

“Takt brings experience with materials and the environment, and we are looking forward to bringing our respective experience together and taking this work even further,” he said.

Takt is known for its ambitious approach to sustainability, focused on driving down emissions primarily through the design of its products rather than operational cuts, to become net zero by 2030.

The company assesses the carbon footprint of its products throughout their entire lifecycle using the EU’s Product Environmental Footprint (PEF) single score, in a bid to bring down its emissions, and claims to be the only design brand to consistently have all of its products marked with the EU Ecolabel.

“I have a background as a scientist, so it was important to me to start measuring things,” Lorensen told Dezeen during our Carbon Revolution series. “The starting point was to get a grasp of the impact of the choices we’re making.”

Lorensen will join Montana Furniture’s board, sharing his experience and perspective on sustainability, while Takt employees will be integrated into Montana’s organisation “as far as possible”, the company said.

By gaining access to the established, international infrastructure of Montana, which has been operating since 1982, Lorensen hopes that Takt’s furniture will be able to reach a larger audience.

“The past few years have been an exciting and instructive journey for TAKT,” he said. “We have built a brand where materials and the environment have been central, and we have collaborated with a number of talented and celebrated designers. “

“Now it is time for TAKT’s next chapter, and we are delighted that it will be written together with Montana.”

#8961. Are Black Cats Modernity’s Icons?

How Manet transformed the misunderstood feline into an emblem of independent thinking; plus, Gay Halloween memes galore!

Centuries of superstition may be to blame for black cats facing among the lowest adoption outcomes at shelters across the US. But these mysterious, furry angels have shed at least part of their witchy stereotype in the modern era — thanks largely to 19th-century French artists, argues Rebecca Rebecca Schiffman, Hyperallergic associate editor. According to Schiffman, who makes a case for the black cat as a modern icon in art history in an essay perfectly timed for Hallows' Eve, painters such as Édouard Manet helped dark-furred felines come to symbolize a Belle Époque “appetite for provocation” and “refusal to be domesticated.”

On a related note, a big, heartfelt thanks to all who joined us at Hyperallergic’s Halloween party last night — you blew us all away with your commitment to the art costumes. (I’m looking at you, “Two Fridas” and “Saturn Devouring His Son.”) Look out for photos from the evening soon!

And in another tradition, Staff Writer Rhea Nayyar rounds up the spiciest Gay Halloween memes this year, a trend that holds a mirror up to our broader pop-culture moment. “I hate gay Halloween, what do you mean we're dressed as Kelly Clarkson and an animatronic bird?”

Every Halloween, black cats return as emblems of witchcraft, bad luck, and the supernatural. Their sinister reputations stretch back centuries: starting in the Middle Ages, people associated cats with heresy and sexual transgression, and their perceived affinity with witches intensified during the trials of Elizabeth Francis and Agnes Waterhouse and their cat Sathan between 1565-1579. But after the Enlightenment, 19th-century French artists and writers began to reclaim the mysterious and devilish qualities foisted onto felines as desirable.| Rebecca Schiffman Read More

#8960. Otis College of Art and Design in LA Offers a Two-Year MFA Fine Arts Degree Program

Refine your artistic vision and join a diverse community at the first professional school of the arts in Los Angeles.

In the MFA Fine Arts program at Otis College of Art and Design, we believe artists thrive when they can explore a wide range of approaches in artmaking and all its related disciplines.

Our program provides an artistic learning environment where artists of different backgrounds and creative practices can flourish together. Our courses, studios, labs, and galleries are welcoming places where everyone in our community can develop as artists and as engaged participants in society.

MFA students have 24/7 access to individual working studios. They are also guaranteed at least one semester of a Graduate Teaching Internship or Graduate Assistantship. Students receive access to painting, sculpture, and lighting studios; state-of-the-art wood and metal shops; photography, video, film, printmaking, and ceramics labs. A mid-residency show, annual open studios, and a final thesis show offer ample opportunities for exhibition over the course of the two-year program.

Distinguished alumni include Carlos Almaraz, Alonzo Davis, Roberto Gil de Montes, Judithe Hernandez, Vita Kari, Alison Saar, Masami Teraoka, and Kent Twitchell.

The Einstein Visiting Artist Lecture Series at Otis College brings distinguished artists, designers, and creative thought leaders to campus to engage with students and the public. Past guests have included Doug Aitken, Kelly Akashi, Dawoud Bey, Njideka Akunyili Crosby, Theaster Gates, Trenton Doyle Hancock, Edgar Heap of Birds, Shirin Neshat, Hank Willis Thomas, Jeffrey Vallance, Kara Walker, Zoe Whitley, and Anicka Yi, among others.

Priority deadline for fall entry is January 15 and October 1 for spring. After these deadlines, applications will be accepted on a rolling basis as space remains available.

#8959. Architect Kae Ito creates a modular ‘secret garden’ for Art Week Tokyo's bar

Japanese architect Kae Ito’s commission for this year’s AWT Bar is called Kuru Kuru, with openwork structures of stainless steel and acrylic © Kae Ito

Since its inception in 2022, the pop-up AWT Bar has become one of the most appreciated hubs of Art Week Tokyo. This year, the architect Kae Ito has been commissioned for the spatial design. Ito opened her independent firm Office Itokae in 2025 after ten years at the Pritzker Prize-winning firm Sanaa / Kazuyo Sejima & Associates in Tokyo, where she worked on notable projects like the Better Co-Being pavilion for Expo 2025 Osaka, the Inujima Landscape Project and myriad exhibition designs in Japan and abroad.

Her AWT Bar, titled Kuru Kuru, she says, is intended to evoke a “secret garden”. Ingenious openwork structures of stainless steel and acrylic are distributed throughout the space, their placement guided by a geometric design on the floor. Multimedia elements by the artist Nile Koetting further enliven the space.

Kae Ito worked at architecture practice Sanaa before opening her own firm, Office Itokae, in 2025 © Office Itokae

Ito recently spent time in Mongolia investigating ger, the traditional nomadic homes of the region, which are designed to be easily folded up and moved. Like those, Kuru Kuru is made of modular, collapsible elements, composed of rings and semi-circles, with a simple locking mechanism to render them stable. Colour-coded acrylic hemispheres have flat upper surfaces that form seats, tables or counters. These exquisitely fabricated units call to mind orreries or models of atoms. An aluminium-covered wall with circular service openings reinforces the science-lab vibe. Ito says, “I’m hoping [the bar] encourages people to have a happy time, eating and drinking with other visitors.”

Chef Ryuichi Yokomizo’s orchestration of the culinary experience at the AWT Bar is a sophisticated inversion of expectations. Following nine years at the Michelin-starred Joël Robuchon restaurant in Tokyo’s Ebisu district, the 30-year-old chef was asked to helm La & Le in Aoyama, which opened in March this year. For Art Week Tokyo, he is presenting two canapés: a gâteau of duck rillettes and pain d’épices, and a tarte tatin-inspired sablé.

Artist cocktails by Natsumi Aoyagi, Mariko Mori and Yoshihiro Suda and edible creations by La & Le are on the menu at this year’s AWT Bar © Saiki

These pleasantly deceiving creations display a beautiful autumnal colour palette, and reward the diner’s attention. The beautifully constructed savoury option layers duck rillettes over dark pain d’épices, finished with foiegras mousse, a paper-thin slice of apple, caramelised walnuts and delicate sprigs of micro amaranth. The tarte reimagines the classic tarte tatin, layering deeply caramelised apple over a sablé Breton base, topped with a quenelle of calvados-infused buttercream and artfully placed micro celery. Each masquerades as its opposite: the savoury rillettes appear at first glance to be a dessert, while the sweet tarte appears savoury.

“I’m deeply interested in the element of surprise in cuisine,” Yokomizo says. “My theme for Art Week Tokyo, Entre, centres on the Japanese ideas of tsunagu—to connect—and aida—the space between,” he says. “Like art, cuisine changes with one’s point of view. I hope to show how simply changing the angle of approach can transform eating into an entirely different experience. I believe that sharing good food and drink in this way can foster deeper communication.”

The artist-devised cocktails on offer are similarly inventive. Mariko Mori’s All That Shinesuses luminous kuzumochi spheres, tapioca balls and rose caviar to evoke “the invisible ripples that are sent out into the world as our souls interact”. For Part-Time Job, Yoshihiro Suda reached back into his past as an illustrator for cider and whisky brands to make a cocktail as bittersweet as his memories. Natsumi Aoyagi’s sudsy Caipirinha de Cinco Sabões (Caipirinha of Five Soaps) is accompanied by a fable that alludes to the drink’s historical rural Brazilian roots. Combining uniquely ambitious design, cuisine and cocktails, the AWT Bar promises an unforgettable multisensory experience.

Getting everything out of my head frees up an astonishing amount of mental space for actually thinking.

#8957. A View From the Easel: Anna Pajak

“I wanted it to feel like a chapel, a place for everything I believe in. My painting chapel.”

Welcome to the 361st installment of A View From the Easel, a series in which artists reflect on their workspace. This week, Anna Pajak paints symmetrical will-o'-the-wisps in the woods of southern Sweden.

Want to take part? Check out our submission guidelines and share a bit about your studio with us through this form! All mediums and workspaces are welcome, including your home studio.

How long have you been working in this space?

I like to start early, with coffee. I lay out the paint and go straight to the canvas. I often imagine that I’ll sit down and thoughtfully plan what I’m going to do, but I’m unfortunately too restless for that. The moment I enter the studio, I just want to squeeze out the paint and get going. The coffee gets cold and forgotten.I usually listen to music while I paint, unless the painting requires too much thinking or measuring, then I need complete silence. I often work on two canvases at once, like sisters standing side by side.I watch the sky outside my window. When the gradient is at its best from orange into light green, it’s usually time to stop for the day, before I get overtired and stop seeing clearly, or start overthinking and invite the critical voice into the room. I wash all the brushes so I can start faster tomorrow.

Just in time for Halloween, John Kenn Mortensen talks dark fantasy, drawing by hand and bringing his distinctive illustrations to FLASK.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Halloween is the time to linger in the dark a little longer, and John Kenn Mortensen is the artist to guide you. His illustrations teem with grotesque creatures, scraggly line work, and unsettling oddballs: the kind of thing you glimpse out of the corner of your eye, then need to stare at and see more of.

“In the dark there are secrets and things to be explored,” he says as he explains his approach to the art and creature design you'll find in FLASK. “I see my work as a dark room, with a door slightly ajar at the end, where a little light comes in.”

That ajar door has made Mortensen a go-to name for the macabre. Now he’s opening it onto video games with FLASK, a dark fantasy roguelike deckbuilder from Chop Chop Games.

Inspired by Jim Henson’s 1986 cult classic Labyrinth and the thrash metal of Slayer, FLASK mixes gruesome fantasy, medieval imagery and black humour. Nightmarish creatures roam, magic is best handled with caution, and even a wizard has to worry about the mortgage on his tower.

For Mortensen, the leap meant taking his pen-and-paper illustrations digital, working with a team of artists to turn his monochrome creations into a playable world. That’s a big shift for an artist who has spent most of his career working solo across books, comics, animation, TV and exhibitions.

I caught up with Mortensen to talk about finding his visual identity, the music behind his monsters, and what it’s like to step into game development for the first time. And, of course, you can download FLASK on Steam this Halloween weekend (and beyond), and follow Mortensen on Instagram for more eerily good art.

Read the full Q&A with Mortensen below, and he's even shared a couple of new creatures coming to FLASK very soon.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

John Kenn Mortensen: It came from within. I have always been drawn to the dark; it is a much more interesting place to work. In the light everything is visible, revealed. In the dark there are secrets and things to be explored. I see my work as a dark room, with a door slightly ajar at the end, where a little light comes in.

JKM: Building on the gameplay mechanics Dario and Michael, co-founders and game developers at Chop Chop Games, already had, I focused on two things: the dark fantasy world of Labyrinth (the Jim Henson movie) and the sound and energy from Slayer (the band). From there, it just started to come alive.

JKM: It has been hard, and I don’t really know... it comes down to the art team; they are amazing to work with, and have been a huge support in bringing my monstrous creatures to life. On my side, I have mostly only worked with pen on paper, very old school.

JKM: Conveying the feelings in my art with colour has been a huge challenge, since most of my illustrations are in black and white. We have added lights, highlights, shadows, and colour, and it’s been really rewarding experimenting with what I’m comfortable with and seeing how we can add more depth when it comes to inserting my drawings into a digital format.

JKM: I tend to lose track of where ideas come from and how they morph into things in the process. But from the start, I wanted it to be dark fantasy mixed with medieval imagery. What’s even more special is that Labyrinth came out 40 years ago, and working on a project so inspired at the time of its anniversary is really rewarding.

JKM: This is my first time doing video games, so Chop Chop’s digital artists really played a huge role in this. First, gameplay had to come in and lay down the foundation, with auto-battler, roguelike, and theory crafting mechanics; then, thanks to the work with the artists, we were able to create a cohesive dark world over the framework of the game.

JKM: Mostly music. I listen to a lot of music. I have an hour every day where I will just walk and listen to music; that is where most of my ideas spring from.

JKM: Now, that is something I can’t take any credit for. We have had artists from outside, and artists on the team, create the card artwork. The rule for the artists working on the card art is that my visual style is the real world, and they have to see themselves as artists in that world and then create. It has been, and still is, a super fun process.

JKM: That, again, is credit to the art team, and it’s such a joy to have a team when I usually work solo. We have the best art team in the gaming world, I think. My art style is not something I have worked on in any direction; it has just sprung out of bad habits and laziness.

JKM: It has been a very different approach than I am used to, but I like that challenge. I always jump from one platform to another in my work: I have done TV shows, animation, live action, books, comics, art shows, and now video games. I see my working life as a big house with a lot of very different rooms where I can hang out and play with the people in them. The only thing I think about before entering is to be as honest and true to myself as possible. There are soooo many new ideas!

Ian Dean is Editor, Digital Arts & 3D at Creative Bloq, and the former editor of many leading magazines. These titles included ImagineFX, 3D World and video game titles Play and Official PlayStation Magazine. Ian launched Xbox magazine X360 and edited PlayStation World. For Creative Bloq, Ian combines his experiences to bring the latest news on digital art, VFX and video games and tech, and in his spare time he doodles in Procreate, ArtRage, and Rebelle while finding time to play Xbox and PS5.

The M5 MacBook Pro is the top of our buying guide for a reason!

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If you look at our guide to the best laptops for graphic design, one comes out on top: the 14-inch MacBook Pro with Apple’s M5 chip. In our tests, it sat at the pinnacle of our Photoshop benchmarks by some margin, and our reviewers found it a lovely laptop to work on in practice.

The catch is, it ain't cheap. So for Amazon to trim it down, with the $1,999 configuration down to $1,839, is a big deal.

That’s a saving of $160, which is not nothing. So if you’ve been nursing an older MacBook, this is a great opportunity to upgrade.

Our favourite laptop for graphic designers combines the M5 chip, a superb display and a solid aluminium build made for daily professional use. Save $160 at Amazon now.

The star of the show here is the M5 chip, which makes everything super-fast. It topped Geekbench’s single-core results when we tested it, and the GPU has also taken a big leap over the M4. If you're running a lot of demanding creative software then, this is the model for you.

Storage is quicker too, with the SSD now running at over 6,000MB/s, almost twice as fast as the previous generation. Finally, the 120Hz display offers excellent colour reproduction, and in our tests it covered 93% of the P3 gamut.

It’s not perfect. It has Thunderbolt 4 rather than Thunderbolt 5, and video and 3D pros may get more from a Windows machine with a dedicated Nvidia card. But for graphic designers, illustrators and photographers, it’s hard to beat. Read our full MacBook Pro M5 review for more.

#8954. Surprise! US Pavilion Needs More Cash to Ship Works Home

Commissioner Jenni Parido sent a letter to donors pleading for "urgent funding" for deinstallation and shipping as the Venice Biennale comes to an end.

With less than a month left until the 61st Venice Biennale closes on November 22, the United States pavilion commissioner Jenni Parido has pleaded for additional donations to ship Alma Allen's sculptures out of Italy.

This week, the New York Times reviewed a letter by Parido, who founded the American Arts Conservancy (AAC) and commissioned Allen's exhibition in Venice. She told potential donors that the Trump administration-aligned arts nonprofit was “facing an urgent funding need associated with the final deinstallation and safe return of the artworks to the United States.”

The time-sensitive fundraising effort falls in line with Parido's financial model for this year's Biennale presentation. After months of opacity surrounding the selection process and funding ventures for the pavilion, Parido told Hyperallergic in April that Allen's exhibition, Call Me the Breeze, received no “corporate or foundation funding,” and that it was facilitated through the “generous support of private citizens who believe in the importance of American artists and cultural exchange.” The AAC also had an online donations portal to help fund the pavilion ahead of the Biennale's opening in May.

#8953. RSHP designs Hetao Alpha skyscraper in Shenzhen with "striking butterfly layout"

British studio RSHP has completed a 45-storey office skyscraper in Shenzhen, China, featuring two angled wings connected by a central core.

Called Hetao Alpha, the 212-metre-tall office building comprises a 37-storey east wing and a 44-storey west wing connected by a central core. The building sits on top of a mixed-use podium.

“The naturally ventilated office tower features a striking butterfly layout with fully glazed east and west wings,” the studio said.

Cantilevered bays extended from the central concrete core on the east and west sides to form the tower’s angled wings, which have 70,410 square metres of office space.

On every 12 levels, mega trusses located on refuge and service floors provide additional structural support.

The Hetao Alpha skyscraper has a fully glazed facade that, together with open floor plates, ensures unobstructed views of the cityscape for the office workers.

Curved double-height glazing at each of the wings’ four corners captures curated viewpoints of the Shenzhen Bay Wetlands to the west and the Hong Kong Mai Po Wetlands to the south.

Lifts are located on the north and south facades in the central volume. These were also fully glazed to offer panoramic views of the surrounding landscape.

“Centred around a concrete core with suspended corner bays, the tower minimises its perimeter structure, creating slender edges and expansive double-height views, forming the distinct structural system that defines the tower’s identity,” said Marco Tessaro, associate at RSHP.

Louvred panels on the facade and vents were incorporated into the glazing to create natural ventilation throughout the building while reducing energy consumption.

This was one of the methods used to help the project achieve China’s 3-star Green Building Evaluation Standard, which is equivalent to LEED Gold.

A six-level public podium is connected to the east wing, creating a roof terrace where half of the space is reserved for greenery.

The studio added extensive vegetation, a feature wall and water elements to improve biodiversity and help create a calm environment for socialising.

“The building’s natural ventilation, green rooftop spaces, and energy-efficient facade define a truly sustainable development that reduces consumption while enhancing wellbeing for both occupants and the wider community,” said Wenchao Zhou, associate at RSHP.

Mega triangular trusses on the podium roof help transfer the load of the east wing to the building’s central core.

Another viewing platform is located on the building’s west wing, which, together with the podium roof terrace, was designed to invite public visitors and private tenants alike to engage in outdoor activities such as observing migrating birds, a popular hobby for the locals.

According to RSHP, one of the challenges of the project was combining two separate briefs from different clients to create an uplifting mixed-use development as well as an office building with a bold and coherent architectural identity.

“Taking a holistic approach to the complex brief, RSHP’s design for Hetao Alpha has created an open and welcoming destination for work, retail, and leisure that achieves a bold architectural identity with a seamless transition between public and private space,” the studio explained.

The 13,640-square-metre public podium houses sports facilities, a library, retail, and a double-height arts exhibition space.

A passageway cuts through the north and south ends of the ground floor, helping to give the podium a floating look that reduces the perceived weight of the volume.

The entrance lobby for the office building can be found inside the podium. This double-height space is supported by a series of slim columns connected to the triangular trusses above on the podium roof.

A metro station was integrated into the basement, which also has a sunken plaza with retail stores.

“Spacious, open, and welcoming, the tower and podium integrate seamlessly to form an elegant composition that maximises connectivity with the wider public realm and the park to the east,” said Richard Paul, director of RSHP.

“With glazed office wings overlooking Shenzhen’s wetlands and a public podium offering diverse activity, the development achieves a serene, flexible environment that accommodates a wide range of uses,” he continued.

Elsewhere in China, RSHP has completed a 186-metre mixed-use skyscraper in central Shanghai, as well as a vast convention centre in Zhengzhou, with 16 exhibition halls connected by a mile-long elevated walkway

Client: SH-STIC, Shenzhen – Hongkong Science and Technology Innovation Cooperation Zone Development CO, LTD Construction cost: £120mSite area: 11,118 square metres Gross floor area: 96,223 square metresLocal design institute: CCDI GroupGeneral contractor: China Railway Construction Engineering Group (CRCEG)Structural engineer: CCDI GroupMEP engineer: CCDI GroupFacade consultant: CCDI GroupLandscape consultant: CCDI GroupLighting consultant: PUDI

#8952. ‘Another way of engaging the city’: centrepiece of Art Week Tokyo sends visitors to venues across the capital

“Even within the same city of Tokyo, each place and space has a completely different face.” The Japanese feminist collective Multiple Spirits is curating a show at Waitingroom Yasuhide Kuge

AWT Focus launched in 2023 as Art Week Tokyo’s centrepiece exhibition platform. Last year it took place at the Okura Museum of Art, where Adam Szymczyk brought together more than 50 artists for What Is Real? For 2026, the format is being radically reconfigured. In collaboration with Curated by, the Vienna gallery festival, Art Week Tokyo has invited curators to organise ten exhibitions across ten participating galleries and art spaces around the city.

The shift brings AWT Focus closer to the structure of Art Week Tokyo itself. Unlike an art fair, the annual event has no central venue: its network of museums and galleries is dispersed across the metropolis, with free shuttle buses connecting participating venues during the week. Running from 4 to 8 November, this year’s fifth full edition will bring together a record 56 museums and galleries.

“From the start Art Week Tokyo was conceived of as an event that would evolve in dynamic response to the city,” says Atsuko Ninagawa, the event’s co-founder and director. The multi-venue AWT Focus, she says, offers “another way of engaging the city and its diverse audiences”. Rather than organising the programme around a single curatorial proposition, “the idea is to bring multiple worldviews to Japan”.

Those worldviews take varied forms. Among the ten projects are Polish curator Maria Brewińska’s presentation of Japan-born, Poland-based artist Koji Kamoji at Take Ninagawa gallery; Ekow Eshun’s presentation of British-Sierra Leonean artist Julianknxx at the Space Un arts and culture venue; and New York-based curator Augusto Arbizo’s intergenerational exploration of painting at Yutaka Kikutake Gallery. Elsewhere, curators Greg Dvorak and Kenji Ono draw on the contrasting post-war histories of eastern and western Tokyo for the latest edition of the recurring exhibition series The Constitution of Japan, at Mujin-to Production, with a second site at Aoyama | Meguro.

For Multiple Spirits, the feminist collective founded by Mai Endo and Mika Maruyama, the dispersed format allows the character of the city itself to enter the programme. “Even within the same city of Tokyo, each place and space has a completely different face,” the collective says. “The location, surrounding environment and flow of people differ from venue to venue”, allowing each exhibition to take shape in relation to its surroundings. The collective also sees potential in moving away from a single curatorial voice towards a more open structure in which “different perspectives by many practitioners” can co-exist.

Multiple Spirits’s exhibition at Waitingroom, Patchwork of Ruffled Wings, draws together zines, textiles and other works through what the collective calls a “vine-like archive”, connecting “girls’ culture, queer culture, artistic movements, underground culture and social movements”. Rather than arranging these histories into a linear genealogy, Multiple Spirits is interested in how cultures are interrupted, inherited or grafted onto others, and how they are shaped by changing social conditions, taboos and forms of resistance. Art Week Tokyo, it suggests, can itself become a site where people with different backgrounds and practices meet, allowing different perspectives to connect while retaining their complexity.

The collective’s own history also complicates any simple division between the “local” and the “international”. Multiple Spirits was founded in Austria and continues to work between Vienna and Tokyo, collaborating with people across national, racial, ethnic and gender backgrounds. Through AWT Focus, the collective hopes to show that the Tokyo art scene encompasses “alternative and diverse activities” that extend beyond any single urban context and are connected through multiple networks.

For the Seoul-based curator Jaemin Shin, meanwhile, working with Tokyo-based artist and poet Natsumi Aoyagi offers another way of reading the city. Shin first worked with Aoyagi for the 2025 exhibition Patchwork! at the WilloW in Seoul. Her AWT Focus exhibition, Possible Words, Possible World, at Misa Shin Gallery, brings together two multimedia installations concerned with systems of recording and ownership.

Language for Our Relation: A Demonstration (2025) by Natsumi Aoyagi Photo: Minji Yi; © the artist; courtesy of The WilloW, Seoul

One takes Tokyo Bay’s artificial islands—territories whose histories begin with administrative records such as land registries—as its point of departure; the other reimagines relationships beyond ownership and Japan’s family-registration system.

Shin sees parallels between the systems of registration and record-keeping, and patriarchal structures in Japan and Korea. But Aoyagi’s work has also altered her perception of the Japanese capital. “Looking at Tokyo through her work, I stopped seeing just a rigid megacity,” Shin says. Instead, she came to see it as “not a singular structure, but one with fluid and fragile boundaries”.

For Shin, the new AWT Focus format creates further opportunities for such readings. An outside curator can translate culturally specific ideas into different contexts, she says, creating new connections, while the dispersed format enables a more intimate engagement with particular parts of the city. Rather than simply presenting artworks, she says, an exhibition can connect to specific urban and social sectors in Tokyo, shifting the curatorial gesture towards “actively inhabiting the city” through artworks and ideas.

For Eshun, who returns to Art Week Tokyo after participating last year, the new structure also creates opportunities for exchange among curators. “Part of the goal for me, in travelling internationally to events like Art Week Tokyo, is to discover how different curators are working and thinking and making exhibitions,” he says. “It’s a great opportunity to meet and talk and build new relationships.”

Installation view of Julianknxx’s What Colours Can We Dream in This Night Filled with Salt (2025) at the 36th Bienal de São Paulo. The artist’s AWT Focus exhibition is titled How Much Light Must I Consume? © Levi Fanan; courtesy Fundação Bienal de São Paulo

His exhibition How Much Light Must I Consume? will be Julianknxx’s first in Japan. The artist’s practice spans geographies and diasporic histories, while the central work draws on oral traditions from Comoros, the small island nation near Mozambique. Eshun resists predicting what connections those histories might generate in Tokyo. “All successful art is predicated on discovery, on unknowing, on the revelation of unanticipated connection,” he says. “The hope is that it sparks new ways of seeing and imagining.”

Art Week Tokyo’s organisers are also looking beyond the encounters generated during a single week in November. Previous editions have recorded rising audiences: overall attendance increased by 33% between 2022 and 2023 and by another 15% in 2024, while international VIP participation has also grown sharply.

Ninagawa argues that the event has helped build networks and visibility that participating institutions and galleries can continue to develop independently. Internationally, she believes Art Week Tokyo has helped “rebrand” a Japanese art scene that had been overlooked in global discourse. Overseas visitors who once came to Tokyo primarily interested in the city as a tourist destination, she says, are increasingly arriving specifically to learn about Japanese artists and art history—and going on to develop projects from those encounters.

Eshun offers a more personal account of that process. Tokyo’s art world may appear smaller than those of some other global centres, he says, “but it runs deep”. He describes himself as still mapping its “paths and roads and streams and tributaries”, with Art Week Tokyo helping him “find my way and keep exploring”.

That metaphor feels particularly apt this year. Until now, travelling across Tokyo was primarily how visitors moved between Art Week Tokyo’s participating institutions. With the new AWT Focus, movement through the city is no longer simply a means of reaching its exhibitions; it has become part of the curatorial proposition itself.

Augusto Arbizo assembles works by six Japanese and international artists into an intergenerational conversation on painting practices that offer a space for quiet concentration amid the frenetic visual culture of the city.

Erika Verzutti’s Study for Dog Sculpture (2025) Photo: Eduardo Ortega; Courtesy the artist and Fortes D’Aloia & Gabriel, São Paulo/Rio de Janeiro

Artist Erika Verzutti and curator Julie Boukobza extend their collaboration for this exhibition of monoprints, which builds on a show of sculptures the two produced for a room at the Hôtel Balzac, Paris, in 2025.

Curators Greg Dvorak and Kenji Ono take charge of the fourth edition of this recurring exhibition using art to reread the Constitution of Japan. This year’s edition includes works by video artist Fuyuhiko Takata, multimedia duo MES and more.

Martin Clark, the director of London’s Camden Art Centre, oversees a new site-specific project by Nobuko Tsuchiya, a UK-based Japanese artist known for her sculptural assemblages of found objects that play on the enigmatic and the familiar.

Veteran US museum director Jeremy Strick presents the first exhibition in Japan of leading Los Angeles-based painter Mary Weatherford, with a focus on recent works on paper accompanied by one of her signature neon paintings.

Korean independent curator Jaemin Shin guides this solo project by emerging artist Natsumi Aoyagi, whose multimedia installations juxtapose poems, moving images, AI-generated imagery, recorded sound and fiction. The resulting works generate multilayered meanings shaped by a speculative imagination.

London-based artist Julianknxx addresses the history of Africa and its diasporas through poetry, performance, film, music and sculpture. The artist’s first exhibition in Japan, curated by Ekow Eshun, will feature multimedia works inspired by salt as well as a series of special choral performances.

Koji Kamoji left his native Japan for Poland in 1959 and went on to become a key figure in the Polish avant-garde art scene. Warsaw-based curator Maria Brewińska has worked closely with the 91-year-old artist to develop an exhibition reflecting on the connection between art and survival.

The queer feminist collective Multiple Spirits uses its eponymous zine as a base for producing artworks, exhibitions and other activities. Patchwork of Ruffled Wings explores the concept of the “vine-like archive” through the presentation of printed matter, textiles and other works by Japanese and international artists.

Sophie Nys’s If Nature Didn’t, Warner’s Will (2012) Courtesy of Galerie Greta Meert, Brussels.

Olivier Mignon, the founding director of Keijiban in Kanazawa, juxtaposes works by two artists at XYZ collective. New York-based photographer Taro Masushio addresses themes of queer embodiment and the politics of the gaze, while Brussels-based sculptor Sophie Nys investigates the relationship between language and objects.

#8951. In South Carolina, Artistic Freedom Is on the Ballot This November

A governor-appointed arts commission has denied funding from two LGBTQ+ organizations and an artist focused on immigration issues.

As South Carolinians prepare for Election Day on November 3, some are considering how their vote could affect the governor-appointed South Carolina Arts Commission (SCAC). In August, the agency established new guidelines prohibiting the funding of work that promotes "any ideology," echoing Trump’s rhetoric, and denied funding to an artist and two LGBTQ+ performing arts organizations earlier this month.

Comprised of nine governor-appointed volunteers, the SCAC has distributed over $132 million in grants to artists, schools, and cultural organizations across South Carolina since Governor Robert E. McNair established it in 1967. Over the past year, the agency has come under scrutiny for singling out LGBTQ+ arts groups in its grant decisions and implementing opaque funding restrictions. After an August 20 board meeting, the commission announced that grantees cannot direct funds to "promote any ideology."

"Without a clear definition of 'ideology' or 'promotion,' the new rule can be used to suppress almost any cultural activity that touches on society, history, identity, religion, science, or politics," the National Coalition Against Censorship (NCAC) wrote in a statement published yesterday, October 28, condemning the SCAC. The grant rule echoes President Donald Trump's targeting of federal grant funding for projects related to "gender ideology," a vague term used to push essentialist and anti-trans concepts of gender.

"SCAC's adoption of a new grant rule after proposals had been independently reviewed and vetted is a problem in itself," Elizabeth Larison, director of arts and culture advocacy at NCAC, added in a statement to Hyperallergic. "But the fact that this rule is vague enough to allow government appointees to veto any projects they don't personally like is a threat to artistic freedom and democratic principles in South Carolina."

#8950. Pipo Nguyen-duy, Beloved Photography Professor, Murdered at 64

"He took a lot of joy in his everyday life. He sought to make really beautiful photos, and strove to make the world a more beautiful place," said his former student.

Pipo Nguyen-duy, a beloved 64-year-old photography professor and the studio art department chair at Oberlin College in Ohio, and his wife, 56-year-old Tran Thi Phong, were fatally shot in their home on Wednesday, October 28.

Nguyen-duy's child and Phong's stepchild, 31-year-old Asia Nguyen-duy (birthname Daniel Jones), has been charged with their deaths and faces six counts of murder, one count of tampering with evidence, and four counts of felonious assault, per Oberlin Municipal Court records.

"I am deeply concerned about the impact of the devastating loss of Pipo to our community," Oberlin President Carmen Twillie Ambar wrote in a statement. "Pipo was beloved. During his years at Oberlin, he touched all of us through his passion for photography."

#8949. MoMA, Centre Pompidou, and M+ Announce Novel Collection Alliance

The partnership between the museums will include intermuseum loans and joint exhibitions.

Leaders at Manhattan's Museum of Modern Art (MoMA), Paris's Centre Pompidou, and M+ in Hong Kong signed an agreement granting unprecedented access to each museum's holdings for increased viewership, more collaborative curation, and additional research.

The alliance emerges on the eve of M+'s fifth anniversary at its physical location in Hong Kong's West Kowloon Cultural District, and just one year into MoMA director Christophe Cherix's tenure. The agreement follows a wave of institutional resource pooling and joint acquisitions that swelled in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic as museums seek to reduce overhead costs while navigating major deficits. In another shakeup earlier this year, the Metropolitan Museum of Art announced its forthcoming merger with Ronald Lauder's Neue Galerie, which is set to commence in 2028.

“Museums must evolve to reflect the complexity of our world,” said M+ Museum Director Suhanya Raffel in a press statement on the alliance.

Previous collaborations between M+, home to the Sigg collection of contemporary Chinese art among thousands of other contemporary works from across Asia, and the other two museums foregrounded this agreement. The Hong Kong-based museum signed a memorandum of understanding with the MoMA in early 2025 that established shared curatorial, conservation, and scholarship objectives. And this spring, M+ and Centre Pompidou entered a strategic partnership to “strengthen the cultural dialogue” between their respective continents through joint exhibitions, collections sharing, and a funded fellowship.

#8948. ‘Mariko Mori anticipated the zeitgeist’: curator Alexandra Monroe on her new show and how Japan's art scene has changed

Mariko Mori’s Birth of a Star (1995) Courtesy Mori Art Museum

The US curator Alexandra Munroe has three decades of experience working closely with Japanese institutions, going back to her landmark survey Japanese Art after 1945: Scream Against the Sky at the Yokohama Museum of Art in 1994. Now she is back in the country as the co-curator of the current Mariko Mori retrospective at the Mori Art Museum in Tokyo. The show is a collaboration with the Solomon R. Guggenheim Foundation, where she is a senior curator at large, and has been co-curated with the Mori Art Museum’s director Mami Kataoka.

The Art Newspaper: How has Japan’s museum ecology changed over the years?

Alexandra Munroe: It’s changed enormously. The Yokohama Museum of Art opened in 1989, anticipating the museum boom of the 1990s when municipalities and prefectures across Japan were opening new institutions with extraordinary buildings designed by architects like Fumihiko Maki, Arata Isozaki and others.

Although there were important precursors like the Museum of Modern Art, Kamakura, established in 1951, and the National Museum of Modern Art, Tokyo, established in 1952, there was remarkably little concerted historical understanding of Modern and contemporary Japanese art and its role in global art history. Around the early 1990s, curators and scholars were piecing together how such art had evolved under the umbrella of post-war society—defeat in the Second World War, reconstruction, Americanisation—as well as through the contributions of Japanese artists abroad like Yoko Ono, Yayoi Kusama and On Kawara. The new museums contributed to the tremendous growth of the field, both within Japan and internationally.

Curator Alexandra Munroe © Solomon R. Guggenheim Foundation, New York/David Heald

Successive institutions have built on that legacy. It’s been gratifying to see the Mori Art Museum develop into a global museum under the trailblazing leadership of Mami Kataoka. The recent Sou Fujimoto exhibition was one of the greatest architectural shows I’ve ever seen, while the solo shows of Louise Bourgeois, Ai Weiwei and Lee Bul, going back 20 years now, are among the most influential for those artists staged anywhere in the world.

All of this has been aided by the simultaneous transformation of the gallery scene, with a proliferation of experimental galleries since 1994, not to mention international galleries representing Japanese artists or movements like Gutai, Mono-ha and Neo-Pop. I also appreciate the role that Benesse Art Site Naoshima has played, through the vision of patron Soichiro Fukutake, in the emergence of Japan as a contemporary art superpower. Only a few hundred people attended the opening of Benesse House Museum in 1992. Now events like the Setouchi Triennale draw millions to the islands when the home population is a few thousand. And Benesse’s commissioning programme has given artists like Yukinori Yanagi, Rei Naito and Shinro Ohtake a platform for staging their most ambitious works.

Recent decades have seen a remarkable expansion of museums in China and Korea, Southeast Asia and the Gulf. At the same time, institutions around the world are facing new challenges with austerity measures and a withdrawal of public support for art. What lessons can Japan offer other art scenes?

I have great admiration—and some envy—for the public funding of Japanese art museums. The Japanese model of collecting regionally yet within an international context is something to emulate. There’s also something to be said for collections focusing on artists whose histories were shaped by the places where they grew up and, in some cases, ran away from. The Nagoya City Art Museum has extraordinary holdings of On Kawara’s works, including rare early reportage pieces, even though he left the region in his teens. The Ashiya City Museum of Art and History’s collection of Gutai is unparalleled in the world. And the Fukuoka Asian Art Museum, under the guidance of curators like Kuroda Raiji, has sought to map and reimagine artistic exchanges in Asia.I commend all the brilliant scholarship that has emerged out of these enterprises.

That said, in recent years Japan has retreated from its post-war identification as an international country. One motivation for doing the Mori show is to stimulate a revival in collaborations that can help bring the work done in Japan into international circulation.

Mariko Mori’s Play with Me (1994) Courtesy Mori Art Museum

Collaborations between Japanese and international institutions typically take the form of touring shows, whereas intensive co-productions are rare. How did the collaboration between the Guggenheim and the Mori Art Museum come about?

It’s called synergy! In the summer of 2024 both Mami Kataoka and I had begun talking to Mariko Mori about staging a retrospective and we combined forces. Mariko rose to meteoric stardom in the 1990s for Cyborg (1994-95), the first of her series of photomurals inserting herself as a cyborg, and later a Buddhist-inflected deity, into digitally rendered settings. That interest in technology subsequently found form in complex multisensory environments like Wave UFO (1999-2002), the first artwork to incorporate brainwave biofeedback.

I was interested in reappraising Mariko’s work in the current context of technology-based art, specifically digital technologies. Technology is not an obstacle to humanism for her, but a means of envisioning a new kind of humanism that allows for higher states of consciousness. At the same time, Mariko’s engagement with [pre-historic Japanese] Jōmon culture, alternative belief systems and the afterlife resonates with Indigenous and First Nations artists incorporating Indigenous knowledge into critiques of Western epistemes of modernity and linear time.

For her part, Mami has a longstanding interest in art that addresses spirituality in the modern era, which opens up a critique of the dominant trends of contemporary art as established by market forces and Western institutions, so I think Mariko’s work felt urgent to that curatorial research and practice.

Yes. Collaboration is integral to Guggenheim programmes like the Asian Art Initiative and the UBS MAP Global Art Initiative. We have consistently partnered with museums, curators and artists across Asia to help us collectively think through the larger argument of global art history and how to present exhibitions that map histories and ideas beyond the Eurocentric canon. The collaboration with the Mori is a direct outcome of that, and I’d say it’s a direct outcome of the Mori’s profoundly international outlook as well.

Alexandra Munroe with Japanese artist Yoko Ono at the AICA (International Association of Art Critics) Awards ceremony, New York, in 2001 Courtesy Alexandra Munroe

A compelling retrospective does not just look back but also shows how the artist was ahead of their time. In what ways have we finally caught up with Mariko Mori?

Mariko’s work resonates with the writings of the contemporary philosopher Yuk Hui, who argues for a holistic understanding of technology grounded in Eastern thought and cosmologies, or “cosmotechnics”, as opposed to its bifurcation in modern Western traditions. Mariko anticipated that zeitgeist as a Japanese woman artist who conducted deep research into schools of thought like Pure Land Buddhism and Jōmon cosmology alongside contemporary sciences of the mind.

These are areas of enormous interest to artists now. Look at LuYang, a young Chinese artist who is a serious practitioner of Tantric Buddhism and uses game engines to illustrate themes of transmigration of the soul, multiple selves and the world as an illusion. The Korean new media artist Ayoung Kim also looks up to Mariko for unabashedly drawing parallels between art and technology as ways to “recalibrate our reality”, as Ayoung told me.

I think there will be an enthusiastic response to Mariko’s work from younger artists who are interested in storytelling and altered states of mind, artists who are seeking to break free of the lingering hang-ups of Western art, and anyone looking to just get away to another world.

• Mariko Mori: All That Shines, Mori Art Museum, 31 October-28 March 2027

#8947. "If AI can do most of what we think an architect does, maybe we have defined the profession too narrowly"

Architects are increasingly, and existentially, anxious about AI. It can already produce images, generate endless options, manipulate form, draft text, analyse information and take on increasing amounts of technical production. The predictable professional response is to become defensive: to identify the bits of architectural work that machines cannot yet do, protect them, regulate them and insist ever more loudly on the special status of the architect.

This is absolutely the wrong response. Architecture has always had a tendency to retreat when it feels threatened: as its actual control over the production of buildings has diminished, it has clung ever more tightly to authorship, professional territory and the idea that certain activities somehow belong uniquely to architects. AI merely makes the weakness of that position more visible.

If AI can do most of what we think an architect does, maybe we have defined the profession too narrowly. If producing drawings, images, options and information constitutes our entire claim to value, we are defining our value in far too limited terms.

We are still, to an astonishing degree, trained to imagine ourselves as mini Corbusiers

The profession has spent decades confusing the production of architectural artefacts with architectural intelligence, and we have run out of road. We are still, to an astonishing degree, trained to imagine ourselves as mini Corbusiers. If we design a back extension, give it a sufficiently enigmatic name, photograph it carefully, attach enough rhetoric, we somehow persuade ourselves that we have made Ronchamp.

Architectural culture has encouraged this inflation for decades, in that every modest building becomes a manifesto, every detail becomes a proposition and every project arrives with the expectation that it should reveal something profound about architecture itself.

But the age of the hero is exhausted. The profession no longer has the cultural authority, the economic power or, frankly, the public attention to sustain this fantasy, however enthusiastically we continue to perform it for one another. AI may simply accelerate the reckoning: if machines can generate endless formal novelty and beautiful images, the architect’s claim to importance can’t continue to rest on being the singular creative intelligence who produces the special object.

Click here to read more about the issues facing architecture in our Performance Review series.

The economic model that supported this fantasy is broken too. Architecture remains notoriously poorly paid relative to the length and cost of its education, the responsibility it carries and the hours it routinely demands. Yet architects have tolerated this for decades because the profession offered another form of compensation – the most important thing of all for architects: recognition, via awards, publications, photographs, lectures, the approval of our peers and the possibility that one small project might provide a tiny share of architectural glory.

We have accepted low pay, long hours, insecure employment and unpaid competitions partly because we have been sold the idea that authorship itself is a reward. If the work is meaningful enough, beautiful enough or visible enough, perhaps the sacrifice will somehow be justified.

That bargain has always been dubious, but it now looks increasingly absurd. Most architects will never become Corbusier, however many evenings they work, and most projects will never become Ronchamp, however much rhetoric is wrapped around them. Architectural status – irrelevant to most outside a handful of people in the profession – has nevertheless become a kind of substitute currency, and architecture has been remarkably successful at persuading people to accept less of the real kind in return.

We need to expand what clients understand architectural value to be, and therefore what they are prepared to pay architects to do

AI makes the bargain even harder to sustain. If the production work on which fees have traditionally depended becomes faster and cheaper, defending the same exhausted model will simply drive fees and salaries down further.

The answer cannot be to produce the same things more efficiently for less money. We need to expand what clients understand architectural value to be, and therefore what they are prepared to pay architects to do.

The more interesting response to AI is not to ask how architects protect what they currently do, but what architects might become capable of doing if some of that work no longer defines them.

With this, architectural intelligence becomes most useful where there is no simple answer. The most interesting projects rarely arrive as neatly defined problems awaiting visually arresting solutions. Instead, they involve conflicting needs, uncertain briefs, difficult sites, volatile markets, limited resources, political constraints and people who want different things. They involve other consultants who know things the architect does not, clients who change their minds, communities whose needs cannot be compressed into a consultation report and materials that stubbornly refuse to behave predictably like lines on a drawing.

This mess is the essence of architecture. The most useful architect is not simply the person who generates a solution, they are someone able to enter an unresolved situation, figure out what the problem actually is, connect different forms of knowledge, make spatial judgements and establish enough structure for something useful to emerge via collective endeavour rather than their own brilliance.

This demands a radically different model of authorship, which is less author and more host. That doesn’t mean becoming a passive facilitator, it means knowing how to bring people together, anticipating problems, establish frameworks within which others can work, exercising judgement, knowing when to intervene, and knowing when to shut up and not be the hero.

It also changes what architects might reasonably be paid for. At present, architecture fees are overwhelmingly organised around a relatively linear journey from brief, to concept, to information, to construction and eventually completion, but much of the work that might make architecture genuinely valuable sits awkwardly around the edges of that process.

Understanding a problem before a brief becomes fixed is often unpaid. Working seriously with communities gets compressed into consultation. Engaging directly with materials and makers is treated as secondary to design. Returning after occupation to understand what worked and what failed is rarely properly funded. Helping a building adapt over years barely appears in conventional fee structures at all.

There is an irony here, because for years architects have tried to make themselves more machine-like

But architects should be paid for diagnosis and briefing, for bringing different forms of knowledge together, for testing possibilities at full scale, negotiating spatial conflicts, post-occupancy work, adaptation and long-term stewardship. Practices should be able to maintain relationships with buildings and communities rather than disappearing at practical completion. Architecture fees might begin to pay for judgement over time, rather than simply production on the way towards an object.

This is not some romantic idea of architects becoming artists, activists or community workers instead of running viable businesses (which contemporary practice is not). Quite the opposite: it is about identifying forms of architectural value that are difficult to automate and, more importantly, are actually useful.

For the past 20 years, our educational initiative Studio in the Woods (pictured top and left) has accidentally provided a small laboratory for some of this. Its significance has never really been the timber structures that emerge over several days of co-production. Instead, the interesting aspect of Studio in the Woods is what happens when people design and make together under conditions in which the answer is not known beforehand, where ideas encounter the friction of weight, resistance, gravity, tools and materials. Where experts and non-experts work together as equals, and leadership moves according to what needs to happen next.

The skill of the architect in these situations is not to surrender judgement, but to exercise it differently. What should be negotiated? What can remain unresolved? Where is precision necessary? Where might uncertainty be productive? Who knows something that I do not? These are much more interesting questions for the future of the profession than whether AI can draw a convincing building.

There is an irony here, because for years architects have tried to make themselves more machine-like: eliminating uncertainty, standardising processes, increasing predictability, producing ever-more information and pretending that buildings can be completely resolved before anybody actually makes them. Now, machines are becoming extremely capable at exactly those things and we are surprised to find ourselves threatened, and we should stop trying to beat them at their own game.

Human architectural intelligence is at its richest when it is situated, relational and embodied. It involves judgement without complete information and responsibility for consequences that cannot be fully predicted. It means understanding materials as part of landscapes and economies, buildings as things that change through occupation, and design as something produced between many people rather than delivered by one.

None of this means drawings, technical knowledge, form or aesthetic judgement cease to matter. They matter enormously, but they are merely parts of architectural intelligence, not its definition.

The architect of the future does not need to be the person with the most original idea and the most charisma. They might instead be the person who can understand an uncertain situation, recognise what matters, establish a framework for action and create the conditions in which something richer than their own initial idea can emerge. AI may make the old version of the architect less necessary, but I’m not sure that is something we should mourn.

Piers Taylor is the founder of architecture practice Invisible Studio and the convenor of Studio in the Woods. He is professor of knowledge exchange in architecture at the University of the West of England and an external examiner at the Arts University Bournemouth, having previously held positions with the Architectural Association and the University of Cambridge. He holds a PhD from the University of Reading. He has presented several architecture shows on television including BBC programmes The House that £100k Built and The World’s Most Extraordinary Homes. His first book, Learning from the Local, was published in 2025.

A living trust is a legal arrangement where you (the grantor) transfer ownership of your assets to a trust entity that you also control (as trustee). It sounds circular, and in practice, during your lifetime, nothing changes about how you use your money and property. The magic happens when you die or become incapacitated.

During your lifetime: You are both the grantor and the trustee. You control everything. You can add or remove assets, change beneficiaries, modify terms, or dissolve the trust entirely. Your Social Security number is the trust's tax ID — there is no separate tax return. For practical purposes, nothing changes about your daily financial life.

If you become incapacitated: Your successor trustee immediately takes over management of trust assets. No court petition needed. No guardianship proceeding. No delay. This is a major advantage over a will, which provides zero protection during incapacity.

When you die: Your successor trustee distributes assets according to your trust document. No probate court. No public record. No waiting 6-18 months. Beneficiaries can typically receive assets within days or weeks.

A living trust essentially creates a private, self-executing transfer system that operates outside the court system entirely. For FI families who have spent years building wealth, this means your heirs receive the full value of your estate without probate eating into it.

The terms "revocable" and "irrevocable" describe whether you can change or dissolve the trust after creating it. This distinction has major implications for control, taxes, and asset protection.

Revocable living trust — the standard choice for most families:

You retain full control. You can amend the trust, add or remove assets, change beneficiaries, or dissolve it completely at any time. Because you maintain control, the IRS treats trust assets as yours — they are included in your taxable estate, and creditors can reach them. The primary benefit is probate avoidance and incapacity protection, not asset protection or tax reduction.

Irrevocable trust — the advanced tool for specific situations:

Once created, you generally cannot change or revoke it. You give up control of the assets placed inside. In exchange, you get benefits that a revocable trust cannot provide.

For most FI families: A revocable living trust is the right starting point. It provides the two biggest benefits — probate avoidance and incapacity protection — while letting you maintain complete control.

Creating a trust document is only half the job. A trust only controls assets that are titled in its name. An unfunded trust is a worthless piece of paper.

Assets you should transfer into your trust:

The re-titling process for real estate: This is the most critical step and requires recording a new deed. You transfer ownership from "John Smith" to "John Smith, Trustee of the John Smith Revocable Living Trust dated January 15, 2024." Contact your county recorder's office or have your attorney prepare the deed. Most counties charge $15-$75 for recording. Notify your mortgage company (they cannot call the loan due under the Garn-St. Germain Act for transfers to a revocable trust) and your homeowners insurance carrier.

Ongoing funding discipline: Every time you open a new bank account, buy property, or acquire significant assets, ask: "Should this be titled in my trust?" Create a simple checklist and review it annually. The most common estate planning failure is a perfectly drafted trust with assets still titled in the grantor's personal name.

A common concern is whether transferring your home into a trust triggers a due-on-sale clause in your mortgage. Under the federal Garn-St. Germain Depository Institutions Act of 1982, lenders cannot accelerate a mortgage when property is transferred to a revocable trust where the borrower remains a beneficiary and occupant. This protection applies to residential properties with fewer than five units. Your lender may ask for a copy of the trust document, but they cannot call the loan. Always notify your homeowners insurance company of the title change to ensure coverage remains valid.

A living trust is most valuable if your net worth exceeds $500K, you own property in multiple states, you want to avoid probate, or you want incapacity protection. If your estate is simple and under $500K, a will may be sufficient.

Online services (Trust & Will $399-$599, LegalZoom $399-$599) work for simple trusts. For complex situations or estates over $1M, an estate planning attorney ($1,500-$5,000) ensures proper drafting and funding.

Your trust document should name your trustee (you), successor trustee, beneficiaries, and detailed distribution instructions. Include provisions for incapacity and specific instructions for each major asset category.

Transfer real estate by recording new deeds. Retitle bank and brokerage accounts into the trust name. Complete the assignment of personal property document. This is the most critical step — an unfunded trust is useless.

Draft a pour-over will that directs any assets not in the trust to pour into it upon your death. This will also names guardians for minor children. Review and update both documents every 3-5 years.

A living trust is a legal entity you create during your lifetime that holds your assets. You serve as trustee and maintain full control. When you die or become incapacitated, a successor trustee you named manages and distributes assets to your beneficiaries — without probate or court involvement.

A revocable living trust costs $1,500-$3,000 through an estate planning attorney, or $399-$599 through online services like Trust & Will or LegalZoom. Irrevocable trusts cost $3,000-$10,000+ due to their complexity. Additional costs include deed preparation ($200-$500) for transferring real estate.

A revocable living trust does NOT reduce estate taxes — assets are still part of your taxable estate because you maintain control. Only irrevocable trusts remove assets from your taxable estate. However, with the federal estate tax exemption at $13.61 million per individual (2024), estate taxes only affect very large estates.

Yes, and you should be. With a revocable living trust, you serve as your own trustee during your lifetime. You maintain complete control over all trust assets — buying, selling, spending, and investing exactly as you did before. Your successor trustee only takes over upon your death or incapacity.

A will goes through probate court (public, 6-18 months, costs 3-7% of estate). A living trust avoids probate entirely (private, days to weeks, minimal cost). A trust also provides incapacity protection, which a will does not. However, a will can name guardians for minor children, which a trust cannot.

Yes. You need a pour-over will to catch any assets not titled in the trust and to name guardians for minor children. The trust handles your major assets and avoids probate. The will serves as a safety net for everything else.

#8945. 10 Years Later, Magenta Plains Is Still Embracing the Unexpected

An anniversary exhibition spotlights the artists who’ve made the gallery one of Lower Manhattan’s most adventurous success stories.

Olivia Smith had a thriving career running Exhibition A on the Upper East Side, a company that sells original contemporary art editions, when artists Chris Dorland and David Deutsch approached her in 2015 about opening a gallery on the Lower East Side.

Smith had worked with hundreds of artists producing limited edition prints, but she had never managed a commercial gallery or negotiated with museums before. Still, she felt a kinship with Dorland and Deutsch, who found a ground-floor storefront on Allen Street and needed help programming it. First they had to agree on a name, as long as it wasn’t their own on the door.

“We wanted something expansive and open-ended,” Smith told Hyperallergic. “We felt Magenta Plains represented a place, but we didn’t know what that place was that we were building yet.”

A decade later, Magenta Plains has helped define what the Downtown contemporary art scene can offer the world. The gallery, which outgrew its original location and currently occupies a 4,500-square-foot space at 149 Canal Street, has featured groundbreaking technology-influenced installations, sculptures, and paintings, selections of which are on display in its 10 Year Anniversary show, up through October 31.

I'm in my fifties and far too old to use youth slang. But even I've come to realise that in recent years, the kids have started using "NPC", aka non-player character, as a term of ridicule for people in real life.

That makes sense, because typically in video games, the people who walk past you on the street are visual wallpaper. They give the impression that other humans are around, but they have no individuality.

This is exactly why the 2021 film Free Guy, in which Ryan Reynolds lives a repetitive, meaningless existence in a video game world, worked so well. We were all already in on the joke.

But now comes Grand Theft Auto 6, and its makers, Rockstar Games, are about to blow the concept of non-player characters right open.

In a cover feature for Edge, Creative Bloq's sister print magazine, the studio reveals it art-directed every one of the game’s NPCs, creating around 600,000 animations in the process.

Normally, procedural systems assemble background NPCs, making them largely interchangeable. Grand Theft Auto VI's non-player characters, however, will have their own personalities. Which means any Free Guy sequel (long mooted, but never confirmed) may have to rethink its premise entirely.

According to the Edge article, Rockstar set up a dedicated LA-based team of writers, directors and producers whose job was to make the pedestrians of Leonida, the game’s fictional take on Florida, feel individually realised.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

In practice, this means NPCs have personality traits that shape how they react to you. These include their temperament and aggression, where they are, what they’ve seen and how you’ve treated them. Different districts even have their own demographic and professional mix.

Rob Nelson, co-studio head at Rockstar North, describes a process of constantly asking how people might behave. “Who’s going to be aggressive? How many people will go for a weapon? How many are going to test me?”

Not only is this making me even more excited to play the game – even more excited than this brilliant GTA/South Park tie-in or these saucy GTA ads – it also says a lot about where we are as a culture. At a time when much of the creative industry is looking for faster, cheaper ways to fill digital worlds, Rockstar has done the opposite. And the rewards, I feel, will be immense.

We all talk endlessly about games being "immersive". But a city doesn’t feel real because of its landmarks. It feels real because of the passer-by who takes offence to something at precisely the wrong moment.

As D&AD’s AI & Creativity Report put it this year, AI has raised the floor, but not the ceiling. GTA 6 looks like an attempt to raise the ceiling the hard way, and I simply can't wait.

Tom May is an award-winning journalist specialising in art, design, photography and technology. He is the author of the books The 50 Greatest Designers (Arcturus) and Great TED Talks: Creativity (Pavilion). Tom was previously editor of Professional Photography magazine, associate editor at Creative Bloq, and deputy editor at net magazine.
