#8910. Seven Sculpture Shows to See in New York, From Modernist Masterpieces to Contemporary Anti-Monuments

In 1979, at the start of her essay “Sculpture in the Expanded Field,” art critic and theorist Rosalind Krauss wrote: “Over the last ten years rather surprising things have come to be called sculpture: narrow corridors with TV monitors at the ends; large photographs documenting country hikes; mirrors placed at strange angles in ordinary rooms; temporary lines cut into the floor of the desert.”

Since then, sculpture has ventured even wider, into realms such as crafts, gardens, and masquerades, all relatively unexplored in Krauss’s time by mainstream Western art. Sculpture can take the form of a bacterial culture, a free clinic, or a virtual world, and The Kiss can now refer to an 1882 marble by Rodin, a 1923–1925 limestone carving by Constantin Brancusi, or a 2003 constructed situation by Tino Sehgal.

How richly varied sculpture can be in our present moment is well illustrated in shows on view in New York this fall, from 15th-century bronzes to Beverly Buchanan’s site-specific memorials. Below are seven sculpture exhibitions on view during Art Week NYC, a citywide festival of art events co-organized by ARTnews, Art in America, and Artforum, taking place throughout the city from November 11 to 14.

To coincide with her inclusion in the 61st Venice Biennale (on view through November 22), Andrew Edlin is showing works by Beverly Buchanan (1940–2015), whose art has recently attracted renewed attention. Curated by Aurélie Bernard Wortsman, the exhibition will include Buchanan’s 1970s abstract paintings, made during a brief but successful career in New York, as well as sculptures produced after her move to Georgia in 1976. These include her handcrafted “shack sculptures” based on the vernacular architecture of the American South, as well as abstract cast-concrete works placed in galleries, her garden, and most famously at the marshland site of an 1803 slave rebellion (Marsh Ruins [Marshes of Glynn, Brunswick, GA], 1981). Often known only through photographs, memorials like this one “resist the idea of monument as something fixed or permanent,” Wortsman told ARTnews, “instead engaging with the passage of time, displacement, and transformation.”

November 6–December 19, 392 Broadway, 2nd floor

Following a well-received solo exhibition last year at Château Shatto in Los Angeles, Charlie Engelman is showing a new group of sculptures at Pietro Alexander. Like the works he presented in LA, these pieces are made from Engelman’s go-to materials—flocked high-density foam, cast aluminum, and 500-year-old redwood—all related to California’s natural and industrial past. Also as before, they derive from the artist’s research into biology, design, and art history while conjuring such quintessentially West Coast products as Arts and Crafts furniture, California Deco buildings, and Hollywood Regency decor. The two redwood sculptures here are said to be homages to Louise Bourgeois’s worktable and ceramic sculptor Ken Price’s banding wheels, respectively, while a winding string of forked polyurethane forms, titled Vene Cava, refers to the large veins that, like miniature biological freeways, carry deoxygenated blood from the body back to the heart.

November 5—January 7, 2027, 59 Wooster Street, 2nd floor

At Paula Cooper, an exhibition of sculptures, drawings, and prints by Pop artist Claes Oldenburg (1929—2022) revisits “Six Themes,” a traveling survey show organized in 1975 that explored a half dozen of the artist’s recurring subjects: a geometric Mickey Mouse head based on the shape of a movie projector seen in profile, a three-way electric plug, a cigarette butt, a clothespin, a typewriter eraser, and a baseball mitt. The most notable of the artists who translated Pop art into sculpture, Oldenburg made versions of each of these subjects in a wide variety of scales and materials over the course of his career. Shown here are works ranging from a four-foot-high stuffed and painted canvas clothespin to an 18-inch-long, cast aluminum cigarette butt.

November 5—December 19, 534 West 21st Street

Born into a family with a ceramics workshop in Cairo, Egyptian-American sculptor Ibrahim Said creates intricately hand-carved clay vessels that bow to multiple religious and craft traditions of the Middle East. References to ancient Egyptian, Coptic, and Islamic art come together in works that combine centuries-old, and even millennia-old, patterns and symbols with contemporary forms. Said’s show at Yossi Milo coincides with the conclusion of his time as one of the three inaugural artists in the Metropolitan Museum of Art and Vacheron Constantin Artisan Residency. A program “recognizing artisanal practices that revive, reimagine, or reinterpret traditional knowledge and technical skill,” the 18-month residency granted Said sustained access to the Met’s collection, resulting in the development of the body of work shown here.

Through January 9, 2027, 245 Tenth Avenue

The blockbuster exhibition “Siena: The Rise of Painting, 1300—1350,” presented at the Metropolitan Museum of Art and the National Gallery, London, in 2024—25, explored Siena’s palmy days, when the Italian city was famed as a center of religious paintings by such masters as Duccio, Simone Martini, and Pietro and Ambrogio Lorenzetti. Its run as a hub of painterly innovation ended with the coming of the Black Death in 1348, which wiped out two-thirds of Siena’s population (including the Lorenzettis) and brought artistic activity there to a standstill. A new show at the Frick picks up Siena’s story 100 years later, after the radically transformed city had reestablished itself as a locus of high art, this time for its bronze figurative sculpture. The exhibition features some 40 artworks—virtually all of the surviving bronzes of the period able to travel—by the likes of Vecchietta, Francesco di Giorgio, and Donatello.

Through January 18, 2027, 1 East 70th Street

Less than a decade ago, Pittsburgh-based sculptor Thaddeus Mosley’s graceful wooden abstractions were relatively unknown beyond his hometown, but his inclusion in the 2018 Carnegie International gained him a wider following. On the heels of its spring show of recent glass pieces by Mosley, who died in March at the age of 99, Karma is presenting a group of his wood sculptures made between 1954 and 1968, along with paintings and collages from the same period. Smaller than the monumental sculptures he is known for, the three-dimensional works here show the artist shifting away from representation while, at the same time, communicating Mosley’s early and abiding interest in African art and how it inspired European modernists such as Picasso and Constantin Brancusi. “Without West Africa,” he once said, “there would be no Cubism.”

From the unlikeliest of materials—used automobile tires, initially scavenged, now gifted to her by companies like Michelin—Chakaia Booker wrests sculptures of baroque elegance. Grounded in the lineage of 20th-century Black abstraction (Al Loving was an early mentor), Booker’s tire works, which range in scale from intimate to room-size, tumble down walls in cascades of ringlets, curl into self-contained tangles, and mount upward in dust devil—like spirals. While her works have been variously read as tapping into African American traditions of reuse, as a commentary on environmental degradation—generally affecting Black communities more than white—or even as a reference to the exploitative rubber trade, Booker herself offers few clues, preferring to leave interpretations to the viewer. A new exhibition of her work at David Nolan showcases Booker’s skills in other mediums as well, combining her signature rubber works with collages, photographs, and a tapestry.

#8908. Rotterdam's Echo is a Tokyo-inspired listening bar inside the brutalist Groot Handelsgebouw

Photography by Sophia van den Hoek

Creative director Jeﬀ Hoogendijk, DJ and producer Khalil Ryahi and architect Paul Cournet have teamed up to open a listening bar in Rotterdam, featuring a bar made from shipping crates and ombré mirrors by Sabine Marcelis.

Inspired by visits to listening bars in Tokyo, the trio envisioned Echo as a flexible space that can host different events and activities, but primarily focuses on the experience of music.

Located on the ground floor of Groot Handelsgebouw, a post-war office block opposite Rotterdam Centraal station, the bar has an interior designed by Cournet’s architecture and design studio, Cloud.

Cournet said the idea was to adapt the concept of the listening bar to the creative energy of Rotterdam.

“We wanted to make it super local,” he told Dezeen.

The main bar, which functions as both a service counter and the DJ area, exemplifies this approach.

Built in collaboration with Barendregt’s Kistenfabriek, a company that manufactures wooden shipping crates, together with carpenter Simon Fitskie, it’s a reminder that Rotterdam is home to Europe’s largest seaport.

Its sides are printed with the words “handled with care”, which became Echo’s tagline.

“We thought it would be so cool make the bar an art crate because we treated everything, from music to hospitality, as if it were art,” said Cournet.

“We always wanted to do everything in the best way possible.”

The space features several works by Rotterdam-based designer Marcelis, who is Cournet’s partner.

Her signature ombré mirrors adorn the walls, reflecting shades of red and gold, while a linear resin lamp hangs above the bar.

Polish brand Tylko supplied much of the furniture, including the modular shelving that extends across the walls to create space for displaying vinyl.

Cournet previously worked with the furniture company on its Berlin showroom, a project that led to a collaboration with audio company Form Follows Frequency.

Together, they developed a colourful system of speakers and subwoofers that slot precisely into Tylko’s shelving, which launched earlier this year.

These speakers form part of the sound system for Echo, along with two sculptural speaker towers that stand either side of the bar.

“There’s a contrast between the rawness of the exposed concrete and the more refined elements, like the sound system or Sabine’s mirrors,” said Cournet.

“When you put them together, it creates a tension that I find interesting. The concrete feels a bit softer.”

ECHO is one of several listening bars to have opened recently – with others including Bar Bardo in Milan and Upstairs at Hausu in London – but it is the first of its kind in Rotterdam.

The space shifts from a coffee shop by day to a bar by night, and includes a curated retail offering.

It can also morph to accommodate exhibitions, listening sessions of 20 to 40 people, or seated dinners for up to 40 guests.

Since opening in early September, the team has invited various local record stores to contribute to the event programme.

“Rotterdam has this really long history with music, with a lot of famous DJs and people who were pioneers in the music scene in the 1990s and 2000s,” added Cournet.

“It feels like the project has really resonated with that community.”

Photography by Sophia van den Hoek

Executive Editor, ARTnews & Art in America

Ukraine’s prosecutor general reported that a Russian lieutenant general has been charged in absentia for ordering a missile strike that caused significant damage to the Hryhoriy Skovoroda National Literary Memorial Museum in the country’s Kharkiv region in the spring of 2022.

As reported by The Kyiv Independent, “According to the Prosecutor General, the Russian lieutenant general who ordered the attack is originally from the village of Chuhuiv in Kharkiv Oblast and commands Russia’s 6th Guards Air and Air Defense Forces Army.” Related Articles Pussy Riot Defiant After Russia Hands Down Harsh Prison Sentences in Absentia Ai Weiwei Brings Art and Activism to Ukraine's Front Line

The prosecutor general wrote, “The (lieutenant) general knew for certain that he was attacking not a military target but a monument of Ukrainian culture. Despite this, he gave the combat order to destroy it.”

The memorial museum dedicated to Skovoroda, an 18th-century philosopher steeped in the Socratic method, was housed in an estate where he lived the final years of his life and died in 1794. The institution was one of many damaged or destroyed during the siege of Ukraine. As ARTnews reported in a roundup of embattled cultural sites in the country, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said, after the attack in 2022, “Last night, the Russian army deployed one of its missiles to destroy the Hryhorii Skovoroda Museum in Kharkiv Region. A missile—to destroy a museum.”

As The Kyiv Independent reported, “Russia has repeatedly targeted Ukraine’s cultural heritage since the start of the full-scale war. As of September 2026, 2,161 cultural heritage sites and 2,665 cultural institutions in Ukraine had been damaged or destroyed, according to data collected by the Culture Ministry.”

#8905. In Reply to Senators’ Amicus Briefs, Austria, Albertina, and Leopold Museum Double Down on Unconstitutionality of HEAR Act

The Republic of Austria, the Albertina Museum, and the Leopold Museum Foundation—the latter two both in Vienna—filed a response Friday to amicus briefs submitted by two US senators, in which they repeat their claim that the updated Holocaust Expropriated Art Recovery (HEAR) Act violates Article III of the US Constitution and the Tenth Amendment.

Austria, the Albertina, and the Leopold are defendants in a suit brought by Timothy Reif, a descendant of Fritz Grünbaum, a Jewish cabaret performer and collector who was killed in a death camp in 1941. Reif is seeking the return of several works by Egon Schiele that he alleges were looted by the Nazis when they seized Grünbaum’s collection. The defendants dispute the claim, arguing that the works in question are part of the same cache that was exported from Austria by Grünbaum’s sister-in-law in the 1930s and then sold to a Swiss dealer in the 1950s. Related Articles Senators Blumenthal and Cornyn File Amicus Brief in Case of Heirs Suing for Nazi-Looted Egon Schiele Works Bolstered by New Laws, Lawsuits in Los Angeles Renew Bids for Restitution of Nazi-Looted Art

Although the defendants had previously argued in several motions that the HEAR Act is unconstitutional, this new filing responds to briefs submitted last month by the Department of Justice and by Senators Richard Blumenthal (Democrat of Connecticut) and John Cornyn (Republican of Texas). Those briefs presented additional legal precedent supporting the constitutionality of the HEAR Act. Friday’s response addresses each of those cases.Though the defendants “respect the work of the Senators and the Government, and their attention to trying to remedy at least some of the horrors of the Holocaust,” they believe that in passing the amended version of HEAR, “Congress exceeded its constitutional bounds,” the filing states.

Blumenthal and Cornyn did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

At the heart of the response are the 2025 amendments to the HEAR Act, which President Donald Trump signed into law last year. Originally signed in 2016, the act was set to expire in 2026; the amendments extend it indefinitely. Other key changes were meant to address several high-profile cases that had failed in court on technical grounds, including statutes of limitations that vary depending on the state in which a case is brought.

The defendants argue that the HEAR Act stops short of creating a federal law for art restitution, akin to federal copyright law, and in doing so “delegates the substantive means to restitute Nazi-looted art to the states,” the filing reads. Courts are then to rely on applicable state laws, but by eliminating defenses based on technicalities, the 2025 changes dictate how courts should rule on the cases before them.

As a result, the defendants argue, the HEAR Act violates both the Tenth Amendment, which states that any power not explicitly granted to the federal government belongs to the states, and Article III of the Constitution, specifically the separation-of-powers doctrine, which gives courts the authority to decide the cases before them and how to rule on them.

“By forbidding the federal courts from any longer considering these equitable defenses, Congress is intruding on the constitutional right and obligation of Article III courts to ‘decide’ such cases and controversies for themselves,” the defendants’ response reads.

One defense eliminated by the 2025 amendments is laches, under which an otherwise valid claim can be dismissed if the claimant unreasonably delayed bringing it. The change bars courts from conducting “any factfinding as to questions of whether ‘inexcusable delay’ by a plaintiff or the plaintiff’s predecessors caused the loss of critical evidence, resulting in ‘unfair prejudice’ to the current owner of allegedly stolen art,” the response states.

The filing adds, “By outlawing the laches defense in particular, which prevents unprovable allegations of Nazi theft from becoming de facto conclusive presumptions of Nazi theft, the HEAR Act unquestionably does compel particular factfinding in favor of plaintiffs.”

In a phone interview, William L. Charron, an attorney for the defendants, said the purpose of Friday’s filing was to respond directly to the additional arguments for the HEAR Act’s constitutionality raised by the Justice Department and Senators Blumenthal and Cornyn.

“The government and the Senators intervened and involved themselves in this case because they wanted to be heard as to their reasons why they believe the HEAR Act is constitutional, and so this was an opportunity for my clients to respond and explain why they respectfully disagree with those positions and respectfully believe the HEAR Act is unconstitutional,” he told ARTnews.

Charron said he believes Reif v. Republic of Austria can be decided without addressing the constitutionality of the HEAR Act. But if the courts decide they must rule on that question, he said, it is the kind of case that could eventually make its way to the Supreme Court.

“I believe these are important and serious issues,” Charron said of the arguments raised in the filing. “We have given the Court a number of arguments and grounds to dismiss the case without having to rule upon these constitutional questions. But if the Court decides that it does need to address the constitutionality of the HEAR Act, I certainly hope that it seriously considers the arguments that have been raised in this filing.”

#8904. What Is ‘Fiber Training’—And Why Should You Be Doing It?

With the fibermaxxing fad encouraging people to prioritize this chronically neglected nutrient, one issue keeps coming up: the side effects. As important as hitting your daily fiber goal is, your body doesn’t always make doing so easy. Fiber is difficult for your digestive system to break down and has to be handed off to bacteria in the colon instead (which is kind of its point), so piling on too much too fast can result in a barrage of painful, awkward, or inconvenient digestive symptoms—bloating, gas, stomach cramps, the whole nine yards.

To be clear, GI distress isn’t a sign to abandon your pursuit of a higher-fiber diet. “Even with fiber becoming a growing trend, people still greatly underestimate its importance and, also, just how many ways it benefits the human body,” Desiree Nielsen, RD, a recipe developer with a focus on plant-based nutrition, tells SELF. You’re probably familiar with fiber’s ability to keep you full, stave off constipation, and support gut health, but it wears plenty of other hats too, like lowering “bad” LDL cholesterol and stabilizing your blood sugar (not to mention reducing your risk for a slew of diseases in the long run). In fact, overlooking fiber is one of the top nutrition mistakes people make, according to experts.

But if you feel apprehensive at the thought of fighting constant stomach discomfort in the process of working to correct a fiber deficiency, we don’t blame you. In fact, it’s a complaint that Lisa Ganjhu, DO, a gastroenterologist at NYU Langone Health, hears all the time at work: “I have a lot of patients that will say ‘I ate more fiber, and now I’m really bloated and crampy,’” she says. Thankfully, there’s a way to curtail those disagreeable side effects so you can (comfortably) continue your fiber journey: a strategy Nielsen calls fiber training. Here’s what that involves, and how to start developing those “muscles.”

Fiber training is exactly what it sounds like: training your body to handle fiber better. It’s all about “slow, consistent increases in fiber to help you build your tolerance…while minimizing the potential symptoms,” Nielsen says.

You can think of fiber training kind of like preparing for a race. “In much the same way that you wouldn’t go out and run a marathon tomorrow if you haven’t run a mile before,” you need to work your way up to a high-fiber diet, Nielsen says. Similarly, Dr. Ganjhu compares it to a weightlifting regimen. Rather than lifting 50-pound weights right off the bat, “you kind of have to adjust slowly,” she says. “You start off with 10. When that becomes easy, you go to 20, then you go to 30”—and so on.

Fiber training is especially critical if you’re constipated at the outset, as many people are, according to Nielsen. Even though fiber can help prevent and alleviate constipation, too much at once can actually make an existing issue worse by overwhelming your gut. “When you add a ton of fiber to an already backed-up system, it’s kind of like a bottleneck on the highway,” Nielsen says: If you try to shoehorn four lanes into one, you’re going to end up with a jam on your hands.

Now that you know fiber training entails steadily increasing your fiber intake, you’re probably wondering what that looks like on a more practical level. Before we share specifics, some context for how much fiber you actually need might be helpful. Per the federal Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2020-2025, women should aim for 28 grams of fiber daily from ages 19 to 30, 25 grams of fiber daily from ages 31 to 50, and 22 grams of fiber daily starting at age 51, though some experts recommend even more—a helpful set of parameters if you’re not sure where to start.

While the ideal amount of fiber to add to your diet while fiber training can vary from person to person depending on health needs (like a constipation issue), most people are “looking at [adding] probably three to five grams at a time,” Nielsen says.

With that in mind, you’ll want to choose a food that has a fiber content in that ballpark—say, an apple (around four grams of fiber), a half-cup of chickpeas (around five grams of fiber), a tablespoon of chia seeds (around five grams of fiber), or two tablespoons of ground flax (around four grams of fiber)—and eat a serving every single day until you feel like your body has adjusted (read: you’re not experiencing any additional bloating, gas, or other GI side effects). This process typically takes around five to seven days, according to Nielsen, but everyone’s digestive system is different, so don’t worry if you need more (or less!) time. “It really is about listening to your body and individualizing the rate at which you increase,” Nielsen says. “You have to follow your symptoms and go slow,” Dr. Ganjhu agrees.

Then, you can tack on another dose—like a second apple, a full cup of chickpeas, two tablespoons of chia seeds, or four tablespoons of ground flax. Continue increasing your fiber intake in these increments (and at this pace) until you’ve hit your daily fiber goal. If you’re a 35-year-old woman starting from scratch, reaching 25 grams of fiber—the recommended daily amount for that age—would take around five five-gram doses, six four-gram doses, or eight three-gram doses, for example.

People who are constipated may want to specifically fiber train with foods that are low in FODMAPs—fermentable carbohydrates particularly hard on sensitive stomachs—according to Nielsen. Like we said above, increasing your fiber intake when you’re backed up can, well, backfire, so low-FODMAP foods are more likely to be a safe bet than their high-FODMAP counterparts. Kiwis, which contain four grams of fiber in a two-fruit serving, are an especially strong option if you fall into this category (and they’ve even been specifically studied as a dietary constipation treatment), Nielsen says. Similarly, she adds, a gentle fiber supplement like Metamucil, which is made from psyllium husk, also “provides a lot of the benefits, but tends to be less irritating to a troubled system.”

Another tip: If you’re constipated, make sure to drink plenty of water as well (though the oft-referenced eight-glasses-a-day requirement is something of a myth!). Because fiber needs water to work its stool-softening magic, insufficient fluids could leave your bowel movements hard and dry, exacerbating the problem.

Whatever new fiber sources you choose, taking this slow-and-steady approach should help ease the transition to a higher intake. “If you’re someone who doesn’t eat a lot of fiber and all of a sudden you start eating 30 grams of it, the colon is just not going to know how to manage that efficiently,” Dr. Ganjhu says. But by leveling up little by little? You can heighten that “colonic fitness”—and sidestep the worst of the awkward stage.

THANKS FOR ASKING. A group of French galleries under the umbrella organization Comité Professionnel des Galeries d’Art (CPGA) have sent a letter of complaint to Art Basel Paris organizers for closing two days early in October due to a planned protest and for failing to consult them, reports Monopol. When Art Basel Paris announced they would close for the weekend of October 24 and 25, the last public days of the fair, they said it was in the interest of safety for all, given the protests planned for Saturday. However, a letter from the CPGA to the fair director, Karim Crippa, claims exhibiting galleries “had not been consulted” about the decision, and questioned the need to close on Sunday, calling it “far less justified.” Indeed, the exhibit “Cézanne et nous” was open Sunday, located on the opposite side of the Grand Palais venue, which also hosts the fair. CPGA members account for over one quarter of exhibitors, many of whom are smaller-scale galleries that rely on weekend sales more than their larger, multinational counterparts. The letter further described the fair’s handling of the early closure as “a sign of disrespect, indeed, of contempt,” and demanded “appropriate compensation” for the loss of business. A burger chain's pixel-art RPG has gamers excited, and there are good reasons for that.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If you’d told me a decade ago that Wendy's would release one of the most talked-about indie RPGs of 2026, I’d have assumed your burger had some dodgy mushrooms. Yet here we are: it's actually happening.

The world's third-largest hamburger fast-food chain has unveiled a turn-based, pixel-art adventure in which its red-haired mascot leads a party of fast-food heroes to save a kingdom in peril. It's called WendyQuest: Legend of the Four Corner Stones. No, this is not a South Park parody. This is a real, playable game.

The branded element isn't just about bigging up Wendy's either: it also takes potshots at rivals. In the game, for example, your enemies include Frydusa, a carton of snake-like French fries, and a gang called the Golden Archers. As a dig at McDonald’s, it's not subtle.

81monkeys, an indie studio in Port Moody, British Columbia, is making the game, and it’s heading to Steam. You might expect something so obviously corporate to either get trounced on social media or get ignored and sink without a trace. At the time of writing, though, gamers mostly seem to be asking… why it looks so good.

There's more. Last summer, Pepsi asked on social media whether it should make a video game. It was buried in replies pointing out that it already had. One came from Kotaro Uchikoshi, now a celebrated visual-novel director (yes, that's a thing now), who'd worked on 1999’s Pepsiman and was offering to reconnect the company with the original team.

Branded games are clearly back on the menu. The question is… why? Well, first it's worth noting that we've been here before.

Domino’s Avoid the Noid in 1989 is widely cited as the first fast-food tie-in game. McDonald’s followed with Global Gladiators, which is considered one of the best platformers of its era. Then there was Cool Spot, starring the red dot from 7 Up’s American logo, which you could play on the SNES and Mega Drive in 1993 and, branding tie-in aside, is a genuinely brilliant 2D platform game.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

The original Pepsiman, though, remains the king of the branded games. Released only in Japan (which always helps cult status), it showed a superhero sprinting through cities to deliver Pepsi cans. And it remains much-loved: these days, copies go for hundreds of dollars on sites like eBay.

Then came Burger King's 2006 experiment. The chain sold three branded Xbox games for $3.99, including the infamous stealth title Sneak King, as long as you bought a value meal (sold separately). BK ended up shifting more than 3.2 million copies in total.

KFC was late to the party, only joining the fun in 2019 with I Love You, Colonel Sanders! A Finger Lickin’ Good Dating Simulator. The parody dating sim got flayed by critics, but players loved it, giving it a 91% positive rating on Steam.

From a branding perspective, what's interesting is that these weren’t just adverts with gameplay bolted on. They were proper games that people actually liked, even if reviewers were somewhat sniffy. So why are they coming back now? It's difficult to say, but I think a few factors are in play.

First, the original branded games' child audience is now an adult audience with money, and nostalgia is a powerful force. Second, it’s far easier to distribute games today. While Burger King once had to manufacture physical copies and distribute them to restaurants, now Wendy’s just needs a Steam page.

Thirdly, traditional advertising is struggling to break through ad blockers, ad-free subscriptions and a general lack of interest. In contrast, people actually like a branded game. They might even actively seek it out.

Finally, there's the backlash against AI. Wendy's Steam page proudly declares its game “100% fresh and 100% human-made” for a reason. As we all drown in AI slop, handcrafted, indie-style pixel art becomes a visual statement of brand values.

None of this, of course, guarantees that these games will succeed. For every Global Gladiators there’s a Sneak King, a game remembered more as a curio than for its gameplay. The brands that get this right treat players as players, not targets for ads.

So will WendyQuest join Pepsiman in the hall of fame, or end up in the bargain bin of history? I have no clue. But if a burger chain can get me excited about a turn-based RPG, its marketing team must be doing something right. And Pepsi, if you’re reading: Uchikoshi’s offer is still on the table.

#8900. Why Are People Taking CoQ10 Supplements for Longevity, and Do They Work?

Coenzyme Q10, or CoQ10, was once a niche supplement, known best in wellness circles for its possible benefits for heart health and fertility. But now the antioxidant’s star is rising for a new reason: its purported longevity-boosting powers.

The appeal of CoQ10 has grown as researchers have explored its effects on various conditions, with small studies revealing, for example, it may help boost insulin sensitivity, cut the frequency of migraine attacks, and alleviate muscle aches from statins used for high cholesterol. But as of late, there’s excitement around its broader anti-aging potential because of how it supports our mitochondria, which you may remember from high school biology as the “powerhouse of the cell.”

That role has punched CoQ10’s ticket into the longevity club, alongside other supplements thought to lend a hand to mitochondria (like urolithin A and nicotinamide mononucleotide, or NMN). There’s even a synthetic derivative of CoQ10 designed specifically for better absorption by mitochondria, which is called mitoquinone (or MitoQ), that’s gaining hype among celeb trainers and athletes for boosting energy, recovery, and “cellular health.”

But is CoQ10 all it’s cracked up to be when it comes to longevity? Read on to learn more before grabbing a bottle of this supplement.

Our cells naturally produce CoQ10, a molecule that acts like a conveyor belt for charged particles inside our mitochondria, enabling them to “efficiently create adenosine triphosphate, or ATP,” the “currency for cellular energy,” Anthony Molina, PhD, a professor of medicine at UC San Diego who studies aging biomarkers, tells SELF. That’s a big deal, as all cells rely on that energy to complete their daily functions. As we age, both the number and energy-producing powers of mitochondria drop off—a process involved in the development of many age-related diseases, Dr. Molina points out. Meanwhile, CoQ10 levels also decline with age, leading to the idea that we should take it in supplement form for better mitochondrial (and, in turn, overall) health.

Beyond its role in energy production, CoQ10 is also an antioxidant that is “very powerful in capturing free radicals,” or volatile molecules that can harm cells, Daria Mochly-Rosen, PhD, a professor of chemical and systems biology at Stanford University and coauthor of The Life Machines: How Taking Care of Your Mitochondria Can Transform Your Health, tells SELF. By stabilizing those molecules, CoQ10 may help to keep that damage (a.k.a. oxidative stress) from piling up and also contributing to aging and the development of chronic disease.

Separately, CoQ10 has potential benefits as it relates to cardiovascular health: It’s anti-inflammatory and may also improve the function of blood vessels, helping regulate blood pressure, JoAnn E. Manson, MD, DrPH, chief of the division of preventive medicine at Brigham and Women’s Hospital and professor of Medicine at Harvard Medical School, tells SELF. These upsides could lower risk for heart disease, the number-one killer in the US.

Despite the promising mechanisms above, “the evidence base just isn’t yet there,” Dr. Manson says. The studies we do have on CoQ10 and longevity are in mice and rats—and while a few suggest a lifespan-extending effect, or a way to reverse some cognitive decline once it starts, others show no anti-aging upsides in healthy animals. Besides, “we find again and again that humans are not just large, non-hairy mice,” Dr. Mochly-Rosen points out, “so we can’t assume the results transfer.”

Studies in people have been focused on CoQ10 as an intervention for specific diseases, particularly cardiovascular ones. All the experts say the strongest evidence for longevity is in those with heart failure, who have low CoQ10 levels—taking the supplement alongside standard treatment has been shown to reduce the need for hospitalization and risk of early death, possibly because of its mitochondrial perks.

But logistically, it’s a lot trickier to prove that CoQ10 prolongs life in healthy people versus in those with a medical condition or known CoQ10 deficiency. In the absence of these studies, it might be tempting to take a logical leap: If we know CoQ10 supports mitochondrial function, and levels of both dip with age and disease, supplementing with CoQ10 seems like it should help you live longer. But the problem is, we don’t know exactly what drives the mitochondrial issues that occur with age, Dr. Molina says. “So maybe you’re not taking a shot in the dark because we know that mitochondria has something to do with healthy aging, but using CoQ10 as the tool is like taking a shot in a dimly lit room,” he says. “It’s not clear whether you’re hitting the right target.”

As with any supplement, it’s best to ask your doctor before adding CoQ10 to your routine. While there’s a good deal of data to suggest it’s safe and well-tolerated, there are some people who shouldn’t take it, generally because of interactions with prescription drugs, Dr. Molina points out. The main concern is with blood thinners (a.k.a. anticoagulants) like warfarin (which are often prescribed after a blood clot)—CoQ10 could make these drugs less effective, Dr. Manson says. It’s also extra important to check in with your doctor first if you take insulin or are receiving treatment for cancer. Though CoQ10 doesn’t usually cause side effects, you could also wind up with some mild GI upset or insomnia, Dr. Manson adds.

There’s also the quality-control problem that comes with any supplement. These are not subjected to the same FDA regulations as medications are, meaning you can’t know for sure that you’re getting what the bottle promises. Studies of certain CoQ10 supplements have found that they contained less of the antioxidant than the amount listed on the label, Dr. Mochly-Rosen notes. Your best defense against winding up with a sugar pill is to find a product that’s been third-party verified, she says—look for the “NSF certified” or “USP verified” stamp.

#8899. Christie’s First Fine Art Auction in Abu Dhabi Totals $8.94 M.

On Sunday, Christie’s hosted its debut fine art sale in Abu Dhabi, “MAWASIM: 20 Years of Modern and Contemporary Middle Eastern Art,” to mark the auction house’s 20th anniversary of its first auction in the United Arab Emirates. The sale totaled $8.94 million.

The evening sale held at the Abu Dhabi Edition hotel featured works by artists from the Middle East and North Africa. Monir Shahroudy Farmanfarmaian’s Variations on the Hexagon (2006) led the auction, selling for $844,800; the painting’s estimate was $150,000 to $250,000. Bidding for the work by Farmanfarmaian, who is currently the subject of a retrospective at the Moderna Museet in Stockholm, lasted for seven minutes. Guiragossian’s Noces (Wedding), 1958–59, sold for $486,400, nearly beating its high estimate of $500,000.

In a joint statement, Christie’s Ridha Moumni, chairman of Middle East and Africa, and Marie-Claire Thijsen, head of sale and specialist at Christie’s UK and UAE operations, said that the auction’s results highlight the “breadth of bidding across the sale demonstrates the international interest this category has achieved today. Its scale reflects the depth of the region’s art sector and its capacity to support a major sale of this kind.” Christie’s reported that more than 30 percent of registrants were millennial and Gen Z bidders, and that 37 percent of the participants were new to Christie’s.

Leading up to the sale at Christie’s in Abu Dhabi, the auction house displayed three major works from its upcoming marquee New York sales on view at Abu Dhabi Edition hotel. The works included Wassily Kandinsky’s Betonte Ecken (1923), which carries a $60 million–$80 million estimate; Mark Rothko’s Untitled (1968), which carries a $10 million–$15 million estimate; and Pablo Picasso’s Tête de femme (1939), which carries a $12 million–$18 million estimate.

Did you ever see the 2021 Leonardo DiCaprio film Don't Look Up? I don't think it's a spoiler to say that its focus on people not looking up was partly a satire on climate change denial. But more broadly, it fed into the idea that nowadays, we're all looking down a lot; specifically at our phones.

I've honestly got no idea if smart glasses – some of which can now project information, images and videos straight at your eyeballs – will end up taking off in future, and replacing the smartphone. But if they do, then it occurs to me that this will be big news for billboards.

You might assume that if more digital tech catches on, physical advertising would be one of the casualties. After all, why look at a poster when your glasses can show you something tailored? But the more I think about it, the more convinced I am the opposite will happen.

Consider this: nobody is going to wear smart glasses to look at their feet. The whole attraction is that you get the benefits of a phone while keeping your eyes on the world around you. And in most towns and cities – even in this smartphone era – that world is already plastered with outdoor advertising.

And if smart glasses can truly take advantage of augmented reality – tech that overlays digital content onto real-world, physical things – then those billboards will suddenly be a lot more exciting to look at.

For over a century, billboards have been essentially a one-way medium. QR codes promised to fix that, but how many of us have actually stopped in the street, taken out our phones and waggled them at a pixelated square? Once or twice, maybe. But on a regular basis? Hardly.

In future, I reckon, you'll be able to point smart glasses at a billboard and get it to do all sorts of useful things, probably by talking to an AI bot embedded in your specs.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

With a movie billboard, for instance, you might want to play the trailer or find out which cinema it's playing at nearby, and when. You might even want turn-by-turn directions to the multiplex to appear in front of your very eyes.

This might sound like Black Mirror-style sci-fi, but it's worth remembering how many old Black Mirror episodes have essentially come true already. And it certainly seems to be the way the ad industry is thinking.

In fact, you can already see a version of this idea in east London. Electric Garden, on Shoreditch High Street, bills itself as “the billboard you can walk into”. It’s a 21,000 sq ft open-air site that sits behind a row of giant digital screens, so brands can run a campaign on the screens and then build a physical world behind them for people to explore.

Its launch campaign, for Activision’s Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, turned the site into a neon-lit, Seoul-inspired alleyway, complete with convenience stores, plastic stools and code-breaking missions. As co-founder Alex Ezen puts it: “A screen can capture attention, but a physical experience gives people a reason to stop, take part and share it.”

Smart glasses could deliver something similar without anyone needing to build an alleyway. That will make the brief for designers all the harder, of course, but personally, that’s the kind of challenge I’d relish.

Recently, I’ve written for Creative Bloq's sister site Digital Camera World about a run of photographic rediscoveries. For instance, F Holland Day’s 1898 series The Seven Words resurfaced in September. Then in October, we saw a newly found cache of photos that document the making of the 1926 horror film Faust. These antiquated forms of physical media sat untouched for a century or more, and yet remain totally viewable. Amazing, really.

Now, let's do a thought experiment. If you're old enough, picture the digital work you made 20 years ago. That might be a website design, assets for a CD-ROM, a vector illustration… whatever.

Ask yourself: could you locate and open those files today? If you’re anything like me, the honest answer is “mostly no”.

It's ironic, really. Because digital work has no tangible physical presence, we tend to think of it as eternal. In truth, though, it's kind of the opposite.

This March, I visited memory card manufacturer Lexar’s facilities in Shenzhen, China. And one moment there has stuck with me ever since.

In a press conference, the company's representative explained that the flash memory used in consumer memory cards and SSDs can start losing data within a year if you leave them in a drawer and don't power them up.

Lexar told me it’s developing a dedicated device to address this issue, but it's early days. In contrast, a print just sits there, being a print.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Meanwhile, if you're putting your work online, there's more bad news. A Pew Research Center study found that 38% of webpages that existed in 2013 were no longer accessible a decade later. Platforms are no safer. Back in 2019, MySpace admitted that a server migration had wiped photos, videos and music uploaded between 2003 and 2015: an estimated 50 million songs from 14 million artists.

Its advice to users was to keep their own backups. But wherever you back stuff up, basically, you're running the same risk. As the sudden closure of Sora highlighted, venture capitalists don't really care about protecting your stuff as much as you do.

There's also the problem of actually opening files in years to come. Built something in Flash in 2012? I doubt you'll be able to salvage it now, after Adobe shuttered the format in 2020, and that's just one example among many.

So what can we do? There are few basic rules we all should be following if we want to be able to access our work in 2030, 2040 and further ahead. The first is to follow the 3-2-1 rule. Keep three copies of anything important, on two different types of storage, with one stored offsite or in the cloud. It's not a foolproof method, but it does reduce the odds of losing stuff exponentially.

Secondly, every few months or so, power up your SSDs and memory cards, so firmware can do its job. Thirdly, export your final files to open formats like TIFF, PNG, SVG or PDF/A, which are more likely to be readable in decades to come.

Fourthly, treat platforms as shop windows, not storerooms. And finally, print your work. As long as you can avoid floods or fires, paper-based storage has a better track record than digital.

Is this seems a bit of a faff, I'd have to agree. But consider this. If future historians end up knowing more about 1926 than 2026, it won’t be for lack of material. It’ll be because we couldn't be bothered to look after it – and what will future generations think of us then?

From the first ever touchscreen on Mac to the super bright and colourful 'PROLED' XDR display, there are quite a few candidates for the headline feature of Apple's new MacBook Pro. But judging by the reaction in the room during the launch in LA last week, the most popular addition might not be that new at all.

Readers of a certain vintage will remember the illuminated Apple logo. The light-up fruit used to adorn every Apple laptop, and was a (somewhat distracting) mainstay of cafes, trains and DJ performances. In 2015, Apple unceremoniously killed the illuminated logo, replacing it with a mirrored version. But as of last week, it's back – and it seems people are happy about it.

Now, the cynical among you might think the reason for the addition is to make the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display stand out as new in public. There's always something to differentiate a new Apple product from the previous generation, even if it's simply new colours. But from a distance, this new MacBook Pro looks almost identical to non PROLED models. How are we supposed to quietly show it off in a cafe? With the 'new' illuminated logo, of course!

But the less cynical among you might see this as yet another sign that under new CEO John Ternus, Apple is rediscovering its sense of fun. From the brand's wild new TikTok presence to the colourful (and cheap) MacBook Neo, Apple seems to be stepping outside of its space grey prison and embracing a sense of friendliness we haven't seen for years. And it's going down well.

#8895. in this video game, moths and wolves play out a nearby climate future

alice bucknell's, the alluvials, take players through burning forests and a sand-covered los angeles to explore a speculative future through non-human lenses.

In 2023, artist Alice Bucknell released The Alluvials, a video work filled with wolves, moths, and sediment that looks at a version of Los Angeles in the near future. In this California city, the sand that had once been characteristic of its beaches has taken over downtown, effectively turning the sprawl of highways and skyscrapers into a desert of dunes and dust. Through this speculative lens on an alternate reality, Bucknell presents both the history and consequences of this dried-up world. The work examines the history of the Tongva people of the Greater Los Angeles Basin while also imagining the water desalination corporation Qwench, a perpetually burning landscape, and an eternity in which the sky remains in its golden hour.

A year later, the project evolved into The Alluvials video game (2024), a multilevel game that explores the world inside the film. With each embodied exploration of its digital realm, the project presents the uncanny and nearly incomprehensible fallout of climate change. In their exploration of a not-so-far-off Los Angeles, Bucknell poses the questions: Is this how we will want to live? And if the answer is no, what modes of action do we have access to in order to reroute our course in the progression of climate change?

Alice Bucknell, still from The Alluvials, video work, 2023 | all images courtesy the artist unless stated otherwiseAlice Bucknell, still from The Alluvials, video work, 2023 | all images courtesy the artist unless stated otherwise

The word alluvial means of or relating to alluvium, which Merriam-Webster describes as ‘clay, silt, sand, gravel, or similar detrital material deposited by running water.’ In the game, Bucknell puts players in a kind of alluvial world, one that results from sand and silt accumulating where there should have been running water. Within it, there are four levels in which the player takes on the perspective of what are usually considered non-playable characters (NPCs). In doing so, Bucknell challenges traditional gameplay dynamics with what they refer to as ‘queer and ecological game mechanics.’

Alice Bucknell, still from The Alluvials, video game, 2024Alice Bucknell, still from The Alluvials, video game, 2024

In one such level, Extinction Burst, the game opens with a bright red forest and a mountain lion sulking down a fuchsia path. The scene gives way to a dried-out basin filled with white particles. On closer inspection, these drifting flakes are revealed to be a form of moth. As you approach a desert tree growing near the center of the basin, a question in blue, hazy letters reveals itself in the sky: ‘ARE YOU MOTH OR ARE YOU TREE?’

Depending on whether you choose the moth or the tree path, you encounter two different perspectives of the desert landscape. In other levels, you walk through a forest fire, become a wolf in a barren, sand-ridden Los Angeles, or pilot an airboat speeding through the Los Angeles River in the evening. By presenting these alternative points of view, the game not only challenges the agency of the player but also offers an embodied understanding of things humans may take for granted: the knowledge of a moth, a yucca plant, or a body of water.

The Alluvials has been exhibited in both film and video game formats in spaces across the US, Europe, and Asia. In each space, Bucknell’s work has come to life in different forms. When the film was shown at LUMINEX in downtown Los Angeles as a four-channel work, scenes of the forest fire lit up the building, creating an uncanny reflection of both the real and fictional city. At HEK Other Intelligences 2025 in Basel, Switzerland, pink camo beanbags were set up on the floor, presenting the game as a two-channel video game that visitors could sit down and play in a space awash in fuchsia.

Within Bucknell’s work, the artist brings together a work of speculative fiction that speaks from an unknown future but carries the threatening tone of a parable lived many times over. True to the worlds they build in game engines, Bucknell makes real the promises, threats, and predictions that the CEOs and climate scientists of our time launch into the news cycle. Yet here, there is an opportunity to progress, level by level, through the very possible consequences of our present-day actions if left unchecked. Here, the posthuman utopia is one in which we leave humanity behind—one that discards the anthropocentric thinking that leads to artificial waters—and instead move forward with a future informed by the logic and processes of the natural world, before it is too late.

date: video work (2023) and video game (2024)

A year ago, a lot of people couldn't quite believe it when Canva made Affinity free. Suddenly, the three paid-for apps obtained through the acquisition of Serif were rolled into a single piece of creative software covering everything from photo editing to vector art and desktop publishing, simultaneously serving as a free Photoshop alternative, InDesign alt and Illustrator alt.

There had to be a catch, and one of the suspicions was that the new Affinity would be unlikely to get regular upgrades or improvements. One year on, Canva seems to be defying those predictions. It added new raw photo editing capabilities last month, with more colour, sharpening and detail adjustments. Today, it's completed things by adding one major element that was still missing for many creatives' workflows: a dedicated Affinity for iPad.

The individual Affinity apps (Affinity Photo 2, Designer 2, Publisher 2) were previously available for iPad before last year's launch of the unified free Affinity for desktop. Users who had bought them could continue using the apps, but they didn't support the new .af file format.

The new single-app Affinity for iPad brings the bulk of the combined desktop software to Apple tablets but designed specifically for a touch-first interface. It also takes advantage of Apple Pencil capabilities like pressure and tilt for sketching or for masking images, as well as Apple Pencil Pro's barrel roll, squeeze and hover features.

The app features Sketch Studio for freehand drawing and sketch-to-vector workflows, and several iPad-first features like a Mask Tool and Sketch to Shapes.

Like on the desktop app, Affinity for iPad uses the same .af file format across sketch, vector, photo and layout processes to make cross-media workflows easier. Non-destructive edits render in real time and there's no need for assets to be exported, converted or remade.

For sketching, there's a brush library with controls to shape each brush, while sketches stay live in the file to build on, rather than trace again. The iPad app also includes Affinity's raw image editing capabilities and the ability to create print-ready multi-page documents.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

AI tools, including Generative Expand, upscaling, denoising, and Decompose Layer to split a flat image into editable layers, are available with a subscription via Canva AI Studio.

An increasing range of major software is now available in the form of dedicated iPad apps, from Adobe's main apps like Photoshop, Illustrator and Premiere to DaVinci Resolve for video editing and Maxon's ZBrush for 3D sculpting. This means the powerful iPad Pro can now be used to its full potential for creative work, allowing more mobile workflows, either for working remotely or simply allowing creatives to take time away from the desk to work in another place before coming back to pick things up on desktop.

Affinity for iPad is is free for individual users and available to download from the iPad App Store now. If you don't already have one, you'll need to create a free Canva account to use the app. A premium Canva subscription is required for AI tools.

The gift tax is one of the most misunderstood parts of the tax code. People hear "gift tax" and assume they'll owe the IRS money for giving a birthday check to their grandchild. That's almost never how it works. The federal gift tax exists to prevent people from giving away their entire estate during their lifetime to dodge estate taxes at death. For the vast majority of Americans, it will never cost them a dime.

Here's what actually matters: in 2026, you can give up to $18,000 to any individual without reporting it to the IRS at all. Give that amount to 10 different people and you've transferred $180,000 completely under the radar. Go above the annual limit and you still won't owe tax — you'll just file a form that tracks the excess against your $13.61 million lifetime exemption.

The gift tax is really a planning tool, not a penalty. Understanding how it works can help you transfer wealth to family members, fund education, reduce your taxable estate, and accelerate your heirs' path to financial independence — all without triggering any actual tax.

The annual gift tax exclusion is the amount you can give to any single recipient each year without needing to file a gift tax return or use any of your lifetime exemption. For 2026, that amount is $18,000 per recipient.

This limit applies per giver, per recipient. That means:

The IRS adjusts this amount for inflation periodically. Here's how the annual exclusion has changed over the years:

The annual exclusion has roughly doubled since 2002, when it was just $11,000. Inflation adjustments are made in $1,000 increments, so the number stays flat for a year or two, then bumps up.

This is the single most important gift tax fact: the person making the gift is responsible for any gift tax — never the recipient. If your grandmother gives you $50,000, she files the gift tax return and uses her lifetime exemption. You don't report it as income, you don't owe tax on it, and you don't need to do anything. Gifts received are not taxable income.

When you give more than the annual exclusion to any single person, the excess counts against your lifetime gift and estate tax exemption — currently $13.61 million per person ($27.22 million for married couples). You won't actually owe gift tax until you've exceeded this lifetime amount.

Let's put that in perspective. If you give your daughter $118,000 in one year, you're $100,000 over the annual exclusion. You file Form 709 to report it, and the IRS subtracts that $100,000 from your lifetime exemption. Your remaining exemption drops from $13.61 million to $13.51 million. No tax is owed.

At the 40% top gift tax rate, you'd need to give away more than $13.61 million over your lifetime before any actual tax kicks in. That puts fewer than 0.1% of Americans in gift tax territory.

Important sunset warning: The current $13.61 million exemption is set to be cut roughly in half on January 1, 2026, reverting to approximately $7 million per person (adjusted for inflation) under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act sunset provisions. This has created urgency for high-net-worth families to make large gifts before the window closes.

Several types of transfers are completely excluded from gift tax rules — no annual limit, no lifetime exemption usage, no Form 709 required:

The education and medical exclusions are especially powerful for the FI community. A grandparent can pay $50,000 in tuition directly to a university AND give the grandchild $18,000 in cash in the same year — all tax-free with no reporting.

If you give more than $18,000 to any single recipient in a year, you must file IRS Form 709 (United States Gift and Generation-Skipping Transfer Tax Return) with your tax return. Filing Form 709 does not mean you owe tax — it simply reports the gift and tracks your lifetime exemption usage.

One of the most powerful gift tax strategies available is the 529 plan 5-year election. The IRS allows you to front-load up to 5 years of annual exclusion gifts into a 529 education savings plan in a single year.

For 2026, that means you can contribute up to $90,000 (5 x $18,000) to a 529 plan for a single beneficiary in one year. A married couple electing gift splitting can contribute up to $180,000 per beneficiary.

The catch: if you use the 5-year election and then pass away during the 5-year period, a prorated portion of the gift returns to your taxable estate.

The gift tax and estate tax share the same $13.61 million lifetime exemption. Think of it as one pool of money that covers both gifts during your life and transfers at death.

Every dollar of lifetime exemption you use for gifts during your life reduces the amount available to shelter your estate from tax at death. However, there's a strategic advantage to giving during your lifetime: future appreciation on gifted assets escapes your taxable estate.

Example: You give your daughter stock worth $1 million today. You use $982,000 of lifetime exemption ($1M minus $18K annual exclusion). If that stock grows to $3 million by the time you die, the full $3 million — including $2 million in appreciation — is completely outside your estate. That's $2 million that will never be subject to estate tax.

The current $13.61 million lifetime exemption is scheduled to drop to approximately $7 million per person on January 1, 2026. For high-net-worth families, this creates a narrow window to transfer wealth at the higher exemption level. If you have a taxable estate anywhere near the future threshold, consult an estate planning attorney about accelerating gifts before the sunset takes effect.

A practical guide to making gifts without triggering tax.

Give up to $18,000 per recipient per year with no reporting, no forms, and no impact on your lifetime exemption. Married couples can give $36,000 per recipient using gift splitting.

Pro tip: There is no limit on the number of recipients. You can give $18,000 each to as many people as you want.

Payments made directly to educational institutions or medical providers for someone else are unlimited and completely excluded from gift tax. These do not reduce your annual exclusion or lifetime exemption.

Pro tip: The payment must go directly to the institution — not to the student or patient. Reimbursing someone for tuition they already paid counts as a gift.

Front-load up to 5 years of annual exclusion gifts ($90,000 individual, $180,000 married) into a 529 plan in a single year. The full amount starts compounding immediately.

Pro tip: If you die during the 5-year election period, a prorated portion returns to your estate. File Form 709 to report the 5-year election.

If you give more than $18,000 to any single person, file IRS Form 709 with your tax return. The excess reduces your $13.61 million lifetime exemption but no tax is owed until you exceed it.

Pro tip: Filing Form 709 is just paperwork — it does not mean you owe tax. It simply tracks your lifetime exemption usage.

If your estate is approaching the lifetime exemption threshold, work with an estate planning attorney. Strategies like GRATs, family LLCs, and intentionally defective grantor trusts can transfer wealth beyond the basic gift tax rules.

Pro tip: With the exemption sunset approaching in 2026, large transfers should be planned now rather than later.

In 2026, you can give up to $18,000 per recipient without any tax consequences or reporting requirements. Above that amount, you file Form 709 but still won't owe tax until you've exceeded your $13.61 million lifetime exemption. Married couples can give up to $36,000 per recipient using gift splitting.

No. The recipient of a gift never pays income tax or gift tax on the gift. The giver is responsible for any gift tax reporting (Form 709) and any tax that might be owed. Gifts received are not considered taxable income. However, if the gifted asset later generates income (like dividends or interest), that income is taxable to the recipient.

You must file Form 709 with your tax return for that year. The amount above $18,000 reduces your lifetime gift and estate tax exemption ($13.61 million). You won't owe any actual gift tax unless your cumulative lifetime gifts exceed the lifetime exemption. Think of it as paperwork, not a penalty.

Yes, though the amount matters. You can give $18,000 per year with no reporting. You and your spouse together can give $36,000. For larger down payment gifts, you'll file Form 709 and use some of your $13.61 million lifetime exemption — but no tax is owed. Your mortgage lender will require a gift letter confirming the money is a gift, not a loan.

No. The unlimited marital deduction means you can transfer any amount to your US citizen spouse completely free of gift tax and estate tax. No annual limit, no lifetime exemption usage, no Form 709 required. If your spouse is not a US citizen, a higher annual exclusion applies ($185,000 for 2026) instead of the unlimited deduction.

Gifts are not reported on your income tax return (Form 1040). If you gave more than $18,000 to any single recipient, you file a separate Form 709 (gift tax return) alongside your income tax return. The recipient does not report the gift on their income tax return either. Gifts are outside the income tax system entirely.

The gift tax affects far fewer people than most assume. With an $18,000 annual exclusion per recipient, a $13.61 million lifetime exemption, and unlimited exclusions for direct tuition and medical payments, the vast majority of Americans can give generously without ever owing a penny in gift tax. The key rules: the giver pays (not the receiver), gifts are not taxable income, and filing Form 709 is just tracking — not a tax bill. For FI families, strategic gifting is one of the most powerful ways to accelerate the next generation's financial independence while reducing your taxable estate.

It's the second most confusing horse illusion I've ever seen.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It's been a while since I saw an optical illusion good enough to share, but I couldn't resist this one, which is like a combination of two of our favourite ever optical illusions. I present: the spinning horse meets the blue/gold/white dress – and it's baffling the internet.

This is a real life video of a horse standing in a stable. And the horse is clearly black... except, it isn't. Apparently it's white. I absolutely cannot see this however many times I come back to it, but people in the comments have learned how the horse is actually in shadow, clicked off and back onto it, and then can see that it's white.

I'll share it below – can you see the horse as its real colour, or are you stuck in the same camp as me?

With 4,500 upvotes on Reddit, the r/opticalillusions subreddit is taken with this illusion.

"I can no longer see it as a black horse but at first it was as black as midnight. Now it's white and I cant make it go back," one amazed comment reads.

"It's the exact same effect as the White/Gold Blue/Black dress," explains another. "It's an image where the subject is in shadow but the background is in bright sunlight and our brain struggles to differentiate the two lighting conditions."

Other comments share tips on how to achieve the effect if you're struggling.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

"Scroll so you can only see the legs," one suggests. "Focus your eyes on the shade that the horse is standing in. You should be able to see that it is white," says someone else.

Has that worked for you? Let us know in the comments. Then check out the original spinning horse illusion that amassed millions of views on our site. And the follow up version that was spotted in real life.

#8891. Apple takes "monumental step forward" with first touchscreen MacBook

Apple has revealed its latest MacBook Pro model, which features the technology brand’s first laptop touchscreen and what it claims is “the world’s best laptop display”.

Sixteen years after Steve Jobs described touchscreen laptops as “ergonomically terrible”, Apple has ventured into the market with its new MacBook Pro, which is available from 6 November at prices ranging from £2,899 to £14,549.

As well as being touchscreen, the laptop features a PROLED XDR display, which Apple said is “the world’s best laptop display”, M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, 128 gigabytes of memory, 16 terabytes of storage, up to 24 hours of battery life and a thinner, lighter design compared to previous models.

It comes in 14- and 16-inch models, weighing three and four pounds respectively. The laptop was designed to be both portable and a powerful tool for professional creatives on the go, whether they’re working on 3D models or playing musical instruments onscreen.

“The new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display is a monumental step forward for the Mac,” said Apple chief hardware officer Johny Srouji.

“PROLED XDR is the world’s best laptop display,” he continued. “And with the magic of Touch coming to MacBook Pro, combined with the game-changing performance of M5 Pro and M5 Max, we’ve created a whole new way for pros to interact with their content, taking their workflows to a completely new level.”

“The new MacBook Pro is the result of the deep integration between Apple silicon, hardware, and software, and there’s simply nothing else like it.”

Aiming to provide an intuitive experience, the Touch technology allows users to scroll through a webpage by swiping, zoom in on a photo by pinching, drag and drop slides in presentations and double-tap a window to fill the screen.

The touch sensor is built into the display panel rather than layered over it, to give the feel of touching the displayed content itself.

To support the Touch feature, Apple redesigned the laptop hinge for better stability and created real-time video stabilisation to smooth the camera feed when using the touchscreen on a video call.

Apple said that the macOS operating system automatically translates touches into clicks, meaning multiple existing apps will work with Touch right away. These include Adobe Lightroom, Blender, Maxon Cinema 4D, Maxon ZBrush, Notion, Canva, Zoom, Microsoft Word, Excel and PowerPoint.

“Graphic designers can now use the entire display as their canvas, no longer constrained by the area of the trackpad when drawing,” said Apple.

“Musicians can play software instruments right onscreen, and app developers can test how Touch performs in their iOS and iPadOS apps directly on the MacBook Pro display.”

Apple said the new PROLED XDR display offers “true-to-life colour and unparalleled brightness and contrast”, made possible by combining OLED technology with algorithms that control light across the display.

“The PROLED XDR display offers tandem OLED technology unlike any other, with deep innovations in its layers that keep brightness and grayscale uniform across the entire display, while minimising internal reflections common in traditional OLED designs,” said Apple.

“It’s all backed by advanced algorithms in the display engine that precisely control each pixel in real time, plus a meticulous manufacturing process and precise calibration of every panel for consistency from display to display.”

The MacBook Pro also has a six-speaker sound system, designed for deeper bass and improved sound clarity compared to previous models, and the Dynamic Island search and notification feature currently used in iPhones.

Other recent releases from Apple include its first folding smartphone, the HomeView dashboard for home controls and the budget-friendly MacBook Neo.

#8890. WOLOLOW 2.0 reinterprets 1960s space age architecture as elliptical bedside light

WOLOLOW night lamp ver 2.0 is a miniature tabletop lamp modeled after matti suuronen’s 1968 futuro house featuring an elliptical porthole hull, angled metal tripod legs, and replaceable 12v mr16 LED lighting.

wololow edited by christina vergopoulou October 31, 2026 3 min

Designed by Arthur Koshatahyan and Kostya Trunov, WOLOLOW Night Lamp Ver 2.0 is a compact luminaire that translates the Space Age architectural language of Matti Suuronen’s 1968 Futuro House into an everyday tabletop object. Directly scaling down the iconic portable chalet typology, the second version of the lamp features an elliptical disc-shaped hull punctuated by a ring of oval portholes, elevated on a slender, angled steel tripod base.

Currently launched on Kickstarter, the updated 2.0 edition retains the original fiberglass-inspired silhouette while upgrading the internal illumination hardware. Replacing the previous generation’s integrated battery, the revised model incorporates a hardwired power connection and a standard, user-replaceable 12V MR16 LED bulb with a GU5.3 base. The fixture accommodates standard warm-white modules as well as aftermarket smart LED bulbs, allowing integration with wireless home automation protocols for dimming and RGB color adjustments. The lamp is manufactured in five distinct shell finishes: white, yellow, orange, sky blue, and mirror chrome.

the lamp directly references the architectural geometry of Matti Suuronen’s 1968 Futuro Housethe elliptical, disc-shaped housing echoes the fiberglass shell of the original prefabricated chaletthe structure is supported by an angled, three-legged steel wire base

designers: Arthur Koshatahyan, Kostya Trunov
