Concept artist Christian Forsgren explains how Arrowhead takes hardware from Blender blockout to in-engine testing.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

With the Scope of Authority Warbond bringing new sniper rifles, ghillie armour, and mine grenades to Helldivers 2, we asked Arrowhead concept artist Christian Forsgren how that kind of hardware goes from Blender blockout to an in-game weapon. The answer is speed. “I can see how it actually handles in a player’s hands straight away, not weeks later,” he says. For weapons and machinery, that matters: a badly judged few centimetres can be the difference between convincing military hardware and something from a toy shop.

Each asset starts with a brief and a team brainstorm. Forsgren then builds a rough 3D blockout in Blender, refines the functionality, materials and finish, and pushes it into Arrowhead’s Stingray engine to see how it behaves in real time.

That loop helps give Helldivers 2 its battered, believable look. Weapons have to be mechanically plausible, and procedural materials add edge wear, grime and volumetric detail “without ever doing a single second of UVs”. Forsgren has also built a Blender pipeline for the game’s Warbond banners, producing renders at a higher fidelity than the game itself can manage, in the series’ propaganda-poster style.

There’s plenty here for Blender users beyond games, too: the scripts and add-ons Forsgren uses to speed up his work, the custom tools Arrowhead uses to move assets between Blender and the engine, and why the studio lets artists build their own workflows. The takeaway is that the best pipeline helps artists make better decisions, faster, with fewer hand-offs.

For more on Helldivers 2, visit Arrowhead Game Studios.

Christian Forsgren: It starts with a brief, then it’s team brainstorming. After that team brainstorm I take over and focus on ideas we have landed on and take it to a point where we can start to iterate. Say I'm building a weapon: I take the agreed upon brief and build the concept model in Blender, sometimes I do simple sketches depending on the asset to bounce around the team but most of the time it's straight into Blender for easy blockouts to help with scale and animation approximations. When that has reached a reasonable state I take it further and focus on functionality, materials, and how we want the finished asset to look like.

When that is greenlit Blender's job ends once the asset's ready to live in the game. We push it straight into Stingray, the game engine, and we're play-testing it in real time so I can see how it actually handles in a player's hands straight away, not weeks later. That's where Stingray takes over: real lighting, real scale, how it sits next to everything else. Then it's a loop with coders, designers, 3D artists and animators until it actually fits the game, not just looks good on its own.

CF: My own setup runs on scripts I've built and collected over time. Everything from camera related addons that help me manage the compositor, HDRI’s, Lights, focal length and Depth of field. Addons that help me create procedural materials in the shader editor. Pie menus to help me speed up access to all different kinds of Blender nested menus. The asset library is an insanely helpful addition to Blender to help me keep track of textures, materials, assets, animations and have them always available without opening a file explorer. The ecosystem's incredible and most problems I hit, someone's already solved it.

At a studio level, Arrowhead's built custom exporters and importers to bridge Blender and our engine. The problem we were solving was speed and consistency. Without that bridge, every asset needs manual rebuilding or re-checking every time it crosses from Blender into the engine, and that adds up fast across a whole team.

CF: Military realism drives a lot of it. Every weapon, like the arm-mounted cannons on our Exosuits (the mech suits players pilot in Helldivers 2), has to be functionally plausible, with every part sized to actually fit how it works mechanically. That attention to real, physical logic is a big part of why it reads as lived-in rather than designed.

Blender's procedural tools do a lot of heavy lifting too. I can generate complex backgrounds like planets and star systems without hand-painting any of it, and Cycles with some simple HDRIs gets me high-quality results without a huge amount of manual tweaking. That procedural system is always handy when it comes to the nitty-gritty textures as well; I can get there very fast with the procedural texturing tools inside Blender. All the nodes available to me make it a breeze to create edge wear, grungy textures and interesting volumetrics without ever doing a single second of UV’s.

For the war bond banners specifically, I built a proper Blender pipeline to replace what used to just be in-game screenshots with simple text put on top; now it has grown to larger marketing material where the most important part of the image is made in Blender in conjunction with studio tools to get in-game assets into Blender to be rendered at higher fidelity than we could ever achieve in-game to really row home that gritty propaganda feel we always strive for.

CF: Because we can export an asset into Stingray and see it working within a few hours, we iterate fast, and the feedback loop with coders, designers and animators continues until the design fits the game.

All games go through late asset iterations, it may be because what we initially thought was something fitting of the fantasy has changed because other assets in the game brought this particular one into the wrong direction so now the concept has to change.

Since Helldivers is such a vast world we often find other uses for assets that maybe not made the cut so we try to salvage things at later stages or for different themes just so interesting ideas don’t get lost but since we built the workflow to use 3D early and iterate on blockouts early it rarely happens.

CF: Blender is my all-in-one package for modelling, animation, texturing,simulation and rendering, so I don't have to jump between programs, which is why I prefer it to other 3D packages which are more specific in their use cases. Blender is also the most user friendly, working with other packages was always way too daunting as a concept

artist, but there was something in the way Blender did everything I wanted in the same package that made it a go to choice.

CF: Arrowhead gives us creative freedom to choose our own tools and workflows but we have some specific ones everyone uses to bridge the game engine and Blender. A lot of the 3D artists at the studio have very different setups based on how they like to work, which I think is really important. Pushing everyone to use the same exact

setup can have some advantages, but giving team members the tools to customise Blender how they like to is what keeps that individuality.

The studio-specific tools are there to get finished work from Blender into the engine, not to dictate how that work is made. Everyone has their own setup when it comes to the tools they like to work with, be it specific add-ons if you are an environment artist or if you are a hard surface artist or character artist. All these use vastly different workflows, so empowering them to use what they think is best is super important, and it also helps create an environment where different disciplines can empower each other.

CF: Honestly, it's being able to push early concept blockouts straight from Blender into the engine and have it working almost immediately. I didn't expect that to become as central as it has. It's changed how fast we can actually iterate, because I'm not waiting around to see if something works now we can test animations, scale and overall look within the engine in the blink of an eye.

CF: What transfers, I think, is the mindset more than any specific tool. We lean on Blender because it's open source and shows what you can do without breaking the bank, whether you're a studio or working completely solo, it gives you real, tangible results rather than something generated for you. Having modelling, texturing and animation all in one place matters most if you're working alone and don't want to juggle five different programs.

The other thing that transfers is freedom in your own process. Arrowhead gives artists a lot of freedom in which tools and workflows they use, and everyone on the team works a bit differently. On my end, that shows up in small ways. Procedural tools save a lot of time by generating things like backgrounds automatically instead of building them by hand, and I do colour and exposure work right inside the render with the Photographer add-on instead of switching to Photoshop.

CF: The industry is always changing, so it is very hard to be on top of what works and what doesn’t. But with the knowledge and connections I possess today, I could more easily create workflows that would be in line with how I can work more closely with the rest of the teams. How can we bridge the gap between artists, animators and designers? For example, it’s an everlasting process of building pipelines, so who knows what is on the horizon.

#8888. "Lady in Blue is as fitting a monument to our era as any I can imagine"

Tschabalala Self’s sculpture is far from being out of place in Trafalgar Square, writes Priya Khanchandani.

Who belongs in public space? How should public art represent who we are? And who deserves to be celebrated, cast in bronze and placed on a pedestal? These are some of the questions that Tschabalala Self’s commission for the Fourth Plinth, Lady in Blue, has raised in recent months, since it was unveiled in September.

I was there that cloudy morning in Trafalgar Square – a space I’d always crossed, probably like most Londoners, without thinking much about what it symbolises. When the black cloth was pulled away, we saw the figure of a Black woman caught mid-stride, one leg pushing through the fabric of her bright blue dress.

Like most of the admirals and generals monumentalised around her, she is cast in bronze. But unlike them she isn’t posed in command, she’s on her way somewhere. Her head, hair piled high, looks straight out into the city towards Whitehall, her left arm and fingers outstretched, moving with intention.

My Instagram post about the unveiling alarmingly attracted more than 6,000 comments, many of them either subtly or openly racist

I couldn’t help but feel satisfaction that a sculpture of a Black woman was there, taking up space in the city, on what is probably the most visible public plinth in Britain, and assumed this sentiment would be widely shared. It turns out I was wrong; my Instagram post about the unveiling alarmingly attracted more than 6,000 comments, many of them either subtly or openly racist and often suggesting the sculpture doesn’t fit its context.

I feel the need, therefore, to address the notion of what and who belongs in public space, and particularly in a space like Trafalgar Square.

Before Trafalgar Square existed, the site was used for the royal stables that served Whitehall Palace. Designed in 1840 by Charles Barry, the square was conceived as a stage for Britain’s image of itself, articulated through the grandeur of neoclassicism, and statues were central to its story. If you linger, you’ll spot George IV in Roman robes, sitting valiantly astride his horse. The generals Henry Havelock and Charles James Napier, whose reputations were made in the violent consolidation of British rule in India (the latter for the conquest of Sindh, where all four of my grandparents happen to be from) stand on two further plinths.

Admiral Horatio Nelson himself, the Royal Navy officer whose victory at the Battle of Trafalgar gave the square its name, overlooks them from 50 metres high atop a granite Corinthian column, guarded by four bronze lions. This composition represents a particular vision of 19th-century imperial power, reflected in the monuments and civic spaces rolled out across the Empire.

The square might be beautiful, and a fitting monument to its time, but it is also a living, breathing entity formed not only through its monuments and buildings, but also through the way it has been used.

Its function and meaning as a civic space keep being shaped by the people who have held festivals, memorials, gatherings here – or even simply walked through it on their daily commute. After it was built, Trafalgar Square quickly became a place for public assembly. From Bloody Sunday to the suffragettes to Black Lives Matter and the Palestine Coalition, it has a long tradition as a space of protest.

The square has been redesigned over and over, most significantly by Foster + Partners and Atkins in a 2003 scheme that closed the road along its northern edge, adding a terrace and turning what was essentially a traffic island into a pedestrianised space.

For some, in recent years the commission has merely settled into a pleasant biennial ritual

Lady in Blue is in dialogue with this context. She echoes the other figures here through her medium, bronze. And yet while the other figures are rooted to their respective plinths, she looks frozen in motion, echoing the movement of the people in the square below rather than the stillness of statues. The vivid blue of the figure’s dress – evoking lapis lazuli, the stone that has been ground into pigment since antiquity – is far from an attack on the Western canon, but rather in conscious conversation with it.

Once intended for an equestrian statue of William IV, the Fourth Plinth stood empty for more than 150 years before it became a space for contemporary sculpture in 1998. Unoccupied, it was always suggestive of a history waiting to be told or – given that the sculptures around it were all commemorating a contemporary moment – a future moment waiting to be solidified in bronze.

The absence of a statue suggested the question of who belongs on a pedestal was always open. Its dedication to contemporary art has allowed for redefinition and offered a chance to bring a quite spectacular historic space, a space of democracy, protest and celebration, into sync with the present.

The Fourth Plinth has become a space where identities are made visible and histories challenged, from Marc Quinn’s powerful Alison Lapper Pregnant, to Yinka Shonibare’s sculpture of Nelson’s own ship in a bottle. Works like these have also, at times, provoked arguments about how the square should be used, and yet each of them has become a part of its changing meaning.

For some, in recent years the commission has merely settled into a pleasant biennial ritual – and yet, this year’s sculpture underscores why it exists and why it’s so necessary right now.

In 2026, when a Black woman crossing this space is one of the most ordinary sights imaginable, Self’s statue validates her as worthy of belonging, not just in the city but here, in a culturally and politically charged public space dominated by white men sculpted by other white men.

Any notion that she doesn’t belong isn’t an aesthetic judgement, so much as a claim about who the city is for

That elevating such a woman into the visual language of the monument should provoke rage is telling, especially when all the figure has done is walk. Any notion that she doesn’t belong isn’t an aesthetic judgement, so much as a claim about who the city is for.

Self has said her work is meant to speak to human experience beyond racial identity. She has described the sculpture as depicting “everywoman”, implying that an ordinary person merits acknowledgement.

In other words, she hasn’t put it into the world simply as a statement about race – though its reception shows how readily the presence of a Black woman in this setting becomes about who is allowed to stand for the universal.

It’s as fitting a monument to our era as any I can imagine. At such a fractured time, I can’t help but feel relieved she is there, elbowing her way through the noise, making room for all of us.

Priya Khanchandani is a writer and curator specialising in contemporary design and visual culture. She was formerly head of curatorial at the Design Museum, where she curated the exhibition The Offbeat Sari and an accompanying book. She was also previously editor-in-chief of Icon, while her writing has appeared in the Financial Times, Frieze, The Guardian and The World of Interiors, as well as numerous books.

#8887. Olaver unveils multi-purpose Laneway Studio with "lantern-like" glass-block facade

Photography by Brook James

In the garden of a Melbourne family home, a facade of glass blocks set within recycled white brick and a concrete band beam tops this two-storey studio by Australian architecture practice Olaver.

Olaver designed Laneway Studio to appear as a “beautiful object” reflecting light into the garden in the day and glowing like a lantern at night. The multi-purpose building was designed in response to the growing needs of the family of five, offering a practical alternative to renovating the existing home.

It houses a study-cum-guest-room with an en-suite and terrace on the first floor and an open-plan living area below, fitted with concealed laundry facilities and a bar.

The new studio block was constructed behind the main house and its newly configured garden, designed by landscape architect Penny Starr to include a pool and areas of planted foliage.

Large glass-panelled sliding doors leading into the garden from both the house and studio create a seamless flow between the interior and exterior living spaces.

Another sliding door on the opposing wall of the studio, made from oak with a steel-clad exterior, connects the studio’s living space with the titular laneway behind the property.

“With large sliding doors on opposing walls, the ground floor can open right through, so it works as an extension of the garden and pool terrace to the laneway rather than a closed room”, Olaver director Emlyn Olaver told Dezeen.

“Open, the space feels far bigger than its footprint, and the family can spread across the house, the pool and the studio as one connected space when entertaining”, she continued.

Inside, the ground floor was designed to be minimal and open-plan to ensure its multi-functionality. It features neutral terrazzo flooring throughout. Oak cabinetry conceals storage, laundry facilities and a TV nook and frames a central bar area with a stainless-steel sink and surround.

“We wanted the studio to be calm, with joinery doing the heavy lifting so each space can change roles without feeling cluttered”, Olaver explained.

“Every space had to do more than one job; a laundry, a living room or a bar depending on the day. That flexibility also gives the building a longer life, because the family’s needs will keep changing as the kids grow up, move out and come back.”

On the first floor’s east-facing wall, overlooking the garden, a facade of glass blocks was installed above a concrete band beam to bypass planning restrictions on the use of conventional windows.

The first-floor interiors were also designed to be multi-functional, comprising a combined study and guest bedroom with an en-suite and small roof terrace. Red wraparound tiling in the bathroom is echoed by red panelling in the nook of the foldable bed, itself concealed behind more oak joinery when not in use.

“The new studio’s interiors echo the existing home’s rich but calm textures,” Olaver said. “Natural materials and tactile elements exist in both spaces, but the studio is slightly more playful in its approach.”

The project tasked Olaver with extending the home of a family rapidly outgrowing their existing space.

“In Melbourne, the usual answer is yet another extension that eats into the backyard,” she said. “Laneway Studio goes the other way, keeping the garden at the centre of the site and showing how a well-designed studio can add flexibility and density to an existing lot.”

More studio developments recently featured on Dezeen include a Camber Sands studio made using waste materials and a green-tiled studio in a London garden.

Photography by Brook James

#8886. chromatic pavilions and modular play structures activate historic istanbul rami library

milimetrik architects transforms the courtyard and interiors of istanbul's historic rami library into a 91,000 sqm environment for play and shared family experiences, welcoming approximately 825,000 visitors in eleven days.

Murat Özgön edited by christina vergopoulou October 31, 2026 2 min

Staged across the historic Rami Library in Istanbul, AileFest 2026 is a temporary spatial intervention designed by Turkish practice Milimetrik Architects. Held from September 26th to October 6th, 2026, the 91,000-sqm installation adapted the site’s historic courtyard and interior halls into an interconnected landscape for family-oriented recreation, education, and cultural programming, hosting approximately 825,000 visitors over an eleven-day period.

The project employs a child-centric, semi-structured spatial syntax designed around ergonomic scales for varying age demographics. Rather than defining rigid play equipment, the studio populated the expansive outdoor courtyard with modular geometric volumes, abstract shelters, and chromatic gathering nodes that allow for open-ended circulation and spontaneous use. Inside the library, the Book Fair departs from standard orthogonal booth layouts, organizing the space with pitched house-shaped pavilions, primary-toned modular display stands, and graphic floor patterns. The intervention establishes continuous circulation between the open-air courtyards and the historic interior galleries, utilizing temporary timber-and-steel fabrications to activate the civic site without altering its heritage fabric.

name: AileFest 2026 | @aile.festivali architect: Milimetrik Architects | @milimetrikarchitects

location: Rami Library, Istanbul, Türkiye

dates: September 26th – October 6th, 2026

#8885. Everyone Wants This Unapproved Weight Loss Drug—And Some Have Found a Way to Get It

For all the hype surrounding GLP-1 weight loss medications like Wegovy and Zepbound, these drugs don’t work for everyone. Nearly 17% of people on these medications are considered “non-responders,” leaving them looking for a different solution. But there’s a buzzy new medication waiting in the wings. While it’s not yet approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), people are already seeking it out.

It’s called retatrutide, and it’s a triple-agonist medication, which means it acts on three different receptors in the body. By comparison, Wegovy (semaglutide) acts on one receptor, while Zepbound (tirzepatide) works on two.

Retatrutide is already being hailed as a game changer in an area of health that’s already welcomed plenty of impressive medications in the past few years. In fact, clinical trial results show that it’s so effective for weight loss that some people have dropped out of the trials because they felt that they lost too much weight.

But retatrutide is still being tested in clinical trials. Eli Lilly, which makes reatrutide and Zepbound, hasn’t even submitted the trial results yet to the FDA for approval. So this is still an experimental medication—and versions of it are being sold online for cheap.

Mir Ali, MD, medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, California, tells SELF that retatrutide is “not really available” for use just yet, short of signing up for a clinical trial. There is no set timeline for when it will hit the market, given that clinical trial results have not yet been submitted to the FDA.

If you’ve struggled with losing weight on a GLP-1 medication or just want to pay significantly less for what appears to be the next big thing in weight loss drugs, it’s understandable to be tempted to add this to your cart. Here’s why doctors recommend resisting the urge.

Retatrutide is similar to GLP-1 medications in a few ways. Namely, it’s used for weight loss and is given once a week through an injection. Like Wegovy, Ozempic, and Zepbound, retatrutide works by reducing appetite and slowing digestion.

But retatrutide has more going on than that. This medication acts on three hormone receptors in the body—glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), gastric inhibitory polypeptide (GIP), and glucagon (GCG). “This is the first one in the pipeline to work on three different receptors,” says Dr. Ali. “The theory is that the more receptors it affects, the more effective the drug will be.”

The medication is currently in phase-three clinical trials, and it’s had some impressive results that suggest it could be the most effective drug for weight loss yet. The latest clinical trial results show that participants lost an average of 28.7% of their body weight on the highest dose of retatrutide over 68 weeks. By comparison, tirzepatide users lost an average of 15% to 22.5% over 72 weeks during clinical trials, and semaglutide users lost 10% to 15% of their body weight over 68 weeks during clinical trials.

It takes a little detective work, but there are some pharmacies that are selling the drug online.

In fact, this has become such an issue that the FDA issued a press release in early February, stressing that it’s illegal to sell retatrutide (and fellow experimental weight loss medication cagrilintide) right now. That includes picking up the medication from a compounding pharmacy.

“Retatrutide and cagrilintide cannot be used in compounding under federal law,” the release states. “Additionally, these are not components of FDA-approved drugs and have not been found safe and effective for any condition.”

The FDA also noted that its officials have issued warning letters to companies that are distributing these medications.

This is hardly shocking, but doctors really want you to take a pass on using retatrutide before it’s FDA-approved.

“People should wait to take medications until they are approved by the FDA to maximize safety,” Richard Siegel, MD, codirector of the Diabetes and Lipid Center at Tufts Medical Center and endocrinologist at Tufts Medicine Weight & Wellness Center–Stoneham, tells SELF. “All scientific data in animals initially and then humans are carefully reviewed by the FDA for any signals that a medication may be harmful.”

That includes side effects you might experience now or in the future, Dr. Ali points out. Compounding pharmacies have become a gray area. They’re able to legally produce and sell their own versions of popular medications when the FDA-approved versions are in shortage. But technically this is no longer legal once the medications are out of shortage.

But compounded drugs aren’t carefully regulated and may not even have the same ingredients or concentration as the medication they’re designed to mimic, Dr. Siegel says. “While these medications may be safe, there is less oversight in their production,” he says.

Dr. Ali warns against going directly through a compounding pharmacy, noting that it’s safer to work with your health care provider if you plan to go this route. “The worst-case scenario is that you’re getting something unsafe or ineffective,” he says.

But, with all medications, Dr. Ali says it’s best to use the FDA-approved version whenever possible. “It’s going to work in a predictable way, and the side effect profile will be well-studied,” he says.

Dr. Siegel points out that there are a lot of options to lose weight right now. And, if you haven’t had success on one, he recommends talking to your healthcare provider about trying a different medication or strategy. If you haven’t had luck while working with a primary care physician, Dr. Ali suggests seeing an obesity medicine specialist who will be more knowledgeable about treatment options.

“Medications for weight management are a powerful tool that should be used together with a comprehensive lifestyle plan focusing on self-monitoring, optimal nutrition, and an exercise prescription, including both aerobic and resistance components,” Dr. Siegel says. Meaning, people who have the best results do more than take medication—they also focus on nutrition and exercise.

If you’re interested in taking a weight loss medication or your existing treatment isn’t working, talk to a healthcare provider who specializes in this area. “These medications are designed for people with significant weight to lose,” Dr. Ali says. “Most likely, they will need to be taken long-term.” That makes getting a well-vetted medication from a reputable source even more important, he points out.

#8884. Meet the WNBA's Next Class of Rookies

The newest class of the WNBA is already stepping into the spotlight. Monday’s draft night delivered all the energy you’d expect from a league entering a pivotal chapter. With a new collective bargaining agreement reshaping conversations around players’ salaries, benefits, and long-term investment, the future of the WNBA is looking bigger, better, and brighter.

This year’s top picks come in with stacked resumes, impressive tournament runs, championship wins, and star power already on the rise. Draft night may be over, but the real story is just getting started. SELF had the chance to get to know some of the league’s newest members before their rookie seasons tip off.

Game day mantra: “Keep going and trust in your work.”

Go-to hype music: Too Much Sauce by DJ Esco

“I’m overjoyed and overwhelmed with emotion and gratitude at this moment. Finally this moment is here, and it happened in the right way. I’m excited for the winning culture in Minnesota. There are MVP-caliber players with a winning coach and program, so I’m excited to get to know a new team and play at such a high level.”

College: University of California, Los Angeles

Go-to hype music: Anything house music, “I like to feel like I’m in a club.”

“People don’t understand the sacrifice we made this year to win the national championship. Sometimes it can feel like you’re not giving enough, or not being noticed to get to where you want to be even though you’re giving up so much of yourself to a team. This makes everything worth it. We won a national championship and now we’re getting drafted. I can’t ask for anything more.”

Game day mantra: “You are what you tell yourself”.

Go-to hype music: Woah by Flau'jae Johnson

Favorite post-game meal: Stuffed salmon with alfredo

“I’m excited for the new community and new people—I’m a people person. Anywhere I’m planted, I bloom. This means so much to me. I come from Savannah, Georgia, and I wasn’t even ranked. Nobody was looking at me, and look at me now. I’m just thankful to be here.”

Game day mantra: “I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me", Philippians 4:13

Favorite post-game meal: Sour straw candy, airheads, and spaghetti

“I’m excited about winning. The Fever have a chance at winning the championship this year and I’m very excited about it. I’m ready to go in there, be a sponge and learn, and I’m ready to learn from vets like Caitlin Clark. I’m going to bring a winning mentality and whatever it takes to win, I’m going to do that.”

Game day mantra: “I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me", Philippians 4:13

Favorite post-game meal: Pasta alfredo or ugali

“I’m so excited about being around some of the greatest players. I’ll be playing with Angel Reese, and it will be great to meet her and learn from her. It means so much to represent my country, to represent Africa and all the young girls back in Africa trying to be like me one day. I’m grateful to everyone who helped me get here today.”

College: University of California, Los Angeles

“Any opportunity to grow and challenge myself is exciting. I’ve been leaning on the people around me to support me, and luckily I have five other teammates going through this exact same process, so it’s been special. Coming off winning the national championship, I’m feeling confident in myself. But it’s important to have a balance of being super humble and trusting the work you put in, while also learning and growing as a rookie.”

Favorite post-game meal: Salmon, sweet potato mash, and veggies

“It’s an honor to be a part of this class that’s coming into such a special time for women’s basketball. I understand the responsibility, and more than anything I’m just grateful. I was in California for a couple years, so I have a lot of people there that I’m excited to see, and my favorite Chinese food spot ever is in San Francisco so I’m very excited about that.”

#8883. Having ‘Boring’ Conversations Is Really Good for You, Psychologists Say

It’s tempting to try to bypass coworkers in the break room or limit small talk with the person waiting next to you in an effort to avoid what you suspect will be a dull conversation. But new research makes a solid argument for leaning into these “boring” chats.

The study, which was published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, found that people who actually engage in these conversations thought that they were much more interesting and enjoyable than they expected. But beyond that, there is data to suggest that having these “boring” conversations could do your mental and physical health a solid.

“These moments are small, but they are not trivial,” Nicholas Allan, PhD, psychologist and assistant professor in the department of psychiatry and behavioral health at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center, tells SELF. Here’s why.

The research focused on nine experiments featuring 1,800 participants. During the experiments, participants were asked to predict how much they would enjoy talking about a range of topics they identified as boring. These included World Wars I and II, nonfiction books, math, onions, the stock market, cats, and vegan diets. These chats happened with either strangers or friends, and were in person or online.

The researchers discovered that while participants said they expected the conversations to be pretty lame, they reported afterward that they enjoyed them much more than they thought they would. This even happened when both people in the conversation thought a topic was boring.

“We decided to conduct this research because so many people avoid conversations they think will be boring. We cancel small talk, dread networking events, and assume that certain topics, like the weather, commuting, or daily routines, just won’t be interesting,” Elizabeth Trinh, lead study author and a doctoral student at the University of Michigan, tells SELF. “If conversations are generally good for us, why do we so often expect them to be dull or draining?”

Ultimately, the researchers found that being engaged in the conversation was what really mattered. “Engagement drives enjoyment more than topic does,” Trinh says. “People assume that interest comes from having a fascinating subject. But in reality, what makes conversations enjoyable is the sense of connection like feeling heard, responding to each other, and discovering unexpected details about someone’s life. Even a mundane topic can become meaningful when two people are actively engaging with each other.”

People are social creatures by nature and connecting over a topic that feels boring, like onions, is still a social connection, Aaron P. Brinen, PsyD, assistant professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Vanderbilt University Medical Center, tells SELF. Thea Gallagher, PsyD, clinical associate professor of psychology at NYU Langone Health, agrees. “Sometimes people will predict that a conversation will be awkward or uncomfortable. But if you try to connect and listen in a conversation, there can be great benefits,” she tells SELF.

As a result, Dr. Gallagher says she encourages her patients to have conversations everywhere they go. “Being a lifelong learner can be very powerful,” she says. “At the end of the day, connecting with humans can make us feel good.”

These chats can seem pointless, but experts stress that they’re actually not. Not only will you likely find that you enjoy “boring” conversations more than you expected, it could keep you from feeling lonely.

“Loneliness is not just about how many people someone sees. It is about whether interactions feel connecting and meaningful,” explains Dr. Allan. Side-stepping a “boring” chat is likely to increase your sense of loneliness, Dr. Brinen says. “Even if you didn’t want to be a part of that conversation, you’re still lonely,” he points out.

Loneliness on its own is a horrible feeling, but it can also have a big impact on your health. Feeling lonely or socially isolated raises the risk of a slew of serious health conditions, including heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes, depression, anxiety, dementia, and early death, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). “When we find a way to be engaged with other people, it meets that need to connect with others,” Dr. Brinen says.

Over time, those small “boring” moments can build on each other, Dr. Allan says. With that, your feelings of loneliness—and health risks that can come with them—decrease.

Of course, some interactions with others aren’t great. “Not all social contact is beneficial,” Dr. Allan says. “More contact is not automatically better. What seems to matter most is whether the interaction feels respectful, reciprocal, and emotionally safe. Positive connection helps. Depleting or hostile interactions do not.”

Ultimately, Trinh recommends keeping an open mind when it comes to future conversations. “We may be missing out on connection because we misjudge how conversations will feel,” she says. “If we avoid talking to someone because we assume it will be boring—like a coworker at the coffee machine, a stranger at an event, or a neighbor in the elevator—we may be unnecessarily depriving ourselves of small moments of connection that could improve our mood and sense of belonging.”

#8882. designboom radar: exhibitions to see around the world this november

explore our monthly round up of must-see art, design, and architecture exhibitions to check out around the world.

November’s designboom exhibition radar begins with an unlikely reunion in Paris, where two Alexander Calder mobiles return to public view after decades. In Zurich, 125 familiar lamps become a walk-through tunnel, while a new gallery in Hong Kong transfers the grain of wood into cast aluminum. Elsewhere, a house lost to Mexico City’s architectural history returns through an imagined botanical setting, and a new museum in Western Sydney opens with exhibitions on flight and water.

Some of the exhibitions highlighted in earlier radars and listings on our dedicated events guide remain on view, giving designboom readers more time to encounter them around the globe.

Visitors can enter Mariko Mori‘s Wave UFO, an interactive work that incorporates brainwave feedback, as part of All That Shines at Tokyo’s Mori Art Museum. Developed between 1999 and 2002, the large, futuristic installation connects neurological activity with visual experience. It appears in a retrospective of approximately 40 works spanning more than three decades of the Japanese artist’s practice.

The exhibition begins with Mori’s early performance-based photography and science-fiction-inspired imagery, including her experiments with cyborg identities in the 1990s. Later works turn toward Buddhist concepts of consciousness and questions about the cosmos, using sculpture and technology to approach subjects that resist direct representation. Together, the installations and moving-image works trace Mori’s changing ideas about the relationship between human perception and technological experience.

name: Mariko Mori: All That Shines artist: Mariko Mori museum: Mori Art Museum location: Tokyo, Japan dates: October 31st, 2026 — March 28th, 2027

More than 400 objects trace the experimental practice of Dutch designer Hella Jongerius at the Museum für Kunst und Gewerbe Hamburg. Whispering Things, organized by the Vitra Design Museum, brings together furniture, textiles, ceramics, and early prototypes to examine how she has approached the making of objects over three decades.

The exhibition moves from commercially produced designs for companies such as Vitra and IKEA to more sculptural investigations of material and color. Sketches, collages, and films reveal the processes behind the finished work, including experiments that resist the predictability of industrial production. Throughout her career, Jongerius has returned to the relationship between craftsmanship and manufacturing, considering how objects can retain the irregularities and physical traces of their making.

name: Hella Jongerius: Whispering Things designer: Hella Jongerius museum: Museum für Kunst und Gewerbe Hamburg location: Hamburg, Germany dates: October 23rd, 2026 — June 13th, 2027

A reconstruction of Charlotte Perriand‘s 1929 domestic prototype, Équipement intérieur d’une habitation, appears at Barcelona’s Fundació Joan Miró in Free to Rethink the World. Produced by Cassina in collaboration with Perriand’s daughter, architect Pernette Perriand-Barsac, the installation revisits a project developed with Le Corbusier and Pierre Jeanneret during Perriand’s early career.

The exhibition follows four decades of work through ten sections, extending from her Parisian interiors to her encounters with Japanese craftsmanship. Photographs and archival documents reveal her interest in creating spaces around the changing needs of their occupants. The presentation also revisits her friendship with architect Josep Lluís Sert, whose building for the Fundació Joan Miró opened in 1975, with Perriand attending its inauguration the following year.

name: Charlotte Perriand: Free to Rethink the World designer, architect: Charlotte Perriand museum: Fundació Joan Miró location: Barcelona, Spain dates: October 9th, 2026 — February 28th, 2027

A monumental paper lantern measuring roughly two meters across takes its place at the Noguchi Museum in New York for No Ordinary Light: Akari at 75. The exhibition traces the development of Isamu Noguchi‘s Akari light sculptures, first conceived in Gifu, Japan, in 1951. Over the following decades, Noguchi developed more than 200 variations of the familiar illuminated forms.

Among the works identified for the presentation is the large-scale 200D, created around 1985, alongside archival sketchbooks and examples of Noguchi’s sculpture in other materials. The exhibition revisits Akari’s appearance at the home of Charles and Ray Eames in 1951 and its later presentation at the 1986 Venice Biennale, following the movement of these paper forms between sculpture and the domestic interior.

name: No Ordinary Light: Akari at 75 artist, designer: Isamu Noguchi museum: The Noguchi Museum location: New York, USA dates: November 4th, 2026 — September 5th, 2027

At the Museum für Gestaltung Zürich, 125 circular IKEA lamps form an eleven-meter-long tunnel in Sabine Marcelis: Light and Color. A mirrored wall with a color gradient extends the installation visually, turning a familiar household object into an illuminated passage. The Dutch designer’s first museum exhibition brings together recent projects and new works conceived for the museum’s Toni-Areal location.

Another room contains eight Mathmos lava lamps, each nearly three meters tall, multiplied through surrounding mirrors. In Sunbeam Captured, developed with Boris Acket, mechanical waves move across a thin layer of water as a shifting light source follows the path of the sun. Material studies accompany the installations, revealing how Sabine Marcelis works with transparency and reflection.

name: Sabine Marcelis—Light and Color designer: Sabine Marcelis museum: Museum für Gestaltung Zürich location: Zurich, Switzerland dates: October 30th, 2026 — April 4th, 2027

A sprawling cast-metal dining table, complete with a sculpted torn napkin and scraps of food, appears among the new works in Misha Kahn‘s All Intensive Purposes at Friedman Benda in New York. Its glass-and-stone surface introduces a surprising degree of order to an object assembled from seemingly accidental gestures. Elsewhere, an onyx table adopts the appearance of a far more roughly constructed piece.

The exhibition marks ten years of collaboration between Kahn and the gallery, following his interest in the unpredictable paths of making. New upholstered furniture incorporates exaggerated forms and graphic surfaces, while multilayered plywood becomes the basis for sculptural objects. The title deliberately alters the familiar phrase ‘all intents and purposes,’ placing the emphasis on experimentation itself.

name: Misha Kahn: All Intensive Purposes designer: Misha Kahn gallery: Friedman Benda location: New York, USA dates: October 29th, 2026 — December 12th, 2026

Two major Alexander Calder mobiles return to public view at Hauser & Wirth Paris in Calder: François Premier, an exhibition devoted to the artist’s years in France during the early 1950s. The presentation brings together Les Granettes (1953), a large standing mobile exhibited for the first time in 72 years, and The Putney Mobile (1954), making its public European debut.

The show takes its name from a seventeenth-century stone house in Saché, where Calder lived and worked after returning to France in 1953. Ink and gouache paintings from this period accompany the sculptures, tracing a particularly productive chapter in his career. There is a geographical coincidence, too: the Paris gallery occupies a historic building on rue François Premier.

name: Calder: François Premier artist: Alexander Calder gallery: Hauser & Wirth location: Paris, France

dates: October 19th, 2026 — December 19th, 2026

Green fluorescent tubes stretch across several meters in Dan Flavin‘s greens crossing greens (to Piet Mondrian who lacked green), one of the works presented in Some Light at the Guggenheim Museum Bilbao. Made in 1966, the installation arranges ordinary industrial fixtures into two illuminated sections, bringing color directly into the surrounding architecture.

The exhibition draws on the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum‘s holdings, with works dating from the 1960s through the 1980s and particular attention to Flavin’s early experiments. Beginning in 1963, the American artist used commercially available fluorescent lights to construct corners, barriers, and corridors. Their arrangement changes the appearance of the gallery itself, allowing visitors to experience color through the spaces the light occupies.

name: Dan Flavin: Some Light artist: Dan Flavin museum: Guggenheim Museum Bilbao location: Bilbao, Spain dates: November 11th, 2026 — April 4th, 2027

With architecture by Moreau Kusunoki, Powerhouse Parramatta opens in Western Sydney on November 7th with five inaugural exhibitions devoted to art, design, science, and technology. Among them is Task Eternal, an ambitious exploration of aviation and space designed by OPEN Architecture. Its more than 850 objects include drawings of flying machines by Leonardo da Vinci and a NASA Moon rock, alongside a new light installation by James Turrell.

Elsewhere, Overflow brings together seven Aboriginal organizations to examine the living systems of Water Country. The Mall, developed with OMA/AMO, investigates the shopping mall as an architectural and cultural form, while Es Devlin presents five immersive installations in The Turning. A fifth exhibition, The Dark, creates an imaginative environment for children. Together, they introduce the museum’s extensive new program.

participants: multiple artists, designers, architects, and First Nations organizations location: Parramatta, Australia dates: from November 7th, 2026

British artist Tai Shani brings M.I.A.S.M.A. to Jupiter Artland outside Edinburgh, transforming the gallery through sculpture and sound. The exhibition revisits the ancient Greek tragedy Antigone, asking how mourning becomes a form of resistance and whose lives are allowed to be remembered. Its expanded title, Moral Injury in the Apocalyptic Sunsets of Modernity disAssociation, gives some indication of the political and emotional territory Shani is exploring.

Developed as an international co-commission, the project was first presented at Kunsthalle Bern earlier this year. Jupiter Artland’s presentation combines imagery with architectural elements to construct an environment shaped by feminist mythology. Visitors can also encounter Shani’s separate installation The Spell or The Dream in the sculpture park’s orchard, where its setting changes with the approaching winter.

name: Tai Shani: M.I.A.S.M.A. artist: Tai Shani gallery: Jupiter Artland location: Edinburgh, UK dates: October 30th, 2026 — April 11th, 2027

Previously unexhibited drawings and photographs offer a closer look at the career of Paul R. Williams in Architect for Living at LACMA in Los Angeles. Working from the 1920s through the early 1970s, Williams designed buildings across Southern California during a period of extraordinary urban expansion. His commissions ranged from private residences to major civic projects.

The exhibition explores this breadth through archival material, tracing a practice that moved between different architectural languages and types of clients. Williams became particularly well known for his houses for Hollywood figures, while his larger body of work included public housing and hotels. Presented alongside related exhibitions at the Getty Research Institute and USC Fisher Museum of Art, the LACMA survey places his architecture within the wider development of Los Angeles.

name: Paul R. Williams: Architect for Living architect: Paul R. Williams museum: Los Angeles County Museum of Art location: Los Angeles, USA dates: November 15th, 2026 — May 31st, 2027

An attempt to capture her mother’s final breath is among the personal investigations revisited in Sophie Calle’s Matrimoni, Rotture e Funerali inclusi at MAXXI in Rome. Bringing together eight projects made between 1978 and 2026, the exhibition follows the French artist’s longstanding interest in the rituals people invent around intimacy and loss.

Photographs and written accounts guide visitors through experiences shaped by separation, absence, and the passage of time. Calle’s projects often begin with a self-imposed rule, whether documenting the end of a relationship or recording encounters with people seeing the sea for the first time. The presentation extends beyond the museum with a new permanent installation at Rome’s Non-Catholic Cemetery for Foreigners, adding another setting to her exploration of how personal histories are remembered.

name: Sophie Calle: Matrimoni, Rotture e Funerali inclusi artist: Sophie Calle museum: MAXXI location: Rome, Italy dates: October 16th, 2026 — February 7th, 2027

A vanished house in Mexico City becomes the starting point for Álvaro Urbano’s Helen at Museo Jumex. The exhibition revisits Casa Cueva, the home and garden created by architect Juan O’Gorman and inhabited with his wife, artist and botanically minded writer Helen Fowler O’Gorman. Built in the rocky landscape of Pedregal de San Ángel, the house brought architecture into close contact with its surroundings.

Urbano draws on Fowler O’Gorman’s 1961 book Mexican Flowering Trees and Plants, imagining the botanical world that once occupied the property. References to Juan O’Gorman’s stone murals and later interventions by artist Helen Escobedo add further layers to the presentation. Through an atmospheric architectural reconstruction, Urbano considers how a building’s history can survive through fragments, images, and the people who lived there.

name: Álvaro Urbano: Helen artist: Álvaro Urbano museum: Museo Jumex location: Mexico City, Mexico dates: October 16th, 2026 — February 7th, 2027

Wood grain appears on the surface of cast aluminum in Precise Play, an exhibition by South Korean designer Jeonghwa Seo at Carwan Gallery‘s new Hong Kong space. Seo uses sand casting to transfer the texture of wood into metal, producing objects that retain traces of the organic material used in their making. The exhibition inaugurates the gallery’s new location.

Bringing together established pieces and newly commissioned works, the presentation moves between sculptural furniture and lighting. Seo also works with resin and natural rush, combining materials with different physical qualities in precisely constructed forms. His objects invite a second look at the relationship between surface and structure, particularly when a metallic piece appears to preserve the grain of timber or a functional object adopts an unexpected sculptural form.

name: Jeonghwa Seo: Precise Play designer: Jeonghwa Seo gallery: Carwan Gallery location: Hong Kong, China dates: November 20th, 2026 – February 20th, 2027

A sea glimpsed through a train window or partially hidden behind trees runs through Yu Nishimura’s Towards a Sea at Lafayette Anticipations in Paris. The Japanese painter’s first institutional solo exhibition in France brings together approximately 50 works from the past decade, including new pieces made for the presentation.

Working in oil and tempera, Nishimura moves between landscape and portraiture, allowing familiar subjects to become blurred or partially obscured. A bicycle wheel might appear alongside a human face, while the boundary between water and sky remains difficult to locate. The exhibition follows the artist’s interest in how places are recalled through imperfect images. His compositions borrow from the language of photography and cinema, and give ordinary scenes the elusive quality of something remembered.

name: Yu Nishimura: Towards a Sea artist: Yu Nishimura museum: Lafayette Anticipations location: Paris, France dates: October 21st, 2026 — January 3rd, 2027

Trees and other natural forms enter the architecture of the National Museum of Qatar in Giuseppe Penone: The Inner Flow of Life. Installed across the museum’s Baraha and Old Palace, the exhibition brings together sculptures and architectural interventions by the Italian artist, whose practice has explored the physical relationship between human bodies and the natural world for more than five decades.

The presentation moves between early works and recent pieces, including Rovesciare i propri occhi from 1970 and Vene di bronzo from 2026. Penone uses materials such as wood and bronze to investigate the forces that shape living matter, often bringing the traces of touch or growth into sculpture. A newly installed public artwork, Idee di Pietra, extends the project to Doha Old Port.

name: Giuseppe Penone: The Inner Flow of Life artist: Giuseppe Penone museum: National Museum of Qatar location: Doha, Qatar dates: October 26th, 2026 — February 13th, 2027

More than 70 works spanning nearly three decades of Rashid Johnson’s practice come together at the Museum of Contemporary Art Chicago in A Poem for Deep Thinkers. The survey brings together photographs, large-scale installations, and films, including his black-soap Cosmic Slops paintings and the expressive faces of the Anxious Men and Broken Men series.

Throughout his career, Johnson has drawn on Black intellectual culture and art history to explore questions of identity, anxiety, and freedom. His 2024 film Sanguine turns toward his own family, examining relationships with his father, brother, and son, and incorporating a poem by writer and activist Amiri Baraka.

name: Rashid Johnson: A Poem for Deep Thinkers artist: Rashid Johnson museum: Museum of Contemporary Art Chicago location: Chicago, USA dates: November 7th, 2026 — April 25th, 2027

An ancient Indian ivory statuette discovered in Pompeii offers a glimpse into the far-reaching connections explored in Global Antiquity at Fondazione Prada in Milan. Bringing together more than 150 artworks and artifacts, the exhibition examines cultural exchange across Afro-Eurasia between approximately 600 BCE and 1000 CE. The presentation occupies the foundation’s Podium building, with exhibition design by Rem Koolhaas and AMO/OMA.

Curated by Salvatore Settis, Anna Anguissola, and Chiara Ballestrazzi, the exhibition considers how objects traveled through systems of trade and political contact long before the modern idea of globalization. Their places of discovery become as revealing as their origins. Together, the artifacts trace connections between distant societies across 1,700 years.

#8881. Atelier Zébulon Perron draws on metabolist influence for Montreal bistro

Photography by Alex Lesage

A monochrome palette and influences from Japanese metabolism characterise Bistrot à Franky in Montreal, Canada designed by local outfit Atelier Zébulon Perron.

The restaurant is a home base for local chef Francis Blais in the city’s hip Mile End neighbourhood.

Atelier Zébulon Perron took what it views as the standard design language of a Montreal bistro – bright lighting and lots of activity – and translated it into a more contemporary design.

For studio founder Zebulon Perron, the monochrome whites and beiges, interspersed with milled aluminium accents and a large zinc bar top, allowed the studio to experiment with textures and lighting to create visual interest and contrast in the dining space.

“With the monochromy of the restaurant, we experimented with textures – shiny versus matte, tile nd and stucco – and how light reacts to those surfaces in different ways,” Perron told Dezeen.

The studio emphasised the postmodern and “retrofuturist” elements of the design, pointing to the custom chandeliers with their illuminated Pyrex tubes and exposed wiring, fabricated by Perron’s long-time collaborators, local lighting design studio Lambert & Fils.

Perron highlighted the milled aluminium wine cellar that sits above the bar face, interspersed with portholes that are a direct reference to Japanese metabolist architecture.

“There’s a postmodern, 1980s aesthetic that naturally rose from everything we were doing,” said Perron.

Visitors enter the restaurant through a red-painted hallway and a metal door and handle carved from butcher block by local cabinetmaker Olivier Doray.

Inside, only the terrazzo floor was a holdover from the building’s former use. Granite tabletops cover some of the larger tables, while the classic bistrot white tablecloths are draped over the smaller tables.

Blond leather banquettes were placed below large mirrors on the wall opposite the bar, and these larger seating arrangements are centred by large butcher block tables, also fabricated by Doray.

Custom walnut chairs were designed by local industrial designer Guillaume Sasseville.

On the walls, white tile is interspersed with stucco and works of art, curated by local filmmaker Xavier Dolan. These artworks give pops of colour and Perron said that the monochromatic design elements allow both the food and the artworks to stand out in the space.

“Since the canvas is pretty neutral, the food and the artwork take centre stage,” he said.

A set of windows opens up the kitchen space to the dining room.

Custom bar seating features white columns with seats informed by transportation design, and Perron noted that the metal details and clean lines of the bar space, as well as the metal fans, also give the interior a streamlined look.

Atelier Zébulon Perron has designed some of the most interesting interior spaces in the city, including Café Constance and the dining areas for the city’s Four Seasons hotel.

It also helped create the pop-up bar staged during the city’s inaugural design week earlier this year.

Photography by Alex Lesage

#8880. Anxiety Tattoos: How Ink Therapy Can Help Ease Mental Health Struggles

Tattoos have long been a flex in personal expression and artistry. For some peeps, they’re the go-to for commemorating life wins or solidifying deep-seated beliefs — from quotes that got you through dark times or portraits of your fave pets.

The act of getting inked can also be a profoundly therapeutic experience. The machine’s buzz and the needle’s sharp sting are part of a ritual that may help bring internal battles to the surface. But is there a link between anxiety and the decision to get tatted? Could framing your fears and anxieties in gorgeous designs help you cope? Continue reading to find out.

For many, tattoos are much more than art. Peeps who have anxiety may get tattoos as a way of taking control over their narrative, including their mental health struggles.

Anxiety disorder makes life challenging, and you may feel you’re stuck in a rip tide of continual worry, fear, and dread. Even if you know it’s the anxiety talking, you can still struggle to contain these overwhelming feelings, and it’s exhausting. Anxiety can trick your mind, tell you you’re unworthy, and there’s no way out.

But here’s where tattoos come into play — they create a visual shoutout to your strength and resilience. Imagine marking your skin with reminders of the battles you’ve won and what you’ve overcome.

Getting inked can feel like grabbing the reins back from anxiety and stress. A tattoo is an affirmation. It can turn your invisible battle scars into something tangible and beautiful, giving a sense of ownership over your body and experiences. This is huge when anxiety tries to convince you that you don’t have a say in your own story.

Whether it’s a poignant quote, a symbolic image, or just a badass design, a tattoo packs a punch of personal significance and your enduring strength. You’ve taken a deliberate, proactive step to help you take greater control over your life, and that should be celebrated.

Psychologically, tattoos are visual high-fives to yourself. For the anxious folks, tats are a way to take those messy, abstract feelings and pin them down in something real and tangible.

There’s also some evidence to suggest that the pain involved in tattooing can be cathartic, offering a physical release for emotional pain. This could explain why people who self-harm or live with substance misuse or eating disorders might be drawn to the tattoo chair — it’s a place where psychological pain is acknowledged and artistically transformed.

Research suggests there may be correlations between tattoos and mental health.

One 2013 study involving 65 female participants living with anorexia, bulimia, and binge eating disorder explored the relationship between eating disorders, self-injury, and tattoos. Around 51% of the participants reported a history of self-injury, and 27% had at least one tattoo. Those with tattoos were more likely to have a history of self-harm, so the authors suggested that tats could be a form of self-punishment.

However, in an interesting twist, 27% of those with tattoos showed no history of self-injury. These peeps reported more positive body image, higher self-esteem, and fewer mental health struggles.

The relationship between tats and mental health is complex and still being decoded. Further research would help confirm the link between the two.

Tattoos can swing either way on the mental health seesaw. For some folks, getting tattooed is symbolic of their healing process. It says, “Hey, I’ve been through some stuff, but look how I’ve grown!” These tattoos often become symbols of a deeply personal journey, spotlighting moments of triumph over anxiety and depression.

But here’s the flip side: if someone gets inked on a whim or during a rough patch without much thought, that tattoo could be a permanent reminder of a not-so-great time.

In a 2011 study of 82 peeps getting their first tattoo, researchers measured their feelings about their appearance and body both before they got the tattoo and then again immediately and three weeks after the tattooing. The findings showed that right after getting their tattoos, folks of all genders experienced a decrease in appearance anxiety and dissatisfaction. Three weeks later, they reported increased body appreciation, a stronger sense of having a distinctive appearance, heightened feelings of uniqueness, and improved self-esteem. However, female folks experienced increased anxiety related to how others viewed their physique 3 weeks post-tattoo, while males reported a decrease in this type of anxiety.

These results suggest that getting a tattoo can positively affect mental health, but of course, the impact varies among individuals.

Tattoos can be an artistic strategy to enhance your mental health game, but it’s crucial to take a beat and really think it through before you get inked.

Whether you’re looking to mark a milestone, manage the mayhem of anxiety, or remind yourself that everything will be okay, a carefully considered tattoo can be a meaningful addition to your narrative, helping you manage anxiety and positively shaping your story.

The number one reason side businesses fail is not lack of funding, bad timing, or tough competition — it is building something nobody wants to buy. Before you spend a dollar on a website, business cards, or inventory, you need to validate that real people will pay real money for what you are offering.

Validation does not require a perfect product. It requires proof of demand. Talk to 10 people who match your target customer. Describe what you plan to offer. Ask two questions: "Would you pay for this?" and "How much would you pay?" If 3 or more say yes with a specific dollar amount, you have a viable idea. If most say "that sounds cool" but hesitate on paying, you have a hobby.

The FI community has a particular advantage here. Many FI seekers have already cut their expenses to the point where a side business does not need to generate massive revenue to make a meaningful impact. Even $500 to $1,000 per month in side business income — invested consistently — can shave years off your FI timeline.

Forget building a $1 million business. Your only goal is reaching $1,000 in total revenue as quickly as possible. That first $1,000 proves three things: people will pay you, you can deliver, and the business model works. Everything after $1,000 is optimization. The FI community calls this the "ramen profitable" stage — your business covers its own costs and generates even a small surplus. From there, you compound both your skills and your revenue.

Side business income is the ultimate FI accelerator because it attacks both sides of the equation. Your day job covers expenses while 100% of your side income goes directly to investments. If your side business generates $1,500 per month and you invest all of it at 7% annual returns, you will have over $450,000 in 15 years. That is not a theoretical number — that is the real math of why thousands of FI seekers build side businesses.

One of the first decisions you face is how to structure your business legally. For most side businesses, the choice is between operating as a sole proprietorship (the default — no paperwork needed) or forming an LLC (Limited Liability Company). Here is the honest comparison.

A sole proprietorship is what you are by default when you start earning money on the side. There is no registration required at the federal level (though you may need a local business license). The income flows directly to your personal tax return on Schedule C. The downside: your personal assets — savings, home equity, investments — are not separated from business liabilities.

An LLC creates a legal separation between you and your business. If someone sues your business, your personal assets are generally protected. Formation costs range from $50 (states like Kentucky and Colorado) to $500 (California charges $800 per year just for the privilege of having an LLC). For most side businesses, an LLC is worth forming once you have paying customers.

Side business income is taxed differently than your W-2 paycheck, and the surprises can be painful if you are not prepared.

Self-employment tax: You pay both the employee AND employer portions of Social Security and Medicare — a combined 15.3% on top of your income tax. On W-2 income, your employer covers half. On side business income, you cover it all.

Quarterly estimated taxes: The IRS expects you to pay taxes as you earn, not once a year in April. If you owe more than $1,000 in taxes from side business income, you need to file quarterly estimated payments (Form 1040-ES) by April 15, June 15, September 15, and January 15.

Deductions that reduce your tax bill: Home office (simplified method: $5/sq ft up to 300 sq ft = $1,500 deduction), internet (business percentage), equipment, software subscriptions, mileage (67 cents per mile), health insurance premiums (if self-employed), and retirement contributions (Solo 401k allows up to $72,000/year). These deductions are a significant FI advantage because they reduce both income tax AND self-employment tax.

The biggest constraint for side business owners is not money — it is time. You have 168 hours per week. Your day job takes 40-50. Sleep takes 49-56. That leaves 62-79 hours for everything else: family, health, friends, and your business. The key is not finding more time. It is being ruthlessly strategic about the time you have.

The 5-5-2 Framework: Dedicate 5 hours per weeknight (after work), 5 hours on Saturday, and 2 hours on Sunday to your business during the launch phase. That is 12 hours per week — enough to build meaningful momentum without destroying your health or relationships. After launch, you can often reduce to 5-8 hours per week for maintenance.

Batch your work. Do not context-switch between your day job and side business throughout the day. Dedicate specific blocks of time to specific tasks: Monday and Wednesday evenings for content creation, Tuesday and Thursday for customer communication, Saturday morning for strategic work.

The FI community offers a unique perspective on this question. Traditional business advice says to go full-time when your side income replaces your salary. The FI approach is more nuanced: your side business does not need to replace your income if your investments are covering the gap.

Consider going full-time when your side business income covers at least 75% of your essential expenses for 6 consecutive months, you have 12 months of expenses in cash reserves, your business is growing (not plateauing), and you have health insurance figured out independently of your employer.

But here is the FI twist: many people in the community deliberately keep their side business as a side business forever. A day job provides steady income, benefits, and 401(k) matching, while the side business provides additional investment capital. This "two-income engine" approach can cut your FI timeline dramatically. If your day job covers all expenses and your side business generates $2,000 per month in investable income, you add over $700,000 to your portfolio in 15 years at 7% returns.

The decision depends on your personal FI strategy. Some people want to build a business that replaces their job and provides fulfillment in early retirement. Others want to maximize total income during their accumulation phase and retire from everything. Both are valid paths — the important thing is making the choice intentionally with the math in front of you.

From idea to first dollar with minimal risk.

Talk to 10 people who match your target customer profile. Describe your offer and ask if they would pay, and how much. Get at least 3 verbal commitments before building anything. If you cannot find 3 out of 10, pivot your idea.

Pro tip: Pre-sell before you build. Create a simple landing page describing your product or service and see if people will put down a deposit or join a waitlist.

Open a separate business bank account (free at most banks). File for an LLC in your state if you are ready for revenue. Get an EIN from the IRS (free, takes 5 minutes online). Set aside 30% of every dollar earned for taxes.

Pro tip: Do not commingle business and personal finances. A separate bank account makes tax time dramatically easier and protects your LLC liability shield.

Create the simplest version of your product or service that delivers value. A consultant needs a one-page website and a Calendly link. A product business needs one SKU, not twenty. A freelancer needs a portfolio with three examples. Launch ugly and improve based on real customer feedback.

Pro tip: Spend less than $200 on your MVP. If you need to spend more, you are overbuilding before you have proven demand.

Your first customers will come from your personal network, not from marketing. Tell everyone you know what you are building. Offer a founding-member discount in exchange for detailed feedback and a testimonial. The goal is revenue and learning, not profit.

Pro tip: Ask every customer two questions after delivery: "What was the best part?" and "What would you change?" These answers shape your product roadmap.

Once you have proven the model works, build systems so the business runs efficiently. Create templates, automate invoicing, document your processes. Find the acquisition channel that produces the best customers (referrals, content marketing, paid ads) and double down on it.

Pro tip: Track your effective hourly rate. If you earn $1,000 in a month and spend 20 hours, your rate is $50/hour. If you spend 80 hours, it is $12.50/hour — below minimum wage. Optimize for $/hour, not just total revenue.

The most powerful FI strategy is not choosing between your day job and a side business — it is running both simultaneously. Your day job covers all living expenses, employer benefits, and 401(k) matching. Your side business generates pure investment capital. If your side business produces $2,000 per month and you invest every dollar at 7% annual returns, you add over $700,000 to your portfolio in 15 years. That is the difference between retiring at 55 and retiring at 45.

Check your employment contract and company handbook for non-compete clauses, moonlighting policies, and intellectual property agreements. Many employers have no policy against side businesses as long as they do not compete, use company resources, or interfere with your job performance. If your contract has restrictions, consult an employment attorney before launching. Transparency is usually the safest approach if your side business is in a completely different industry.

Most service-based side businesses can launch for under $200: a domain name ($12/year), basic website hosting ($5-$15/month), and a business bank account (free). Product businesses may need $500-$2,000 for initial inventory. The FI approach is to minimize upfront investment and validate before spending. If your idea requires $10,000+ to test, consider whether there is a simpler version you can launch first.

Businesses with flexible hours and no geographic constraints work best: freelance writing, web development, consulting in your area of expertise, online tutoring, bookkeeping, virtual assistance, and digital product creation (courses, templates, ebooks). The key criteria are: work can be done on your schedule, no physical storefront needed, and revenue can grow without proportional time investment.

Report all income on Schedule C of your personal tax return. Pay self-employment tax (15.3%) plus income tax on profits. File quarterly estimated taxes using Form 1040-ES if you expect to owe $1,000 or more. Deduct legitimate business expenses: home office, internet (business %), equipment, software, mileage, and health insurance premiums. Consider a Solo 401(k) to shelter up to $72,000/year from taxes — this is one of the most powerful FI tools available to self-employed individuals.

Start as a sole proprietor during the validation phase (no cost, no paperwork). Form an LLC once you have paying customers and revenue. An LLC protects your personal assets (home, savings, investments) from business lawsuits and debts. Formation costs range from $50-$500 depending on your state. California charges $800/year minimum, which may not be worth it until you are earning at least $10,000/year from the business.

Dramatically. If your day job covers all expenses at a 50% savings rate, you reach FI in about 17 years. Add $2,000/month in side business income invested entirely, and your effective savings rate jumps well above 60% — cutting your FI timeline to roughly 12-13 years. At $3,000/month side income, you could reach FI in under 10 years from starting. The key insight: side business income has nearly 100% savings rate because your day job already covers expenses.

Starting a side business while working full-time is one of the most powerful financial moves you can make on the path to FI. Validate your idea before spending money, set up basic legal and tax infrastructure, launch an MVP quickly, and focus relentlessly on reaching your first $1,000 in revenue. The beauty of the side business approach is that your day job covers all expenses while your business income goes directly toward building wealth. Even modest side income of $1,000 to $2,000 per month, invested consistently over 10-15 years, can add hundreds of thousands of dollars to your portfolio and cut years off your timeline to financial independence.
